authors: Zahra Hirji, Ari Natter, Jennifer A Dlouhy
description:
The US Environmental Protection Agency is expected to formally rescind carbon pollution standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants as soon as Monday, according to people familiar with the matter.
The Trump administration’s latest major climate rollback is expected to come on the sidelines of a Group of 20 energy ministers’ meeting in Houston, said the people, who asked not to be named because the details aren’t yet public.

description:

text:
An unglamorous but important side of the electric vehicle boom is taking off.

Used EV batteries in Yancheng, Jiangsu, are being dismantled and processed so valuable metals can be recovered and reused after reaching the end of their first lives.

Here's what to know

Shanghai Eye (@ShanghaiEyeMagic) detailed the booming industry in a report on its YouTube page .

According to the outlet, the process unfolds in stages.

"Copper and aluminum are first separated, and then the battery powder, rich in lithium, nickel, and cobalt, is fed into a hydrometallurgical production line for deep purification," the narrator noted.

Shi Liyong told Shanghai Eye that the process is rapidly gaining in efficiency.

"The capacity utilization increased by 20% compared to the start of this year," Liyong said. "Recoveries of nickel and cobalt are up to over 99%."

Commenters interpreted the improvements as hugely positive.

"Recycling is valuable for planet earth and even a profitable industry," one wrote.

More background

Battery recycling is drawing attention as EV adoption rises worldwide, meaning more battery packs will need to be replaced, repaired, or retired.

If those materials can be recovered efficiently, manufacturers can return copper, aluminum, lithium, nickel, and cobalt to the supply chain rather than relying on newly mined resources.

Recovering metals from used batteries can reduce pollution tied to mining and lower the risks associated with improper disposal. It can also create more stable battery supply chains, which could support lower costs for EVs, grid storage, and other technologies that depend on those materials.

What's being done?

Another sign of momentum is growing capacity. ShanghaiEye said in the video that recycling companies in China are expanding, with production lines being added to meet demand.

The hydrometallurgical company expects to continue to build capacity, reaching triple its annual capacity in the coming years. That development is important.

"Experts predict there will be 655,000 tons of used electric vehicle batteries globally this year and expect there to be over 2 million tons in 2030," the video noted.

If recyclers can consistently recover large amounts of materials, the process is both a waste solution and supply solution. It can create jobs while reducing pressure on raw material markets.

"This is the answer for EV doubters," one commenter said.

Where can I learn more?

The work in Yancheng is part of a much bigger push in battery recycling. Companies, scientists, and manufacturers are trying to recover more materials, cut costs, and ease pressure on mining as more EV batteries reach the end of their first lives.

• In China, CATL is looking to expand EV battery recycling beyond its home market.

• Scientists are testing cheaper ways to recover lithium-ion battery materials from scrap.

• Across the industry, battery reuse and recycling are becoming essential to sustainable growth.

• Elemental Recycling has turned waste plastic into graphite that can feed battery manufacturing.

• Despite mining concerns, EVs remain better than gas cars as supply chains improve.

text:
The UK and US are set to sign two new agreements at the Global Fusion Summit in London on Monday 14 September, helping to bring fusion power closer to reality and deliver over 10,000 UK jobs in the sector by 2030.

The first agreement will launch a new supercomputing partnership between the UK Atomic Energy Authority and Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, combining world-leading expertise in AI, computing and fusion to accelerate the development of commercial fusion.

The summit will also see the UK and US sign a Joint Statement committing to closer cooperation on regulating fusion energy, helping to attract investment and support growth of the sector.

Fusion replicates the process that powers the sun, combining hydrogen atoms to release vast amounts of energy. It has the potential to provide a secure source of clean energy for generations to come, without producing carbon emissions during operation, while creating thousands of skilled jobs, backing British businesses and unlocking significant economic opportunities for the UK.

Minister for Energy, Michael Shanks, said:

Fusion has the potential to provide virtually limitless clean energy while supporting more than 10,000 jobs across the UK by 2030, attracting investment and creating major opportunities for British businesses.

By strengthening our partnership with the US we’re accelerating the race to commercial fusion, turning cutting-edge research into economic growth and cementing Britain’s position as a world leader in fusion energy.

FCDO Minister for the Americas, Chris Elmore said:

The UK’s relationship with the United States supports growth and thousands of jobs at home.

By bringing together world-leading expertise in fusion, artificial intelligence and advanced computing, we’re helping British businesses and researchers access the investment, knowledge and international partnerships needed to succeed in the industries of the future.

On top of the UK-US agreements, The University of Birmingham, Electric Power Research Institute and industry partners have secured a £2.63 million collaboration on fusion materials, strengthening UK industrial capability and supporting international collaboration in one of the world’s most promising emerging technologies.

Japan’s largest fusion company, Kyoto Fusioneering, will also invest up to £3 million in the UK through Project ALBION, supporting the development and testing of materials for the UK government-backed STEP programme, which is designing a prototype fusion power plant.

The announcements come as the UK publishes its UK Fusion Investment Prospectus, setting out the UK’s offer for companies and investors today and preparing to capture the opportunities in a future global fusion market estimated to be worth between £3 trillion and £12 trillion, establishing the UK as a leading destination for fusion. The prospectus will help turn Britain’s world-leading fusion research into a new clean energy industry, attracting companies to invest, build and create skilled jobs in the UK.

Notes to Editors

In June 2025, the government announced a record investment in fusion energy of over £2.5 billion over 5 years, as part of its SR allocation: Funding breakdown for fusion energy - GOV.UK.

The University of Birmingham, EPRI and industry partners have secured a £2.63 million collaboration on fusion materials, through the FURESHMA (Fusion Reactor Shielding Materials) programme.

The UK is enabling industry growth by publishing its Regulation Landscape, clarifying the regulations and processes needed to deploy a fusion power plant. Alongside this the Environment Agency and Health & Safety Executive have published an Early Engagement Process to formalise engagement with industry and provide confidence to developers and investors.

The UK has signed a Letter of Intent with the State of Tennessee agreeing potential areas of collaboration including R&D, skills and workforce development, regulation, and access to supply chains.

The UK published A New Energy Revolution: The UK’s Plan for Delivering Fusion Energy in March 2026, setting out its ambition to accelerate the growth of the UK fusion industry and maintain Britain’s leading position in the global race for fusion energy.

The UK is investing £180 million in the Lithium Breeding Tritium Innovation (LIBRTI) programme, a globally unique facility that will help address one of the key technical challenges facing future fusion power plants.

The government is investing £125 million in the AI Growth Zone at Culham, including £45 million for the SUNRISE supercomputer, helping place the UK at the forefront of using AI and advanced computing for fusion research.

The UK was the first country to establish a dedicated regulatory framework for fusion energy and has since published a draft Fusion National Policy Statement to support the future deployment of fusion power plants.

In March 2026, the UK became the first country to commit to developing a dedicated market framework for fusion energy, aimed at providing certainty for investors and supporting future commercial deployment.

text:
Britain and the United States are preparing to enter into two formal agreements designed to deepen bilateral co-operation on artificial intelligence and fusion power, in an effort to accelerate a breakthrough in clean energy generation.

Representatives from both nations will officially seal the arrangements during the Global Fusion Summit taking place in London on Monday.

Replicating the natural atomic process that powers the sun, fusion combines two hydrogen isotopes under extreme temperatures to release massive quantities of energy without generating planet-warming carbon emissions.

Researchers worldwide have dedicated decades to mastering this technology as an unlimited source of zero-carbon power, although no experimental reactor has yet achieved net energy output.

Under one of the new accords, a supercomputing partnership will be established between the UK Atomic Energy Authority and the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory.

The joint venture seeks to integrate capabilities in artificial intelligence, advanced computing, and fusion research to hasten the development of a commercially viable energy source.

In addition, the London summit will feature a joint statement committing both governments to closer regulatory alignment on fusion energy.

Officials noted that shared regulatory frameworks will assist in driving financial investment and encouraging broader growth across the sector.

In the UK, fusion technology is increasingly regarded as a key industry within the Oxford-Cambridge Growth Corridor—a Government strategy aimed at boosting innovation and economic performance across the region connecting the country’s leading academic institutions.

Energy minister Michael Shanks said: "Fusion has the potential to provide virtually limitless clean energy while supporting more than 10,000 jobs across the UK by 2030, attracting investment and creating major opportunities for British businesses.

"By strengthening our partnership with the US we’re accelerating the race to commercial fusion, turning cutting-edge research into economic growth and cementing Britain’s position as a world leader in fusion energy."

The new deals sit within a wider framework of nuclear co-operation between the two nations, occurring alongside noticeable differences in their overarching energy policies.

US President Donald Trump has publicly criticised the UK’s focus on accelerating the green energy transition as his administration supports fossil fuels, yet both sides have established common ground regarding their ambitions to advance nuclear fission and fusion.

Chris Elmore, foreign minister for the Americas, said: "The UK’s relationship with the United States supports growth and thousands of jobs at home.

"By bringing together world-leading expertise in fusion, artificial intelligence and advanced computing, we’re helping British businesses and researchers access the investment, knowledge and international partnerships needed to succeed in the industries of the future."

Prior to the summit, £2.63 million in funding was awarded to the University of Birmingham, the Electric Power Research Institute, and commercial partners to collaborate on developing fusion materials.

Meanwhile, Kyoto Fusioneering, Japan’s largest fusion firm, is set to direct up to £3 million into the UK through an initiative known as "Project Albion".

This scheme will assist in testing and developing specialised materials for the Government-backed "spherical tokamak for energy production" programme, which aims to design a prototype fusion power plant.

The UK is also publishing a dedicated fusion investment prospectus detailing current opportunities for commercial investors while outlining strategies to capture market share in a future global fusion sector estimated to be worth between £3 trillion and £12 trillion.

This follows a commitment announced by the Government last year to allocate £2.5 billion to fusion energy over a five-year timeframe.

text:
Global energy demand is outpacing supply highlighting the need for diversified, reliable energy sources and expanded generation and transmission infrastructure. Energy is a deeply interconnected system and steel is fundamental to every segment of its infrastructure.

Global energy demand is outpacing supply highlighting the need for diversified, reliable energy sources and expanded generation and transmission infrastructure.

Energy is a deeply interconnected system and steel is fundamental to every segment of its infrastructure. As demand for energy continues to grow, supply chain reliability for constructing energy infrastructure will be essential. Nucor is supporting that expansion with a robust, reliable, domestic steel supply chain, providing the materials and expertise to build the future of energy infrastructure.

Constructing oil and gas pipelines. At every stage of the oil and gas value chain, the industry relies on high-strength carbon and alloy steels used in oil country tubular goods (OCTG) and cross-country line pipe, designed to withstand extreme pressures, high temperatures and corrosive environments.

Beginning with the extraction stage, plate, sheet and bar steel products are used for drilling rigs, tools and well casings designed to endure deep-well pressure and mechanical stress. During transport and storage, welded or seamless pipeline-grade steel offers exceptional toughness and corrosion resistance for the safe movement of crude oil and natural gas. For the refining and processing stage, facilities depend on corrosion-resistant plate, pressure vessel quality (PVQ) steel and heat-treated alloys that maintain performance under sustained high-temperature operation.

What steel products are essential for the growth of natural gas energy generation?

·Natural gas (NG): A critical transition fuel, natural gas infrastructure relies heavily on corrosion-resistant welded and seamless steel pipe, plate and structural shapes for efficient and safe transport.

·Liquefied natural gas (LNG): LNG terminals and processing plants require steel that can withstand cryogenic temperatures and high pressure, often using durable plate, cryogenic rebar and specialized alloy steel products for storage tanks, containment systems and piping networks.

·Combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT) power plants: A highly efficient system that uses gas and steam turbines to boost electricity output more efficiently. Starting with a gas turbine that generates electricity, the resulting exhaust gases are used in a heat recovery steam generator (HRSG) to produce steam, which drives a second turbine to generate more power. CCGT plants rely on a range of specialized steels to withstand high temperatures, pressure cycles, thermal fatigue and corrosive environments, including high-strength steels for structural components and specialty alloys within the turbines.

American-made steel can deliver the consistent quality, material traceability and safety assurance that critical infrastructure demands, while meeting project timelines and strict requirements.

Steel is infinitely recyclable, so end-of-life products can be transformed into new construction projects using the electric arc furnace (EAF). Discover how steel scrap from decommissioned oil rigs can enable the future of data centers here.

Building nuclear energy. Nuclear energy relies on materials that can withstand the most demanding environments on the planet. Every component, from containment structures to pressure vessels and reactor support systems, must meet exacting standards for strength, heat resistance and long-term performance.

Domestic steel manufacturing provides a decisive advantage for this sector. Producing safety-critical materials within the United States ensures full material traceability, regulatory compliance and alignment with nuclear-grade quality certifications. A domestic steel supply chain also reduces logistical risk through shorter project timelines and strengthens national energy security.

Emerging technologies like small modular reactors (SMRs) and fusion energy are redefining how nuclear power is built and deployed. These intricate systems rely on high-performance steels, including plate, rebar and structural steel products that can be precisely fabricated, transported and assembled while maintaining exceptional integrity under high temperature and pressure.

Developing clean energy. Clean energy systems rely on steel to operate at scale with the goal to reduce carbon emissions. Steel enables that progress, providing the strength and durability needed to support large-scale generation in demanding environments.

In solar energy, galvanized and other coated steels provide corrosion resistance for racking, framing and mounting systems across both utility-scale and distributed installations. Similarly, hydroelectric facilities depend on high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steels to withstand the immense pressures of flowing water used in dams, gates and turbines that convert natural force into consistent power. Emerging carbon capture projects also depend on advanced domestic steel products, from storage tanks and pressure vessels to specialized pipeline systems capable of managing high pressure while resisting corrosion.

Domestic steel mills play a pivotal role in ensuring these clean energy structures are built with reliable, high-quality materials that meet all OSHA and EPA regulations and support local job creation nationwide.

Connecting America’s energy grid. Modernizing the U.S. energy grid ensures that we can meet growing demand by supporting new energy generation sources and improving energy infrastructure.

According to the American Iron and Steel Institute (AISI), the average high-voltage transmission structure contains about 40,000-60,000 pounds of steel (“New and Expanding Demand for Steel in Energy,” 2025). Transmission and distribution networks depend on steel for the utility poles and the steel within the wires that carry electricity across vast distances. American-made steel offers consistent quality and predictable performance, which are key factors for long-term durability in demanding outdoor environments.

As utilities upgrade or replace aging infrastructure, domestic supply helps ensure the timely completion of projects and adherence to national standards. From transmission and distribution poles to transformers and storage facilities, domestic steel provides the foundation for a stronger, more resilient power system that connects energy generation to the communities and industries that rely on it.

Nucor’s Towers & Structures business plans to add 130,000 tons of finished steel transmission pole capacity by 2030. Steel poles help build new lines and modernize existing ones to deliver additional power — all manufactured and fabricated using American-made steel.

American steel is the backbone of modern energy infrastructure. Steel provides the strength, durability and adaptability required to construct the infrastructure needed to expand generation, store energy and deliver power.

While steel is produced globally, American-made steel offers many advantages:

·Supply chain assurance: proximity to domestic steel mills improves overall project delivery timelines and mitigates geopolitical and logistics risks.

·Project agility: U.S. producers provide responsive technical support and custom metallurgical solutions alongside production scheduling flexibility to align with complex construction demands.

·Product breadth and compliance: American steelmakers offer a broad spectrum of grades and products for energy applications, engineered to meet stringent mechanical, performance and regulatory standards.

·Economic and regulatory assurance: sourcing domestically eliminates potential tariffs while simplifying compliance with federal requirements and supporting American jobs and industry innovation.

·Reduced embodied carbon: About 70% of domestic steel manufacturers use electric arc furnaces (EAFs) to produce new steel and steel products. Nucor’s circular EAF process emits on average 0.77 tons of CO₂ per ton of steel produced, resulting in less than one-third of the greenhouse gas (GHG) intensity compared to the global average of blast furnace-basic oxygen furnace (BF-BOF) steelmaking (Worldsteel).

By integrating American-made steel early in the project lifecycle, developers can build energy infrastructure that is stronger and more strategically secure for the nation’s future energy needs.

DID YOU KNOW?

Through Nucor’s advanced material recovery methods, we recycle reclaimed steel and non-ferrous metals such as copper, aluminum and titanium to meet the growing demand for electricity without the need to source overseas.

Dependence on imported materials creates delays and supply uncertainty — challenges that slow the pace of grid modernization. With a reliable domestic supply chain and a breadth of sustainable steel products, Nucor can be a proactive partner for energy developers and utilities to help them build faster, expand smarter and prepare for the growing demand ahead.

title: Citizens 'have no seat at the table' on data centers, says organizer - Yahoo

"If a community wants a data center, then by all means, vote in the people who are going to approve, permit it, build your data center and there you go.

text:
BOYCE — Amy Kremer told a small crowd gathered on a parking lot that she isn't against artificial intelligence or technology, but it should be left to people to decide whether they want to welcome data centers into their communities.

"This technology is the most powerful technology in human history," she said. "It's been built on American data, American land, American resources, American energy, and many times with American taxpayer dollars. Yet the American people have no seat at the table, no voice in the fight on how the technology affects our lives now, how it will impact us in the future.

"And now they're coming into our communities and shoving their infrastructure down our throats, and it is wrong."

Kremer is the chair of Humans First, which bills itself as a grassroots conservative group "fighting for an America First AI policy," according to a news release.

Kremer and her AI Data Center Revolt tour arrived in Boyce on Saturday evening, the second stop on a national tour of cities that's set to end Sept. 16 in Washington, D.C. It started in Dallas at the mini Republican convention last week, then had its first stop in Austin before heading to Rapides Parish.

Applied Digital announcement: AI project coming to Central Louisiana to create high paying jobs

"Go home!" People express skepticism, opposition to Boyce AI factory data center

'Y'all should have asked us first': Save My Louisiana leads protest against Applied Digital data center

The reason it stopped in Boyce is because of the $3.6 billion AI factor data center, Data Forge 1, under construction not far outside of the town on former farmland. It is being built by Applied Digital, a Dallas-based company.

At a June public meeting in Boyce, representatives from Applied Digital, regional economic development organization Louisiana Central and Cleco, which is set to power the center, spoke with citizens about what the project is, how it would operate and what it might bring to the parish.

But the outreach mostly was met by skeptism by those in attendance, and that was mirrored Saturday in the words of those who spoke.

Kremer said her group doesn't support moratoriums on data centers, either on the federal or state level.

"What we believe is that the communities should decide what they want in their own community. We believe in local control," she said to applause. "If a community wants a data center, then by all means, vote in the people who are going to approve, permit it, build your data center and there you go. That's the American way."

For Gary Musgrove, president of grassroots group Save My Louisiana founded in 2025 to oppose carbon capture sequestration projects, it's questions about Cleco's ability to provide power to the center.

He said Cleco has been contracted to provide 430 megawatts of electricity, which he said translates to 250,000 homes or 25% of the company's output.

"Our question is, where is Cleco gonna come up with this power?" he asked.

Musgrove worries that surrounding land could be expropriated for the project. Eminent domain issues are why the group turned its attention to the data center, he said, even though it hasn't been an issue so far.

He cited President Donald Trump's comments about data centers, that communities fighting them are going to miss out on economic development and that the centers will be responsible for generating their own electrical power.

"If that's the case, I'm very concerned with the fact that Cleco is gonna be short 430 megawatts of electrical generation power," Musgrove said. "Where are they gonna get that from? If they're going to use eminent domain and build out the infrastructure to get this power to them, or is this community gonna listen to 196 generators running to compensate for the 430 megawatts that is required?"

He said questions about that, asked at the June forum, weren't answered because the company said it was propriety information.

Dustin McAnn, a teacher and rancher who lives in LaSalle Parish but works in Rapides, saw a survey stake in a median near his barn. He discovered that power company Entergy is planning to install a transmission line that will feed Hyperion, the massive Meta data center being built about 30 miles east of Monroe.

That was news to him.

"How could this happen?" he asked. "I literally moved out here to get away from people, and here they all come to try to move transmission lines and everything else on top of me."

McAnn began reaching out to his state representatives and the Louisiana Public Service Commission. With his neighbors, they found other survey stakes and contacted the landowners.

From that, they formed the Louisiana Landowners Coalition, which opposes efforts by Entergy and Meta to expropriate property for the Richland Parish project.

"Private property should never be expropriated for private enterprise," he said. "I don't think it should be expropriated period, but certainly not for a billionaire and his corporation. If he wants it, he can get one less yacht, he can get with Entergy, spend the money it takes to build the power plants right there at Meta, and have a field day."

McAnn said he believes the landowners will be getting offer letters soon from Entergy for their land.

"We've told our membership to say no, to stand together, locked shoulder to shoulder, and let's make this as difficult on Entergy as we possibly can," he said.

name: EPA
title: Beneath an invisible umbrella: Protecting what protects us | KPMG Perspectives
authors: KPMG Perspectives, Siegfred Bueno Mison, Lito U. Gagni, Rick Olivares, Octavio Peralta, Ricky Gallardo, Ma. Stella F. Arnaldo, Bruce C, Al S. Mendoza, Justine Xyrah Garcia
description:
While these innovations delivered significant social and economic benefits, their long-term environmental consequences were not fully understood at the time.
Even the systems that sustain life can be pushed toward a breaking point when long-term consequences are overlooked.
From the food we consume to the ecosystems that regulate our climate, the ozone layer quietly supports functions that are often taken for granted.
As we observe World Ozone Day, let us remember that the shield above us has never asked for recognition.
It simply performs its role day after day, quietly protecting life beneath it.
text:
CONSIDER an umbrella that has been used for years through heavy rains and intense heat. Its fabric is torn and worn, but it still offers some protection from the sun.

Now imagine that the umbrella protecting the entire planet was beginning to wear out.

Unlike an umbrella we can see and hold, Earth’s most important shield is largely invisible. Suspended high above the atmosphere is the ozone layer, a thin blanket of gas that quietly absorbs most of the sun’s harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation before it reaches the surface. Day after day, year after year, it performs this function, creating conditions that allow people, wildlife, and ecosystems to thrive.

Ironically, its importance became most apparent only when it came under threat.

For much of modern history, humanity viewed the sky as limitless, believing that the atmosphere could absorb the effects of industrialization without consequence. Refrigerators preserved food, air conditioners cooled homes and workplaces, aerosol products became commonplace, and industries rapidly expanded to meet growing consumer demands. While these innovations delivered significant social and economic benefits, their long-term environmental consequences were not fully understood at the time. In many ways, the ozone layer serves as a reminder that decisions made to address immediate needs can create risks that only become apparent years or even decades later. What few realized was that many of the chemicals powering these conveniences were making their way into the atmosphere, where they would gradually weaken one of the planet’s most vital natural defenses.

Unlike environmental disasters that arrive suddenly and dramatically, ozone depletion unfolded quietly. The damage accumulated over decades, hidden high above the clouds. By the time scientists discovered the alarming thinning of the ozone layer and the formation of the Antarctic ozone hole, the world had already learned a sobering lesson: the true impact of today’s decisions is not always immediately visible. Even the systems that sustain life can be pushed toward a breaking point when long-term consequences are overlooked.

The implications extended far beyond the atmosphere itself. According to the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), increased exposure to UV-B radiation is associated with heightened risks of skin cancer, cataracts, and suppression of the human immune system. The same radiation can also affect crops, terrestrial plant life, and aquatic ecosystems.

Research has likewise shown that elevated UV radiation can impair phytoplankton productivity, disrupt marine food chains, reduce agricultural yields, and weaken ecosystem resilience. From the food we consume to the ecosystems that regulate our climate, the ozone layer quietly supports functions that are often taken for granted. What appears to be a thin layer of gas above the Earth is, in reality, one of the planet’s most important life-support systems.

Fortunately, the story did not end there.

What could have become one of humanity’s greatest environmental failures instead became one of its most remarkable success stories. Through the Montreal Protocol and its Kigali Amendment, governments, industries, and researchers united to phase out ozone-depleting substances (ODS) and reduce the use of climate-warming refrigerants. These efforts demonstrate the power of collective action in addressing global environmental challenges, as well as the importance of grounding decisions in science, foresight, and long-term thinking. Commemorated each year on 16 September, World Ozone Day embodies this spirit of cooperation. Guided by the 2026 theme, “Global Action for a Cooler Planet: Celebrating 10 Years of Sustainable Cooling under the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol,” the observance highlights the enduring link between ozone protection and climate action.

The Philippines has likewise advanced ozone protection efforts through the Philippine Ozone Desk (POD) under the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), which oversees the country’s implementation of the Montreal Protocol and related regulations on ODS and hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs). These efforts are aligned with the country’s goal of achieving the total phase-out of ozone-depleting cooling chemicals by 2030 while accelerating the adoption of climate-friendly and energy-efficient alternatives. Through strengthened policy implementation measures, the Philippines continues to contribute to global ozone recovery while advancing national priorities on climate resilience, energy efficiency, and sustainable development, recognizing that environmental considerations are increasingly linked to long-term economic and societal outcomes.

This is where the private sector becomes indispensable, as today’s business decisions will help shape environmental outcomes for years to come. The recovery of the ozone layer presents a meaningful lesson for businesses. Many of the substances known to contribute to ozone depletion were introduced to solve real challenges. Refrigerants, for example, transformed food preservation, cooling and industrial efficiency. Yet at the time, the long-term consequences of their widespread use remained largely unknown until scientists uncovered their role in ozone depletion decades later.

What this highlights is the importance of looking beyond immediate benefits when making decisions. As organizations navigate an increasingly complex operating environment, understanding the long-term impacts on a large scale has become an imperative of responsible decision-making.

Consequently, organizations are facing growing pressure to address environmental risks associated with greenhouse gas emissions, as such risks become increasingly embedded in governance and long-term business strategy. What was once viewed primarily as a compliance issue is rapidly becoming a strategic consideration. Much like the lessons learned from ozone depletion, organizations are increasingly expected to look beyond immediate benefits and evaluate the broader, long-term impacts of their decisions on the environment, society, and business resilience.

At R.G. Manabat & Co., we help clients navigate these evolving expectations by integrating environmental considerations into business decision-making, assessing emerging risks and opportunities, and identifying initiatives that enhance resilience and support long-term value creation. Beyond our client engagements, we continue to support and collaborate with organizations that champion environmental stewardship, recognizing that meaningful progress requires collective action across sectors.

This reminds us that some of humanity’s greatest achievements are not measured solely by what we build, but by our ability to anticipate and manage the consequences of our actions. What was once considered an invisible problem became proof that global cooperation can repair damage inflicted upon systems far beyond our immediate sight.

As we observe World Ozone Day, let us remember that the shield above us has never asked for recognition. It simply performs its role day after day, quietly protecting life beneath it.

Like the worn umbrella carried under a scorching summer sun, its value becomes most apparent when we consider the consequences of losing its protection altogether.

For the shield above our planet, we only have one chance to keep it intact.

But Johnson, R-La., said congressional approval is needed.

Majorities also disapprove of his handling of the economy and immigration, issues that were central to Trump’s election in 2024.
text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump’s proposal to send $5,000 to every American adult if his Republican Party maintains control of the House and Senate in the November election needs congressional approval, House Speaker Mike Johnson said Sunday, while pledging to try to make it happen.

Trump made the unusual pitch at the party’s midterm convention in Dallas last week, promising a “Trump Dividend” if voters keep the GOP in power on Capitol Hill. The president later told CBS News Texas that he did not think Congress would need to authorize the payments, though he did not specify how he could spend more than $1 trillion without lawmakers’ authorization.

But Johnson, R-La., said congressional approval is needed. “I would assume, yes, he’d need Congress to act, and that’s a creative idea,” he said.

A few hours later, Trump said he would deliver on his promise. “The 5,000’s going to happen, 100%,” he told reporters before boarding Air Force One in Ireland, where he attended a pro golf tournament at his resort.

Johnson, meanwhile, said he would work to get Trump’s proposal through Congress despite a small Republican margin.

“He’s the big idea’s president. We’re going to try to implement everything we can,” he said. “I commit that Congress will work through it and find consensus on that like they have to do everything else.”

The dubious election-year gambit could cost more than $1 trillion, putting further strains on the country’s nearly $1.8 trillion annual budget deficit and exacerbating concerns of inflation. The economy is confronted by persistent inflation and increasing interest rates, a tough combination for governing Republicans as they seek to hold on to control of Congress.

The president argues that payments would be possible because of the strong economy, but consumer sentiment is weak as gasoline prices rise because of the war with Iran and wages struggle to keep pace with inflation.

Trump told reporters earlier Sunday that the payments would be “easy enough” because the United States has a strong economy.

“We can easily handle that because we’re taking in so much money,” he said. “We’ve never done better.”

Just one-third of U.S. adults approve of how Trump is handling the presidency, according to a July poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. That compares with 37% in June and 42% who approved of his work when he took office. Majorities also disapprove of his handling of the economy and immigration, issues that were central to Trump’s election in 2024.

It dominates commercial sodium-ion cells and their precursors.
text:
General Motors is aiming for a domestic battery supply chain within two to three years, its battery chief said in an interview published on Saturday, four days after the Trump administration attacked Ford for licensing Chinese technology to make cells in Michigan.

GM imports finished battery packs for its cheapest electric car from China, and reports last year identified the supplier as the same company at the centre of the case against Ford: the world’s largest EV battery maker, CATL.

“We’re developing a supply chain such that, two years from now, three years from now, it will be domestic,” Kurt Kelty, GM’s VP of Battery and Sustainability, told CNBC. “That’s what we’re aiming for. When we get into market, we’ve got a domestic source for that.”

Kelty was speaking about a sodium-ion cell for stationary energy storage that GM is developing with the startup Peak Energy and does not expect in commercial production until around 2029.

A GM spokesperson told CNBC that the company would apply the same priority to cells for future electric vehicles, without giving a date.

Asked about Ford days before the Transportation Department’s letter, Kelty said: “They’re following a different path. We think it’s more valuable to develop this all domestically, take advantage of domestic supply chains, and develop a technology that’s actually better than the incumbent technology.”

The Bolt

GM said in August last year that it would import electric vehicle batteries from China to power the Chevrolet Bolt.

Reuters and other outlets identified the supplier as Contemporary Amperex Technology Co (CATL), citing people familiar with the arrangement.

“For several years, other US automakers have depended on foreign suppliers for LFP battery sourcing and licensing,” GM said at the time. “To stay competitive, GM will temporarily source these packs from similar suppliers to power our most affordable EV model.”

A person familiar with the arrangement told Reuters it was a stopgap until GM could make its own lithium iron phosphate cells, which the company said would begin in the United States in 2027.

Whether the packs still come from CATL has not been confirmed.

The distinction GM draws is between importing finished Chinese packs, which it does, and licensing Chinese process technology to make cells on American soil, which Ford does and which Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy attacked.

In his letter to Ford CEO Jim Farley, released on September 8, Duffy said the department remained “deeply alarmed by Ford’s continued reliance on licensed technology from Chinese battery manufacturer CATL” at Marshall, Michigan.

Ford called the letter “a wrongheaded attempt to capture headlines”, said the arrangement is “a limited technology-licensing and services agreement, not a joint venture or foreign-owned manufacturing operation”, and noted that it owns the plant and employs its 1,700 workers.

The White House then posted that Ford is “a GREAT American company”.

GM Looked at the Licence Too

GM explored CATL technology twice.

It considered a plant in Illinois under a licence structured like Ford’s, abandoning it in 2023 after the backlash against Marshall, according to two people involved in the talks who spoke to Crain’s Detroit Business in June 2025. GM declined to comment on the project.

Separately, Reuters reported in September 2024 that GM was in talks to buy cells based on CATL technology from a US plant that Japan’s TDK would fund and operate.

Bill Ford, Ford’s Executive Chairman, said in June 2025 that “others in our industry are trying to submarine” the Marshall plant, calling it “sour grapes”. He did not name GM.

Four people familiar with the matter told Crain’s that GM was behind lobbying for tighter foreign-entity rules and for budget language targeting licences of the Ford-CATL type.

GM spent about $8.2 million on lobbying in the first quarter of 2025, a record for the company.

“GM has been investing in a resilient critical minerals and battery supply chain to support American innovation, manufacturing and economic security,” GM spokeswoman Liz Winter said then.

China’s Sodium-ion

Sodium-ion replaces lithium and ferrous sulfate with sodium derived from soda ash, which the United States has in quantity.

Kelty said the chemistry tolerates a wider temperature range, letting cells run without active cooling and removing a major cost in stationary storage.

The trade-off is density. Sodium-ion cells are larger and heavier for the same energy, which is why the application is the grid rather than a car.

“The better thing to do is try to leapfrog, come up with a different technology that’s actually better that we can actually source here,” Kelty said.

China leads there too. It dominates commercial sodium-ion cells and their precursors. CATL said deliveries of its large-scale sodium-ion storage system begin in China this month, with a gigawatt-hour targeted by the end of the year.

LG Energy Solution, GM’s cell partner, was reported in January to be building a sodium-ion pilot line at its plant in Nanjing, chosen in part for Chinese cathode suppliers, though the company said its plans were not final.

Peak Energy has been buying commercial sodium-ion cells from Chinese suppliers while its own US factory is built, IEEE Spectrum reported in July.

The date has also moved. When the Peak partnership was announced on June 9, GM said it aimed to commercialise the cells by 2028.

CNBC now reports commercial production around 2029.

A Shrinking EV Business

GM sold 27,395 electric vehicles in the United States in the second quarter, down 40.7%, taking them to 3.8% of its deliveries from 6.2% a year earlier. First-half sales fell to 56,679 units, leaving GM second to Tesla.

The Chevrolet Equinox EV remains its best seller and fell 62% in the quarter. In January the company announced a $6 billion charge to cut electric vehicle capacity.

Its vehicle battery plans have shifted twice in two years. High-nickel cells run at Warren, Ohio. Lithium iron phosphate for vehicles is due at Spring Hill, Tennessee, in late 2027, on lines that began making storage cells this year after a $70 million retooling.

Lithium manganese-rich cells with LG, claimed at 33% more energy than the best LFP at comparable cost, are due in 2028 and are not yet made at automotive scale anywhere.

description:

But the Granville Harbour Wind Farm, with 30 turbines, is much smaller than what's proposed for Whaleback Ridge.
Questions over use of public land Bob Brown Foundation campaigner Scott Jordan said the project was "terrible", and he questioned why public land would be allowed to be used for a large-scale private development.

text:
On the numbers, the Whaleback Ridge wind farm proposal is enormous.

With a planned capital spend of almost $3.5 billion, Westcoast Renewable Energy (WRE) wants to build 280 wind turbines, each up to 250 metres tall at the blade tip, across a 40,000-hectare tract of public land to the north and west of Zeehan, on Tasmania's west coast.

WRE said once it was operational, after a decade-long construction timeline, the wind farm would be capable of generating 2.8 gigawatts of power, which is more than the state-owned electricity generator Hydro Tasmania's capacity.

The company claims the development would be an economic boom for Zeehan, with up to 350 jobs based in town during construction, and 90 ongoing positions.

In Zeehan, some residents are excited for that prospect, but a wildlife foundation is critical of the use of public land for a wind farm it believes will threaten native wildlife.

West coast wind a 'unique advantage'

The company has previous form in large-scale wind farm developments, having built and sold the Granville Harbour Wind Farm, which is visible from Whaleback Ridge and started generating power in 2020.

But the Granville Harbour Wind Farm, with 30 turbines, is much smaller than what's proposed for Whaleback Ridge. And it was built on private farmland.

The bulk of the Whaleback Ridge proposal, north and west of Zeehan, is to be built on three reserves: the Meredith Range, Parting Creek and Mount Heemskirk regional reserves.

WRE chief executive Stephen Casey, a former TasPorts and Incat boss and a former BHP mining executive, compared the quality and consistency of wind on the west coast to a rich iron ore seam in Western Australia's Pilbara desert:

Mr Casey said the company intended to privately finance the entire multi-billion dollar project, and had no plans to seek public funding.

He said that pending state and federal government approvals, the company hoped to start construction on the first phase — 70 turbines capable of generating up to 432 megawatts — in late 2028.

He also said energy-hungry data centres, several of which are currently being planned or built in Tasmania, were being considered as potential users of the project's power.

Whaleback Ridge is currently being assessed under the federal Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act, and in 2024 the state government declared the proposal a major project, meaning it will be assessed by a Tasmanian Planning Commission panel at the state level.

The project has been downsized substantially since 2024, when it was aiming to build 500 turbines and create hundreds of permanent jobs and thousands of construction jobs.

Earlier this week, WRE announced former Tasmanian premier Peter Gutwein as its chair.

Questions over use of public land

Bob Brown Foundation campaigner Scott Jordan said the project was "terrible", and he questioned why public land would be allowed to be used for a large-scale private development.

He said it would put at risk native Tasmanian species such as the wedge-tailed eagle and the critically endangered orange-bellied parrot.

He also dismissed the company's claims that its turbines and associated works would only disrupt 500 hectares of the 40,000-hectare site.

"If we put a tower in the middle of the [MCG], its footprint is going to be fairly small, but you can't play football anymore," he said.

Mr Jordan said the foundation was not opposed to renewable energy projects, but that they must not come at a cost to the environment.

"If the profit is coming before the environment, then their credibility doesn't stack up," he said.

Mr Casey said the company had been surveying the site for several years and had chosen specific turbine locations to avoid the orange-bellied parrot's migration route.

"We know the path of the birds, and we're making sure we're building further away from there," he said.

He said the company was committed to building its turbines where they had the least environmental impact, and that it would continue to have conversations with its opponents.

Cautious hope to see Zeehan 'thrive again'

In town, some residents are cautiously optimistic about the economic claims WRE has made.

Luke Munro moved to Zeehan about a year ago to buy land and start a barber shop, which he said people were lining up for even as he was still building the shop's fixtures.

Mr Munro said wind farms were "majestic", but that "nothing is perfect" when it comes to renewable energy production.

"I know a lot of people don't share that same thought, but I think it's a lot better than digging up dinosaurs and burning them," he said.

Andrew Cronin is familiar with Zeehan's storied history as a mining town and the one-time economic centre of Tasmania, and has hope for its future.

title: The global EV adoption map just fractured in three - ArenaEV
description:
13 September 2026 The EV sales data for August 2026 is impressive - 1.83 million plug-in vehicles finding homes worldwide, a 2% tick upward year-on-year.
Look at the total of 13.4 million units registered year-to-date, up a modest 4%, and it seems the EV transition has settled into a predictable highway cruise.
Yet European EV registrations exploded by 36% (year-on-year) to 380,000 units.
Ottawa’s first six-month import window for lower-tariff Chinese-built electric vehicles drew to a close on August 31 with 24,500 import permits up for grabs.
That pushes cumulative exports past 3.3 million vehicles for the year.
text:
13 September 2026

The EV sales data for August 2026 is impressive - 1.83 million plug-in vehicles finding homes worldwide, a 2% tick upward year-on-year. Sure, almost nothing to talk about. Look at the total of 13.4 million units registered year-to-date, up a modest 4%, and it seems the EV transition has settled into a predictable highway cruise. But walk through the dealership doors wherever you live, and you realize the global market is no longer moving as one. It has split into three distinct geopolitical realities, each playing by its own rules, and nursing its own wounds.

Start with the Old World, where the numbers defy every traditional piece of motor-trade wisdom. August across Europe is normally a commercial ghost town - the factory lines idle, showroom lights dim, and the entire industry packs its bags for the coast. Yet European EV registrations exploded by 36% (year-on-year) to 380,000 units. Deliveries slid 15% month-on-month because nobody signs a finance lease while sitting on a beach in the Algarve, but pushing total year-to-date growth up to 29% in the dead of summer is huge.

The fuel feeding this European bonfire is no secret - it is government-backed cash on the hood. Take Spain, historically one of Western Europe’s slower adopters. Madrid finally threw out the clunky, bureaucratic paperwork nightmare of its old regional MOVES III programme and launched the centrally administered "Auto+" scheme on August 4, smartly backdating eligibility to January 1. Armed with a £341 million budget through 2026, the scheme drops a base subsidy of up to £3,800 straight onto the invoice of a new electric runabout. Unsurprisingly, Spanish EV penetration climbed from 18% in 2025 to 20% year-to-date. Combine that with France hitting a 41% EV penetration rate in August alongside strong German and British numbers, and you see a European consumer base that is happily embracing the plug - as long as the state helps a bit.

The mood in North American showrooms could not be more polarized. Sales of electric cars plummeted 33% year-on-year in August to just 140,000 units - that’s the steepest tumble the region has seen all year (year-to-date volumes down 21%). If you listened only to the doom-mongers, you would think the American public had staged a mutiny against charging cables. But context, as always in this game, separates panic from reality.

The United States is going through a brutal hangover of a buying binge. Wind the clock back twelve months to August and September of 2025. With the federal EV tax credit officially set for termination at the end of September 2025, American buyers stormed dealerships like shoppers on Black Friday, pulling forward months of demand to secure that sweet government kickback before Washington pulled the plug. Measuring August 2026 against that spike makes today’s market look like a crater. Month-on-month, US electric sales actually ticked upward slightly in August. But with federal incentives gone, buyers staring at window stickers between £32,800 to £44,000 are taking a breath - and retreating straight into the arms of petrol-electric hybrids.

North of the border, the Canadian market is in its own regulatory bind. Ottawa’s first six-month import window for lower-tariff Chinese-built electric vehicles drew to a close on August 31 with 24,500 import permits up for grabs. The final score? Automakers claimed only 15,603 permits - roughly 64% of the allocation. The leftover balance of nearly 8,900 permits has now been rolled into the second window, creating a pool of over 33,000 permits running through February 2027. Rather than a sudden Canadian distaste for affordable EVs, this was an administrative bottleneck: the established brands already operating in Canada took a cautious approach, and the fresh Chinese brands planning to flood the market have yet to organize their dealer and service networks.

And finally - China, the king of the electrified landscape, where the raw numbers reveal a bit of a contradiction. Domestic sales dipped 11% year-on-year to 1.03 million vehicles in August, widening from a 5% drop in July. Pundits love to scream about popping bubbles, but that reading misses the forest for the trees. Month-on-month, domestic Chinese deliveries actually rose 4%, and New Energy Vehicle penetration stayed firmly north of 60% of the passenger car market for the fourth consecutive month. This isn’t an electric collapse - it is simply a saturated market grappling with tough year-ago comparisons. Internal combustion engines are being starved out of Chinese cities simply because the math of running an EV on cheap domestic power makes burning petrol look financially absurd.

Because the domestic Chinese market has turned into a knife fight of razor-thin margins and wild discounts, manufacturers in Shenzhen and Shanghai are shifting their sales abroad. Chinese exports of New Energy Vehicles didn’t grow in August - they detonated, surging over 150% year-on-year to a monthly record of nearly 520,000 units. That pushes cumulative exports past 3.3 million vehicles for the year. BYD, China’s premier export powerhouse, has already bumped its full-year overseas sales target upward for the second time this year. If domestic demand is hitting a plateau, China’s industry will simply build transport ships and send the surplus abroad.

That export tsunami feeds into the most eye-opening metric in the entire report: the "Rest of the World" column. Across Southeast Asia, Latin America, and parts of the Middle East, electric vehicle deliveries exploded by 97% (year-on-year) to 290,000 units in August. These are emerging markets not held back by decades of loyalty to Detroit or Bavarian badges. Drivers there want smart, affordable, reliable daily transportation with tiny running costs - and Chinese carmakers have exactly the hardware they are looking for.

Where does this leave us? We are watching the definitive end of the global automotive monoculture. The old playbook - where an automaker could engineer a single crossover platform, stamp it out across three continents, and expect tidy sales - is dead. Today, regional politics and fiscal policy hold the steering wheel. Subsidize the cars in Madrid and Paris, and showrooms hum. Pull the safety net in Washington, and buyers run right back to hybrid safety blankets.

text:
The United States' existing dams could produce an additional 15.2 terawatt-hours of electricity per year, enough to power more than 1.4 million homes across the country. A new study from Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Idaho National Laboratory found that by retrofitting select dams that are not already outfitted for hydropower production could prove to be a critical and efficient source of clean energy at a much lower cost than traditional hydropower projects.

These findings are based on modelling through a new software called HydroGenerate, developed by researchers at the Idaho National Laboratory. The 'multi-stream data architecture' model crunches water flow data from the U.S. Geological Survey and from Oak Ridge to determine potential power production from a given dam by inputting turbine performance curves and hydraulic head.

The combination of these various data sets provides a much more accurate view of hydropower potential than ever before. The modelling takes into account optimal turbine design, seasonality, and existing structural realities, among other critical factors relating to the individualized characteristics of these existing dams. "Many of these dams already serve other critical purposes, and their operational constraints - such as flood control or navigation - can significantly limit hydropower development," Carly Hansen, the project's principal investigator and lead author of the report, was recently quoted by Interesting Engineering. "We've worked to reflect those limitations in a way that hadn't been done before."

Even when accounting for the many limitations presented by working with existing infrastructure, the findings indicate that there is an abundance of exploitable, emissions-free energy sitting dormant across the nation. Most of the dams that the analysis identified as suitable for hydropower retrofitting are in the Great Lakes basin and the upper Mississippi River, and 86 percent are federal facilities.

Adding this identified additional capacity would change the geography of hydropower in the United States and bring this clean energy resource to regions that are currently underrepresented in the sector. In 2025, the top hydropower producing states in the U.S. were Washington (27 percent of U.S. total conventional hydroelectricity net summer generation capacity), California (13 percent), Oregon (10 percent), New York (6 percent), and Alabama (4 percent).

At present, just 3 percent of the United States' dams are equipped for power generation, but that could soon change. Last month, the United States Department of Energy's Hydropower and Hydrokinetic Office (H2O) - the same office supporting the HydroGenerate project - awarded $5.5 million in funding across 11 U.S. National Laboratory projects to help speed up and simplify the licensing process for hydropower facilities.

"For over 100 years, hydropower has been a pillar of American energy, supplying reliable, affordable power across the nation," H2O Director Nichole Fitzgerald said in a press release. "The projects selected today will not only help ensure the continued operation of America's hydropower plants but also keep permitting and relicensing costs down for operators so they can pass those saving along to ratepayers."

This initiative has enjoyed broad bipartisan support in the United States House of Representatives as well as in the Senate, a vanishingly rare occurrence for clean energy development. "It's rare to see so many lawmakers from different parties and regions united on behalf of a common cause, but that's what makes hydropower so unique," said the National Hydropower Association's senior director of legislative affairs, Matthew Allen. "Hydro's dependable power and critical infrastructure can help lower Americans' bills and provide good jobs for generations of families. But the current, outdated licensing process is slowing down new construction and threatens around 16 gigawatts (GW) of hydropower going through relicensing in the next decade."

By Haley Zaremba for Oilprice.com

text:
Egyptian Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly witnessed the signing of a contract to establish an electric battery manufacturing plant in Egypt through a partnership between Egyptian battery manufacturer BME and China’s Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL), one of the world’s largest electric battery manufacturers.

The agreement was signed by Maged Wahib, chairman of BME, and Luo Haining, director of international investment at CATL, in the presence of Industry Minister Khaled Hashem, project manager Amin Karim Ghobour, and BME board member Lotfy Tadros.

The factory will be established as an industrial base for manufacturing battery systems in Egypt, initially focusing on batteries for heavy commercial vehicles. The first phase will have an annual production capacity of 1 gigawatt-hour (GWh), with initial investments exceeding EGP 2bn.

Under the project’s second phase, production capacity is planned to increase to 5 GWh annually. The expansion is expected to include batteries for passenger vehicles and energy-storage systems for renewable energy generated from solar and wind power.

The project targets a local content ratio of 40% and is intended to supply both the Egyptian and international markets, while supporting the development of local manufacturing capabilities and technical skills.

BME was established by Egyptian transport manufacturer MCV and Auto D for Industry, Trade and Supplies. Through its partnership with CATL, the company plans to manufacture battery systems locally for vehicle manufacturers operating in Egypt.

Local production is expected to reduce reliance on imported battery systems and lower some of the shipping and logistics costs associated with imports, while allowing battery systems to be supplied closer to vehicle production lines.

Madbouly said the government is looking to accelerate implementation of the project and move quickly towards the next executive steps, describing the agreement as part of efforts to support and localise battery manufacturing in Egypt.

The prime minister also highlighted CATL’s experience and capabilities in battery manufacturing, saying the government expects the project to contribute to developing Egypt’s industrial capacity in the sector.

Industry Minister Khaled Hashem said that the factory represents a step towards establishing new domestic manufacturing capabilities in battery production as the global automotive industry shifts towards electric vehicles and energy-storage technologies.

He added that automotive component industries are a key element of Egypt’s national automotive industry development programme and can help attract global vehicle manufacturers to the country.

Amin Karim Ghobour, the project manager, said the agreement follows the government’s efforts to deepen local manufacturing and localise modern technologies, particularly in automotive components, electric vehicles, and battery systems.

He said the partnership would combine CATL’s battery technology, production equipment, and technical support with Egyptian manufacturing and engineering capabilities. The cooperation is also expected to support technology transfer and the development of a local supply chain for battery manufacturing.

Ghobour added that BME’s plans extend beyond the initial production of battery systems for heavy commercial vehicles. The company aims to establish a broader battery manufacturing platform that could eventually cover passenger vehicle batteries and energy-storage solutions.

The project is expected to serve growing demand for battery systems in Egypt’s transport and energy sectors while creating new manufacturing and investment opportunities and supporting the development of technical skills required for the electric mobility industry.

Why are researchers turning waste paper into battery anodes

Scientists at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, have developed a technique that turns waste paper into carbon anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The discarded material can come from packaging, paper bags and cardboard boxes. The researchers use carbonisation to convert the paper fibres into pure carbon. This carbon can then be made into electrodes for rechargeable batteries. According to NTU, the resulting batteries could be used in mobile phones, medical equipment and electric vehicles. This gives waste paper a role in battery production rather than simple disposal. The researchers also found that the carbon anodes had durability, flexibility and electrochemical properties.

How carbonisation changes paper fibres into pure carbon

The key step is carbonisation, which involves exposing paper to high temperatures without oxygen. Before heating, the researchers laser-cut sheets of kraft paper into lattice-like structures, some resembling a spiky piñata, to shape the material before it's carbonised. The paper was then heated to 1,200°C in a furnace without the presence of oxygen. Under these conditions, the paper is reduced to pure carbon, while water vapour and oils are also produced. According to the university, the oxygen-free process results in negligible carbon dioxide emissions. This makes it a greener alternative to disposing of kraft paper through incineration, which produces substantial amounts of greenhouse gases.

How long can the waste-paper battery anodes last

The carbon anodes made by the team showed several properties that matter for rechargeable batteries. Laboratory tests found that the anodes could be charged and discharged up to 1,200 times. NTU said this was at least twice the durability of anodes used in current phone batteries. The researchers also reported in the tests that the material was flexible and had strong electrochemical properties. These results indicate that the carbon made from waste paper can function as an electrode material while remaining durable through repeated battery use.

What makes waste paper a low-cost battery material

Beyond durability, the NTU team said their method also uses less energy-intensive processes and fewer heavy metals than current industrial techniques for manufacturing battery anodes. Since anodes account for an estimated 10% to 15% of the total cost of a lithium-ion battery, using a low-cost waste material like paper could help bring down the overall cost of battery manufacturing. The approach also gives discarded kraft paper another use instead of treating it solely as waste. By converting its fibres into carbon, the process creates a material that can serve a practical role in rechargeable battery production while making use of an otherwise unwanted material.

How could waste paper reduce the environmental impact of battery production

The research presents waste paper as a material for rechargeable battery components. Instead of sending kraft paper for incineration, the process converts its fibres into carbon that can be used for electrodes. Carbonisation also produces water vapour and oils that can be used as biofuel. NTU said the process emits negligible carbon dioxide because it takes place without oxygen. The battery tests further showed that the resulting anodes could withstand up to 1,200 charge and discharge cycles and absorb crushing energy up to five times better than their counterparts.

title: Trump's coastal power grab should alarm all Americans - The Hill
authors: Christine Todd Whitman, opinion contributor, Christine Todd Whitman, opinion contributor
description:
Having administered environmental laws in state and federal leadership, I am extremely concerned how the Trump administration is manipulating this model law to impose a federal takeover of California’s coast.
It began when Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick ordered the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to reopen the routine evaluation of California’s coastal management program done, but not finalized, under the Biden administration.
The Coastal Zone Management Act grants coastal states authority to balance national interests with their distinct priorities.
There is more: The Trump administration is targeting California because the state’s coastal management is widely recognized as the nation’s best and strongest.
Our love of the ocean is universal, so the right to manage the coast should remain equal under the law for all coastal states.
text:
Environmental laws are often criticized for being one-size-fits-all mandates imposed on Americans who know how to govern their own affairs.

A prime example to the contrary is the Coastal Zone Management Act. Signed by former President Nixon, it empowers 35 states and territories along the coast and Great Lakes to advance their own priorities in federal decision making about the coast and ocean while standing up for local economies, natural resources and communities they know best.

Having administered environmental laws in state and federal leadership, I am extremely concerned how the Trump administration is manipulating this model law to impose a federal takeover of California’s coast. The best results come from state-federal partnership, not presidential fiat.

Arbitrary governance of the coast places our entire nation’s economy at risk. If coastal counties were a country, its gross domestic product would rank third in the world — behind only the United States and China.

A clean and healthy coast is an economic, cultural and ecological asset. Gambling with it to benefit currently favored industries is foolish, sacrifices the freedoms of nearly 130 million coastal Americans, and risks needless economic harm. The administration must chart a smarter course.

Under the guise of expanding offshore oil drilling and space launches, along with the establishment of seabed mining, this effort is supported by some of my Republican friends. But political pendulums inevitably swing, and this short-sighted initiative creates a dangerous power grab for future presidents of any political stripe to exploit.

It began when Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick ordered the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to reopen the routine evaluation of California’s coastal management program done, but not finalized, under the Biden administration. Lutnick’s order, citing economic factors and favoring select industries, signals this duplicative review is rigged.

The Coastal Zone Management Act grants coastal states authority to balance national interests with their distinct priorities. Following certification by NOAA, states assess and shape proposed federal plans and projects affecting their coastal zones.

With this authority, California has successfully worked alongside 10 presidents to manage its coast as an economic engine and iconic natural feature attracting visitors and entrepreneurs from around the world. As it grew into the world’s fourth largest economy, California also expanded access to its coast, preserved coastal parkland and wildlife, and ensured local governments have a voice in the approval of federal projects, including subsea fiber optic cables, offshore oil and gas production, and military training exercises.

This is what Californians stand to lose. So, let’s consider Lutnick’s claims that the state blocks the nation’s economy and innovation.

Over nearly 50 years, California has reviewed more than 3,700 federal actions impacting its coast and, in 96 percent of cases, either negotiated improvements or approved projects as submitted. Clearly, the state-federal partnership has worked.

Furthermore, as the home of Silicon Valley, California creates tomorrow’s technologies. It is the foremost destination for venture capital, drawing three times more than the rest of the nation combined during the first half of this year. The state also ranks second for commercial space launches and seventh for crude oil production. These achievements have occurred while protecting nearly 22 percent of its coastline as state parkland and growing a $60.5 billion coastal economy supporting more than 600,000 jobs built on tourism, recreation, transport and fishing.

This formula for success falls apart if Washington can supplant California’s priorities with its own, especially if the Trump administration’s rush for new offshore drilling results in oil spills. We’ve seen time and again that such spills close fisheries, beaches and harbors, and transform vibrant coastal communities into ghost towns overnight.

In this context, the administration’s review of California reflects an approach less interested in facts and science than one focused on delivering a specific outcome for this president, who stands to gain significant power over 840 miles of coast just by changing California’s standing under the Coastal Zone Management Act.

There is more: The Trump administration is targeting California because the state’s coastal management is widely recognized as the nation’s best and strongest. If it falls first to a federal takeover, then like dominos, other states will easily follow, destroying one of our best examples of federalist governance.

This should alarm every American. Our love of the ocean is universal, so the right to manage the coast should remain equal under the law for all coastal states. Instead we see the administration play favorites, demonstrated by the abandonment of its oil drilling plans off the Atlantic coast after significant opposition from the region’s Republican leaders.

As the old saying goes, Washington doesn’t have a monopoly on wisdom. Hopefully, we won’t have to relearn this lesson the hard way.

Christine Todd Whitman served as governor of New Jersey from 1994 to 2001 and administrator of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency from 2001 to 2003.

text:
