text:
Australia-Based A1 Lithium Plans Emery County, Utah, Production Operations

Critical minerals company A1 Lithium Inc. plans to establish operations in Emery County, Utah. The $569 million project is expected to create 138 jobs.

The investment will include the construction of a new lithium carbonate production facility located in Utah’s Paradox Basin, which will produce high-purity, battery-grade lithium carbonate for the U.S. electric vehicle and energy storage markets.

“Apart from the advantageous geological conditions of the Green River Lithium Project, A1 Lithium decided to invest in Utah due to the high-level support for the development of critical mineral projects to meet the strategic objective of re-establishing supply chains in the USA,” said Anson Resources President Bruce Richardson. “Utah’s transparent mining policies and aim of making quick application determinations were also a factor in this decision. We have received an unprecedented level of support from GOED and UIPA as well as other Government of Utah agencies for which we express our appreciation. We are excited to proceed with this project that we expect will bring about a generational change in the economy and livelihood of the people of Green River and south-eastern Utah.”

To support the project, the Utah Governor’s Office of Economic Development (GOED) awarded A1 Lithium a post-performance tax reduction through the state’s Rural Economic Development Tax Increment Financing program. The Utah Inland Port Authority (UIPA) board also approved an incentive for the project.

“Developing domestic supply chains for critical minerals is a key focus of both state and national energy infrastructure strategies,” noted GOED Commissioner Jefferson Moss. “The Green River Lithium project in Emery County marks a significant advancement for rural economic growth in Utah. It establishes a sustainable and long-term industrial base, creating well-paying jobs in rural areas and strengthening Utah’s role in producing energy materials domestically.”

A1 Lithium Inc. is the U.S. subsidiary of Australia-based Anson Resources, a critical minerals company focused on developing lithium resources. The company specializes in lithium brine development and direct lithium extraction, with plans to produce high-purity, battery-grade lithium carbonate for electric vehicles, energy storage, and other advanced technology markets.

“A1 Lithium’s investment in south-eastern Utah will be transformational for the City of Green River, Utah’s production of critical minerals, and our nation’s broader reindustrialization efforts,” added EDCUtah Executive Director Ryan Starks. “EDCUtah is proud to support A1 Lithium as they grow and expand, and our network looks forward to continuing to support the company as they invest in the region and create long-term opportunities.”

“UIPA is helping Green River translate private investment into long-term economic capacity,” said UIPA Executive Director Ben Hart. “This post-performance incentive aligns A1 Lithium’s growth with regional priorities and ties public support directly to actual investment and job creation.”

text:
A Quinnipiac University poll of Pennsylvania voters this summer found that 74% say they would oppose building an AI data center in their community, while 16% would support it, with 10% not offering an opinion. This compares to Quinnipiac’s February poll, when 68% said they would oppose an AI data center in their community and 20% would favor it, with 12% not offering an opinion.

Guardrails on PA data centers

Governor Josh Shapiro in August issued an executive order demanding that data center developers meet energy affordability, community engagement, economic development and environmental protection standards. If they don’t, he said, the commonwealth will not give them permits to build and operate.

Click to resize

PA data center permit tracker

In correlation with the governor’s executive order, Pennsylvania’s Department of Environmental Protection has created a “data center permit tracker.” You can check it out online.

Community solar update

Community solar projects are legal and operating in 44 states. But Pennsylvania — heavily influenced by the fossil fuel industry — is not one of them. A bill that would make community solar legal here has passed the state House of Representatives. Its fate now rests in the Republican-controlled Senate where it is mired in committee. Community solar allows renters and others who can’t put solar panels on their roofs to invest in a local solar array. The energy generated by the array is sold to the electric grid and the proceeds typically knock five-to-20% off an individual investor’s home electric bill.

Energy recommendations

PennFuture, an environmental advocacy group, in August produced recommendations for Pennsylvania’s energy future. They include: (1) requiring 35% of electricity to be generated by renewable energy sources; (2) passing Community Solar enabling legislation; (3) Incentivizing solar development on rooftops of warehouses, fulfillment centers, and large government buildings; and (4) promoting sustainable economic development by leveraging environmental standards attached to financial resources.

PA lawmakers rated on conservation

Conservation Voters of Pennsylvania has created a “scorecard” showing how state legislators voted on key bills impacting the environment in the last two years. The 2025-26 Pennsylvania Environmental Scorecard gives each member of the legislature a score on their environmental voting. Just enter your address and you can see the score for the lawmakers that represent you in Harrisburg.

Changing national forest rules

The U.S. Department of Agriculture plans to end a 25-year-old rule limiting road building and logging on 44 million acres of national forest land. That includes the half-million acre Allegheny National Forest in Pennsylvania. The Forest Service will accept, until midnight Sept. 21, public comments before a final decision is made. To comment, go to Regulations.gov. The Roadless Area Conservation Rule currently protects 25,000 acres in Pennsylvania from logging, mining and other destructive human activities, according to PennEnvironment.

Clean energy second-quarter growth

Clean energy investments in the U.S. surged in April, May and June reaching the second-largest quarterly investment in history just behind the third quarter of 2025 when people were hurrying to buy EVs before tax credits ended. That’s according to the Rhodium and MIT Clean Investment Monitor. Nearly all of the increase came from retail sales of rooftop solar and home battery storage systems.

text:
Public has right to know what data centers are doing

I am writing regarding the Environmental Protection Agency’s recent actions to gut pollution controls for artificial intelligence data centers.

Modern AI data centers can use enormous amounts of electricity, as much as a city in one location. Local grids struggle to keep up with such demands. EPA’s efforts to deal with this problem come at the expense of clean air and the public’s right to know what is happening in their community.

Specifically, the Trump administration allows construction to begin before obtaining air permits; AI data centers to run their dirty generators more frequently; certain power plants to not install any pollution controls for acid rain; and companies to seek and receive “minor source” air permits without gathering public input.

Limiting the transparency and accountability of the buildout of these dirty data centers will have real consequences. Large-scale generators at AI data centers are usually powered by diesel, polluting the air we breathe with dangerous chemicals. The public deserves clean air and has a right to know what kind of pollution data centers are pumping into our communities. It's your right to know.

Marcia Schulz, Silver Lake

People with disabilities at risk as services are cut

I’m angered by the Department of Justice’s recent memo authorizing states to institutionalize more people with disabilities. This means removing people from society and shutting them into nursing homes, psychiatric hospitals, segregated schools and sheltered workshops, rather than funding community- or home-based care which offer more autonomy, undoing decades of law and Supreme Court precedent. SinceOlmstead v. L.C., in 1999, states have been required to support disabled people in the most integrated setting. Institutionalization is supposed to be the last resort.

Sadly, states have already started slashing disability services because of Donald Trump’s Medicaid cuts. The budget’s advocates professed that safety-net programs for the “most vulnerable Americans,” would be safeguarded, but children and people with disabilities have been hit hardest.

The DOJ’s memo is part of the administration’s sweeping series of changes impacting how disabled people learn, live, work and otherwise interact with society. For example, the Education Department’s responsibilities for special education and civil rights have been reassigned to the Department of Health and Human Services, raising concerns about whether children will continue to have access to free, appropriate public education. We must resist this and every attempt to make America’s most vulnerable invisible.

Charlotte Onderick, Stow

Blessed to ride with March on Washington activists

I had the great benefit of grabbing a seat on a bus with the Urban League to attend the 63rd anniversary of the March on Washington and Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” speech. Though I don’t know anyone who’s ever enjoyed the physical trip to D.C. on a bus itself, due to its unavoidable, uncomfortable nature, I consider the experience to have been a gift of a lifetime.

What made the trip special were all of the young Americans, the UAW members from all over Ohio supporting Sherrod Brown and Dr. Amy Acton, and, most of all (for me) was the chance to relax and talk with a few dozen members of the marvelous Delta Sigma Theta Sorority from all over the country.

These proud women and avowed social activists are part of a historic sorority that was born in 1913, and had, as their earliest dedicated mission, the women’s suffrage movement. Their wisdom, accomplishments and kindness to an old guy like me from Cuyahoga Falls reminded me that a day on a bus with almost no sleep was meaningless in comparison to the blessings I received in return.

Todd Schneider, Cuyahoga Falls

Remembering what the rubber workers stood for

I do hope it does not offend anyone, when I say: It’s about time.

The rubber industry of Akron has been reported on, in glowing terms in the recent past. As well it may, but a key component, labor, has nearly been completely overlooked. Just why did the workers resort to various kinds of disruptive behavior? Because they were really Communists? They just wanted to tear down the thing of beauty that had been created by General, Goodyear, Firestone and Continental? Absolutely not.

Their employers were using them as they used all other factors of production. Buy an input and use it up, as cheaply as possible. Their living expenses were paid for by trading their skills and labor for their weekly paycheck. The workers were simply looking for an equitable trade in the process.

As has happened to some degree throughout history, when people find that they are in need or hurting they band together for the common good. The United Rubber Workers resulted.

Also, please note that while Akron has enjoyed the URW as an International Union, it is not the only one. Please do not overlook the International Chemical Workers Union that originated in about 1937, about two years after the United Rubber Workers Union. It is still located in the Mitchell Building on West Market Street. (The ICWU is now a part of the United Food and Commercial Workers Union, UFCW, while the URW is now a part of the United Steel Workers Union).

Philip Kroll, Akron

The state of things under Donald Trump

So Dear Leader Don wants to rename New Mexico (we won't even mention Lake Ontario), but why stop there? Just be done with it and rename the states Trump 2 through 51. You might ask why not 1 through 50? Well … we all know who Number 1 is, don't we?

Once Trump is gone, the new president can create CURDS (Commission to Undo Really Dumb Stuff).

Chris Walker, Fairlawn

Akron needs more rules for more people

The city of Akron and the mayor keep coming up with new rules for the police to follow. It has to be tough for the police to think of so many rules in the heat of the moment.

Maybe the mayor and the city should come up with rules for the criminals. This way the criminals would have to think more about committing their crimes.

text:
Hyundai Motor Group and the African Development Bank (AfDB) signed a letter of intent on September 8, 2026, in Seoul to develop projects in Africa focused on clean energy, transportation, electric mobility, and industrialization.

The agreement was signed at Hyundai’s headquarters by Jaehoon Chang, the group’s vice president, and Kevin Chika Urama, chief economist and vice president of the AfDB responsible for economic governance and knowledge management. The bank’s delegation was in South Korea for the 8th Korea-Africa Economic Cooperation Ministerial Conference.

The two partners identified six areas for medium- and long-term cooperation. These include the transition to clean energy, particularly green hydrogen, sustainable mobility solutions, transport and logistics infrastructure, the development of an electric vehicle value chain, strengthening industrial and manufacturing capacities, and talent training.

In terms of infrastructure, Hyundai and the AfDB aim to explore road, rail, and port projects. For electric mobility, the agreement includes plans to investigate value chains based on critical African minerals, to better connect the continent’s resources with transformation, assembly, and production activities.

At this stage, the partnership does not include a total announced financial envelope or a definitive list of projects. Both institutions express their intention to identify concrete investment initiatives and establish implementation frameworks by sector, combining development financing with private capital.

Hyundai emphasizes a mixed financing mechanism that links public or economic policy funding with private capital, featuring mechanisms designed to mitigate investment risks. The automaker believes that such a structure could facilitate projects in mobility, energy, and infrastructure.

On its part, the AfDB contributes its development financing instruments, capital mobilization, and project preparation. Kevin Chika Urama described Hyundai as a strategic partner whose technological capabilities can support the continent’s industrial competitiveness and economic transformation.

Following the signing, the AfDB delegation visited Hyundai’s facilities in Yangjae, where the group showcased mobility and robotics technologies, including the Security X Spot and DAL-e robots.

description:
Concerns over Gulf fish farms are wide-ranging, from nutrient pollution due to excess food and fish waste to the potential for escape.
Manna Fish Farms, a New York-based company, is proposing to install 12 to 14 net pens more than 20 miles off Pensacola.
It would be the first such commercial fish farm in U.S. federal waters, said Manna Fish Farms CEO Donna Lanzetta.
He notes, however, that a true commercial fish farm would have to be far, far larger.
“You're able to actually kind of promote and show people that this is Gulf seafood.
text:
The redfish were biting out in the Gulf, but not in the way they’re usually caught.

Instead, about 1,000 of them in total, all around 10 inches long, were in an artificial pen enclosed by netting, a machine on the surface tossing out tiny food pellets every five minutes.

Ashley McDonald, the scientist managing what is currently the only finfish farm in the Gulf’s open waters, stood atop a yellow platform surrounding the wind-swept pen, waves lapping against its sides. She reflected on the small-scale but compelling aquaculture experiment.

“We can grow fish because we have funding to do it,” she said. “Does that mean that that’s actually economically viable?”

It is a question rooted in a rising moment of peril for the Gulf, and it holds high-stakes consequences for Louisiana and the rest of the states along its shores.

The floating aquaculture platform operated by the Dauphin Island Sea Lab off the coast of Alabama is scientific in nature, designed to shed light on whether such small projects can be ecologically and economically sound. But it may offer a glimpse of the future.

A warming climate, overfishing, economic opportunities and Americans’ voracious appetite for seafood are building momentum for large-scale fish farming in the Gulf of Mexico, which President Donald Trump has renamed the Gulf of America.

It would mark a monumental shift in the country’s commercial fishing industry, as well as for a water body more known for its oil rigs, barrier islands and beaches. For supporters, it is a way to reduce the huge number of imported seafood consumed by Americans, currently around 85% of the total by some counts.

But industrial-scale Gulf aquaculture is intensely controversial, with serious environmental considerations, the risk of hurricanes and concerns from traditional commercial fishermen, including Louisiana’s struggling shrimpers.

Some large-scale aquaculture operations in other countries have led to escaped fish, the spread of disease, the misuse of antibiotics and harmful pollution, among other problems. Those pushing for fish farms in the Gulf say such problems have been accounted for and overcome in their plans, while noting the strict requirements for federal permits and related regulations.

Are large fish farms a necessary and inevitable means of adapting? Or a recipe for disaster? That debate is raging — and the eventual outcome is no longer a far-off possibility.

Another demonstration project in the Gulf, in federal waters off Sarasota, Florida, was recently granted final permits and hopes to be in the water early next year, with a plan to grow up to 20,000 redfish, which are officially known as red drum. That project is a pilot and far smaller than what would be needed for a true commercial operation, but its aim is to help open the path to large-scale fish farms.

A far larger proposal for a commercial-scale fish farm off Pensacola is pending as the plans advance through the country’s byzantine permitting process. And separately, the federal government has identified three areas off Texas as potential sites for aquaculture.

Louisiana has much at stake. The state is still the nation’s second-leading seafood supplier behind Alaska, with an annual economic impact of more than $2.4 billion, despite its rapidly declining wetlands habitat, according to state data.

At the same time, future conditions may only worsen. One recent study projected that increased drought related to climate change could periodically lead to big decreases in Gulf catch.

“I do see aquaculture as being one of the top solutions to the need for proteins for humans. It’s surprisingly hard to do it right,” said Benjamin Kirtman, dean of the University of Miami’s Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric and Earth Science and a co-author of the study.

“You want to make sure you do it in such a way that you don't disrupt the rest of the ecosystem. All of that takes an enormous amount of time.”

‘What I liked about the fish business’

Harlon Pearce’s love of the outdoors is obvious from a look around his office, where mounted bass and deer heads adorn the walls. But seafood is also his business, as it has been for more than 60 years.

His career straddles the industry’s rugged past and the rapidly shifting currents of today.

Below him are the cavernous warehouses for Harlon’s LA Fish, where workers were busy on a recent day slicing filets from slimy mounds of whiskered catfish. Pearce, 80, still shows up at 4:30 a.m. to prepare for deliveries to his plant in Kenner, not far from Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport.

While attending Loyola Law School, he decided he enjoyed the seafood business more than being a lawyer. Early on, he worked for legendary seafood dealer Preston Battistella, whose business had its roots in the heyday of New Orleans’ French Market, before starting his own company.

“I didn't like law, didn't like the reading,” Pearce said.

“I didn't like having to go back to somebody's case to tell me what I could and couldn't do. What I liked about the fish business is I could make a difference and make a change, because nothing was written in stone.”

He recalls the bonanza days, when commercial fishing for redfish was still legal and gill nets were allowed for speckled trout, helping New Orleans build its reputation as a culinary cornucopia. That all changed in the 1980s and beyond as population declines for those species and others became apparent.

Pearce laments the state of the business now. He largely blames commercial fishing regulations, which he calls too restrictive, though recreational anglers and fisheries biologists would certainly disagree.

While still dealing largely in local seafood, Pearce has adapted to include purchases of imports and out-of-state product. His main local supplies include catfish, sheepshead, black drum, shrimp, crab and oysters.

He laments that prices for certain types of wild-caught, local seafood have spiked while regulations have put popular species out of reach for commercial fleets.

It is partly for that reason that Pearce is not opposed to aquaculture in the Gulf. He feels that it would offer a lifeline to the industry if done responsibly. He calls it absurd that New Orleans restaurants serve redfish farmed in ponds in other states, mainly Texas.

“If we don't have the production that we need, to do what we need to do, we're dead,” he said. “So anything that helps us get production, and especially in a moderately priced way, I'm all for. I don’t care what it is.”

But where Pearce sees a lifeline, others sense a potential catastrophe.

Concerns over Gulf fish farms are wide-ranging, from nutrient pollution due to excess food and fish waste to the potential for escape. To make them economically viable, they would necessarily have to be large-scale, and opponents note the Gulf already suffers from an annual "dead zone" created by nutrient pollution flowing down the Mississippi River.

Manna Fish Farms, a New York-based company, is proposing to install 12 to 14 net pens more than 20 miles off Pensacola. Each one would be capable of holding 500,000 pounds of fish, but the company intends to stock them at half their capacity, or 250,000 pounds, to avoid overcrowding.

Each net pen would be 9,000 cubic meters, or the volume of about three and a half Olympic-sized swimming pools. The initial plan is to grow redfish there, and the pens could be submerged 40 feet below the water’s surface.

It would be the first such commercial fish farm in U.S. federal waters, said Manna Fish Farms CEO Donna Lanzetta.

Acy Cooper, president of the Louisiana Shrimp Association, said local shrimpers have been fighting the prospect of offshore aquaculture for years. Even small-scale farms are unacceptable to him, he said.

“That right there is the beginning of the end,” said Cooper, whose organization still has around 500 members despite the local shrimping industry facing numerous challenges. “If it starts, you’re never going to stop it.”

For environmental organizations like Healthy Gulf, concerns are similar. Healthy Gulf was among the groups that filed suit to try to stop the experimental project now set to move forward off Sarasota.

Christian Wagley, a coastal organizer with Healthy Gulf, noted the loss of habitat for wild fish, ranging from the disappearing marsh of Louisiana to the dying seagrasses and oyster beds in other areas of the Gulf Coast. He said the country should focus on restoring that habitat and supporting traditional commercial fishermen instead of pushing for fish farms.

“There will never be one fish farm only in the Gulf, and they'll never be small, because you have to have the economies of scale,” said Wagley. “And so I think for them to make it profitable, they would have to have literally miles and miles of industrial-scale fish farms.”

‘Producing more of this ourselves’

The emerging industry, however, argues the main concerns involving large-scale aquaculture will be overcome through water quality monitoring, careful food management and secure pens, among other measures. They appear to have an ally in the current administration.

Trump, in his first term, signed an executive order on “promoting American seafood competitiveness” that in part aimed to ease the highly complex permitting process for aquaculture.

There is also support in Congress, where a bill known as the MARA Act has been introduced aiming to establish a framework for sustainable offshore aquaculture.

More recently, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration identified 13 “Aquaculture Opportunity Areas” as holding potential for fish farms. They included 10 off California and three in the Gulf off Texas.

Three areas of Louisiana had been identified as potential sites earlier in the process, but those were later removed amid objections from commercial fishing organizations and environmental groups.

Even so, the areas that did make the cut are largely symbolic. Aquaculture development in the Gulf is by no means limited there, and that is beginning to be made emphatically clear.

After an eight-year permitting process, Hawaii-based company Ocean Era recently received the final green light for a pilot demonstration project around 40 miles off Sarasota, Florida.

The so-called Velella Epsilon project will grow up to 20,000 redfish in a net pen measuring 55 feet in diameter and about 23 feet deep. Like the Dauphin Island experiment, its nets are designed to be strong enough to resist sharks, and the entire structure can be submerged in the case of storms.

Neil Sims, Ocean Era’s CEO, hopes the project can be in the water early next year. The company has run two similar pilots off Hawaii.

It wanted to start with a smaller project “that wasn't going to scare anybody in terms of its scale, its potential impact, and allow the Gulf fishing and boating community to see for themselves what offshore aquaculture actually looks like,” said Sims.

He notes, however, that a true commercial fish farm would have to be far, far larger. The pilot off Florida is only about 1% of what would be needed, said Sims.

But Sims is an unapologetic evangelist for the industry. He believes the country has no choice, and he contends that monitoring has demonstrated that if you put the pens in deep enough water, far enough offshore, there is no significant impact on the surrounding ecosystem.

He points to what labels itself the country’s only commercial fish farm operating in the open ocean, run by Blue Ocean Mariculture and producing 900 tons of kanpachi per year in state waters off Hawaii. Sims helped found what later became Blue Ocean.

“It's a great way for us to start to produce the seafood that we need,” said Sims, mentioning the large amount currently imported.

“We need to be producing more of this ourselves, and we need to be creating jobs and building an industry here.”

There are numerous onshore or coastal aquaculture farms, including in Louisiana, growing everything from catfish to oysters. But onshore aquaculture does not carry the same risks to the surrounding ecosystem as open water finfish farms.

Not all environmental groups oppose open ocean aquaculture. But they stress that it must be done responsibly, and with utmost caution.

‘Grow great things’

The small “AquaFort” fish farm off Alabama’s coast comes into view like a sturdy raft floating atop the Gulf’s waters, black piping and a yellow platform framing its perimeter. In a reminder of the Gulf’s industrial legacy, a hulking gas rig looms in the far-off distance.

The Dauphin Island Sea Lab, in partnership with other institutions, won a federal grant for up to three years to operate it, and it is modeled after a similar project off New Hampshire. The scientists overseeing it are hoping to find out if it can be sustainable and ecologically sound, potentially providing traditional commercial fishermen with the option of operating their own for a supplemental source of income.

The platform is actually moored to the seafloor, and it is surrounded by netting to keep the redfish in and predators out. It is part of a dual system of protection that initially included copper mesh, but that will soon be changed to a lighter plastic version.

It is divided into two pens, each one 20 feet by 20 feet, at a depth of 12 feet. The feeder that tosses out pellets for the redfish is solar-powered, and an underwater camera system allows the scientists to monitor the fish remotely.

Cages along the sides hold oysters and algae being grown alongside the fish. The idea is that the oysters can filter the water, and the algae can absorb the excess nutrients being produced by the fish.

Part of the experiment involves whether those, too, can be harvested and marketed, though the current location does not allow for the oysters to be sold.

In June, the scientists returned with commercial fishermen to harvest the redfish. Afterward, they distributed them to seafood markets for free this time and collected feedback.

They would have to be labeled as farmed, but would allow Alabamans a chance to buy redfish from the Gulf.

Like Louisiana, Alabama bans commercial fishing for the species, whose numbers plummeted by the 1980s, though they are farmed in ponds, particularly in Texas.

It will all be a test to gauge interest in the idea — and, potentially, an entirely new industry. McDonald sees the smaller-scale projects like her own as holding potential for wide acceptance.

“We can grow great things in the Gulf. They're local, they're right here, we know how they're grown, we know where they came from,” she said.

“You're able to actually kind of promote and show people that this is Gulf seafood. This didn't come from Indonesia or South America.”

title: Louisiana, Ohio, and Kentucky pass industry-backed bills blocking community air data in ...
description:
New laws in Louisiana, Ohio, and Kentucky, however, limit how much that locally gathered information can matter in requests for regulatory enforcement, according to Floodlight.

Community health protections hinge on air monitoring and on whether governments are willing to act when pollution is found.
text:
Residents near factories sometimes rely on inexpensive air sensors of their own when official monitors are too few or not close enough to major industrial facilities.

New laws in Louisiana, Ohio, and Kentucky, however, limit how much that locally gathered information can matter in requests for regulatory enforcement, according to Floodlight.

Here's what to know

Lawmakers in Louisiana, Ohio, and Kentucky started enacting closely aligned bills in 2024 with support from chemical and manufacturing trade associations.

Under those measures, enforcement cases cannot be based on air readings unless they come from monitors built to EPA-approved standards, devices that can run into the tens of thousands of dollars.

West Virginia has seen similar proposals, but none have been enacted.

Federal grants for the system have dropped by more than 35%, after adjusting for inflation, and the number of government air monitors across the country has been cut by nearly half. That reduction formed the backdrop for these new laws.

Monitoring for toxic pollutants has thinned even further, with networks measuring vinyl chloride, chloroprene, and benzene each declining by more than half from 2004 to 2025.

Chet Wayland, a former longtime leader of the EPA's Air Quality Assessment Division, acknowledged that the network was "showing its age" and "getting smaller over time," Floodlight reported.

Nearly 60% of U.S. counties have no public air monitor at all, according to a 2025 study co-authored by Penn State assistant professor Nelson Roque.

More background

The people most affected are often those already living alongside major industrial operations.

Floodlight found that 71 of the 100 largest industrial polluters it reviewed across Kentucky, Louisiana, Ohio, and West Virginia released, as their top chemical, a substance no government air monitor in that state measures.

Kentucky approved House Bill 137 in March 2025, after Louisiana passed the Community Air Monitoring Reliability Act, and Ohio adopted a comparable limit through its budget bill.

Under Kentucky's law, air testing must use "scientifically defensible" methods.

"When we take away the ability for those folks to have a reasonably priced monitor … for their own protection, we've just taken any tool they had right out of their hands," said Miranda Leppla, a lawyer who sued Ohio over its new rule on behalf of environmental groups, per Floodlight.

Donna Ballinger, who lives near a steel plant in Middletown, Ohio, told Floodlight what she worried about most.

"My fear is cancer," she admitted.

What's being done?

The Environmental Integrity Project says that once the EPA required refineries in 2018 to track benzene at their fencelines, the number above the agency's benzene action level fell by half within five years.

In California, residents of fenceline communities have received funding for monitoring equipment and training, and the state set aside $1.4 billion between 2017 and 2025 for communities that have long carried heavy pollution burdens.

Colorado now requires four industrial plants to conduct real-time fenceline monitoring.

In Texas, the Commission on Environmental Quality and its contractors run 33 automated gas chromatographs that deliver near-real-time measurements of volatile organic compounds.

A court challenge is pending against Ohio's law, while community organizations in places including Louisiana continue pressing for stronger local air data despite funding setbacks.

Reonda Victor, in Louisiana's industrial corridor, told Floodlight, "Without information, we don't know."

Where can I learn more?

Questions about who can document pollution — and what regulators can do with that evidence — reach beyond Louisiana, Ohio, and Kentucky.

Elsewhere, lawmakers and major companies are also trying to shape when air violations lead to penalties and when enforcement gets tougher.

• In Kentucky, lawmakers advanced limits on air pollution penalties for self-reporting polluters in 2024.

• In Detroit, Stellantis pursued a workaround to avoid state particulate emissions rules the same year.

• In Delaware last year, lawmakers approved major restrictions for big corporations by expanding pollution fines.

Community health protections hinge on air monitoring and on whether governments are willing to act when pollution is found.

text:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly on Sunday witnessed the signing of a contract to establish a plant for manufacturing electric batteries in partnership between Egyptian battery maker BME and China’s Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL), the world’s largest electric battery manufacturer.

The agreement was signed by BME Chairman Maged Wahib and CATL Director of International Investment Luo Haining, in the presence of Industry Minister Khaled Hashem and BME board members Amin Karim Ghabbour and Lotfy Tadros.

BME was established by Egyptian transport manufacturer MCV and Auto D for Industry, Trade and Supplies.

The new plant aims to establish a specialised industrial base for battery systems in Egypt. It will initially produce batteries for heavy commercial vehicles, with plans to expand into passenger-car batteries and energy-storage systems.

The project is designed to support Egypt’s growing transport and energy sectors, while strengthening local manufacturing and export capacity.

The first phase will have an annual production capacity of 1 gigawatt-hour, with initial investments exceeding LE2 billion ($39 million). The second phase will increase capacity to 5 gigawatt-hours a year and add production of passenger-car batteries and systems for storing solar and wind energy.

The project targets a local component ratio of 40 per cent and is expected to supply both domestic and international markets. It will also create jobs and help develop technical skills among Egyptian workers.

The partnership will combine BME’s local manufacturing and engineering capabilities with CATL’s advanced battery technology, production equipment and technical expertise. The plant will supply locally manufactured battery systems to vehicle producers in Egypt, reducing reliance on imports and cutting shipping and logistics costs.

Speaking at the signing ceremony, Madbouly welcomed the agreement, describing CATL as a global leader in battery manufacturing with extensive expertise and capabilities.

He said the government expected work on the project to begin soon and would take the necessary measures to support battery manufacturing and technology localisation in Egypt.

Hashem said the plant marked an important step towards building Egypt’s domestic battery manufacturing capacity as the global shift towards electric vehicles and energy-storage technologies accelerates.

He said automotive component manufacturing was a cornerstone of Egypt’s national programme to develop the automotive industry and attract major global carmakers.

The agreement with the world’s largest electric battery manufacturer, he added, also demonstrated the ability of Egypt’s industrial sector to meet international manufacturing standards and produce competitive, high-quality products.

Ghabbour said the agreement was part of efforts to deepen local manufacturing, localise advanced industries and technologies, and strengthen Egypt’s capacity to produce automotive components, particularly for electric vehicles and battery systems.

He said the partnership would combine CATL’s advanced battery technology with Egyptian industrial and engineering capabilities, supporting technology and knowledge transfer and helping build a local battery supply chain.

Ghabbour added that BME aimed not only to manufacture battery systems for heavy commercial vehicles but also to lay the foundations for an integrated battery industry that could eventually expand into passenger-car batteries and energy-storage solutions.

Such expansion, he said, would create new investment, manufacturing and export opportunities and support Egypt’s ambition to become a regional hub for emerging industries.

name: Clean Energy
title: IFA Berlin Recap Part 2: More Diverse Sustainability Approaches - CleanTechnica
description:
If there was a consistent theme around clean technology, it was that sustainability is not just one thing, but a diverse range of approaches.
Heat pumps seemed to be the norm.
Energy efficiency tended to be an expectation more than a differentiator to highlight.
Gorenje had one of the largest displays dedicated to sustainability, with efforts extending from sourcing, materials and manufacturing to energy efficiency and packaging.
Midea highlighted the switch to R290 refrigerant (propane) for their heat pumps, which is far more environmentally friendly than many traditional refrigerants.
text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

Earlier this week, IFA Berlin wrapped up. If there was a consistent theme around clean technology, it was that sustainability is not just one thing, but a diverse range of approaches.

Some of the innovations that we focus on in the US have become routine in Germany. Although I had not been to IFA before, I got the sense that sustainability was not as prevalent in messaging as it was in the past. Heat pumps seemed to be the norm. Induction cooktops greatly outnumbered gas or resistance. Energy efficiency tended to be an expectation more than a differentiator to highlight.

However, clean technology still seems to have a strong appeal in Europe. That showed up in diverse ways through multiple products, some of which are highlighted here.

Bosch showed off their Green Collection, with up to 50% less CO2 from production materials. Although we have tended to focus on efficiency, appliances are heavy and contain a large amount of material. The matte black finish also looked sleek and a bit different than typical kitchen appliances.

Ferre dedicated space to the sustainability of their packaging, made from recycled materials.

Gorenje had one of the largest displays dedicated to sustainability, with efforts extending from sourcing, materials and manufacturing to energy efficiency and packaging. The company makes a range of efficient appliances in their factory in Slovenia, as the fourth largest appliance manufacturer in Europe. In talking with one of their product people, they said that one of the main ways that they foster sustainability is by improving the performance of electrified options, including high-output induction cooktops and electric pizza ovens. While many in the US are not familiar with Gorenje, they are part of Hisense, and also manufacture for several other brands. If you buy an appliance made in Slovenia, there is a good chance that it was made by Gorenje.

Midea highlighted the switch to R290 refrigerant (propane) for their heat pumps, which is far more environmentally friendly than many traditional refrigerants. However, while they gave it the most attention, they were not alone. Europe appears to be transitioning to R290 rapidly.

Chigo/iCongo also showed off their R290 air conditioners, with sustainability-focused messaging. The brand claims 30% energy savings thanks to “AI-powered dynamic adjustments.” That is an impressive claimed efficiency improvement that I would like to see further test results to support.

While heat pumps were dominant, Eurom displayed their infrared home heaters. While not as efficient as heat pumps on a per-BTU basis, these heaters can invisibly radiate long-wavelength infrared onto the surfaces where it is needed. Like how the sun warms the earth. For example, the heaters could be focused on a seating area in an open concept living room, providing a level of comfort while not having to heat all the air in the entire room or entire home. As such, an entire home could be kept at a lower overall temperature, while the areas with occupants could be heated with infrared. Integrating sensors and intelligence could extend the concept. It was an interesting idea that has some potential.

Moving on to materials, REEDEE displayed recycled TPU and PET plastic films to be used as screen protectors. While many people put plastics into recycling bins, they often end up in the landfill or are burned anyway. Providing paths to recycle plastics reduces both pollution and the amount of plastic needed in the first place.

Gforest, or Ningbo Green Forest Electronic Technology, manufactures a range of products, often for white label. They had their food recyclers on display, which break down and dry food to be used in a garden, utilizing a high-efficiency heater. In addition, they showed off mister fans that use a fine spray of water to cool evaporatively. While not an outright replacement for air conditioning, they can provide needed relief when it is not available. Especially in many European homes, where air conditioning is not common, but periods of extreme heat are increasing in prevalence and intensity. One current model places a fan on top of a water tank. However, they also showed off a prototype that adds misting capability to an adhesive puck that can mount to the center of an existing fan case, with a water tank that attaches to the central pole. It is a simple idea, but people would not need to buy a new fan, and they could put off investing in energy-intensive air conditioning a little longer. Not all clean technology needs to be complicated.

Beyond the new technology, there was also some attention to repairing existing electronics. Repartly offered parts and repair of electronics and appliances, available within Germany. This can make repairs faster and more affordable, while reducing shipping costs and emissions. Although you likely would not want to keep an inefficient model for an extended time, by repairing electronics, rather than throwing them away, the embodied energy needed for manufacturing is reduced, while waste management becomes less of a challenge.

In terms of EVs, beyond XPENG and Xiaomi, Volkswagen had their new ID.Polo and ID.Cross on display. The ID.Polo model gets back to their design roots and looked attractive, if not groundbreaking. While the ID.Cross enters the fiercely competitive crossover segment, the smaller ID.Polo could prove to be popular on the tight roads of Europe. If you needed something even smaller, Volkswagen also licensed their brand to an e-bike available for test rides.

Overall, even in markets where sustainability isn’t the primary focus, there are many ways it can be integrated into products and services. From major brands to regional manufacturers. From material suppliers to repair and recycling. There isn’t one silver bullet that will provide a single simple solution to all our challenges. However, the diversity of approaches also creates a diversity of ways to make an impact. IFA, which stands for Innovation For All, demonstrates that all of us have an opportunity to engage with sustainable innovations, through our businesses, our purchases and how we live our lives.

name: Clean Energy
title: Mapped: the £150bn megaproject that aims to protect Britain from energy shocks
authors: Alex Clark, Jillian Ambrose, Ashley Kirk, Tom Calverley
description:
Household energy bills are to rise in the short term to pay for the grid transformation, at a time when politicians are pledging cost-of-living support.
Grid upgrades will be largely paid for through household energy bills, coming on top of electricity prices that have risen sharply after global energy shocks.
Some argue there are ways to reduce the sharpness of this investment “hump” through a different approach to grid upgrades.
Neso forecasts full decarbonisation would have a sizable benefit: shielding against energy shocks.
It has modelled the hypothetical impact of a 2022-style energy shock after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on a fully decarbonised energy system in the UK.
text:
Britain is embarking on one of the largest overhauls of its electricity grid in generations – a megaproject in which five times more infrastructure will be built by 2030 than was constructed during the previous three decades.

Tens of billions of pounds are being spent on new pylons, subsea cables and converter stations to connect a growing fleet of wind and solar farms and carry clean power to where it is needed.

It comes after successive global shocks – Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, then the Iran war – have exposed the vulnerability of the UK’s energy system to international market volatility and galvanised plans to bolster domestic low-carbon generation.

The cost of electricity in the UK has surged in recent years, far beyond that of comparable countries, largely because expensive gas-fired generation sets the price most of the time.

This volatility has accelerated efforts to transition away from fossil fuels, in the hope homegrown renewables can shield UK households from future shocks.

Yet that green drive is now being limited by Britain’s ageing grid, which, after decades of underinvestment, is often unable to transmit the new energy being generated.

“If we don’t have enough transmission network capacity, we won’t be able to make full use of renewable energy resources. We will then be more dependent on fossil fuels, with greater vulnerability to fossil fuel price shocks and higher CO2 emissions,” said Keith Bell, professor of electronic and electrical engineering at the University of Strathclyde.

Unblocking these bottlenecks will require well over 4,000 miles of new power lines by 2041, alongside significant improvements to cables already in place, Guardian analysis of official recommendations shows.

Much of that expansion will be visible, cutting across the countryside and bringing construction to rural communities along the way. It has prompted protests, with some residents claiming they face an “energy invasion” owing to the scale of the planned infrastructure.

Household energy bills are to rise in the short term to pay for the grid transformation, at a time when politicians are pledging cost-of-living support.

Britain’s National Energy System Operator (Neso) recently estimated that £64bn of investment will be needed for transmission projects by 2030 and a further £89bn beyond that – more than £150bn, which will be largely paid for by surcharges on household bills.

While these investments will eventually help lower costs by reducing reliance on expensive gas generation, on Friday the National Audit Office warned the government that dozens of grid projects risked delay, potentially placing further strain on consumers.

But a failure to build also has costs – as the below visual explainer sets out.

Grid upgrades will be largely paid for through household energy bills, coming on top of electricity prices that have risen sharply after global energy shocks.

The energy regulator Ofgem has announced that the energy bill price cap will rise by 4% from October to its highest level in three years, driven by increases in wholesale gas prices.

On the day of the price cap announcement, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, was challenged about whether “the drive towards net zero” was also costing people more. She replied: “Absolutely not.”

But Fahnbulleh went on to acknowledge that paying for upgrades would be unavoidable, saying: “For a decade and a half, under the last government, we didn’t invest in our energy system, we didn’t invest in the grid, and we’re going to have to deal with that. So for the grid to operate properly, we’ve got to upgrade it.”

Andy Burnham has attempted to reduce energy bills since entering Downing Street, with his first big policy announcement being a cut to VAT on them from 5% to 0%.

In the absence of further government intervention, rising network costs will soon add an extra £130 to a typical household’s energy bills by 2030, according to one forecast.

Ofgem has pointed out that households would still be paying more by 2030 if grid upgrades were not undertaken, due to the cost of curtailing renewables.

“While upgrades will require investment, failing to invest would also increase costs for consumers through higher constraint and balancing payments caused by grid bottlenecks,” a spokesperson said.

Many experts also agree that spending more on grid upgrades now alongside growing the UK’s low-carbon power capacity will lead to lower energy costs in the future.

Neso forecasts that full decarbonisation that meets the UK’s net zero targets could lead to energy spending falling from more than 10% of gross domestic product to less than 5% by 2050, owing to the wider use of cheaper renewables and lower waste.

Spending falls further than in a scenario with far less decarbonisation, in which the UK falls short its legally binding 2050 target, though it is initially higher because of the investment needed to increase renewable capacity.

Some argue there are ways to reduce the sharpness of this investment “hump” through a different approach to grid upgrades.

The Conservatives recently claimed transmission costs could be reduced by focusing on a smaller number of large nuclear and gas plants over many renewable sites, in turn reducing the number of new cables.

Others dispute those findings, pointing out that emissions would be higher – building nuclear sites requires large upfront costs and has proven to be difficult in recent years – and that gas prices are likely to exceed the assumptions used in their analysis.

Neso forecasts full decarbonisation would have a sizable benefit: shielding against energy shocks.

It has modelled the hypothetical impact of a 2022-style energy shock after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on a fully decarbonised energy system in the UK.

The original shock cost an extra 1.8% of GDP – equivalent to tens of billions of pounds. In a full net zero transition scenario it would have been closer to an extra 0.3%, more than six times smaller.

“Our analysis suggests that delivering net zero by 2050 could halve energy-related spending, whilst also providing greater protection from global price spikes in the process,” a Neso spokesperson said.

However, experts say getting to that point will require more than just new cabling projects.

“Transmission is only one piece of the puzzle, though – greater storage, demand flexibility, and potentially green hydrogen production would all help drive down curtailment costs and cut dependence on expensive gas,” said Collett-White.

“A better, not just bigger, grid should be the goal.”

With the geopolitical landscape looking increasingly turbulent, ministers may be convinced that making households pay for a better grid – and the protection it affords – will be worth it in the end.

A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Decades of underinvestment in the grid has left us overexposed to fossil fuel markets and unable to realise the full potential of clean, homegrown energy to lower bills for households.

“That’s why we’re building a decarbonised energy system that can bring down bills for good.”

A spokesperson for National Grid said: “Investment in upgrading the grid is supporting jobs, skills, and supply chains across Britain, while creating opportunities and benefits for local communities.

“We work closely with local people, consult extensively, and consider all technology options as we develop proposals for the infrastructure needed to support a secure energy future.”

title: Hyvolution 2026: Hitachi Energy highlights energy planning for green hydrogen growth in Chile
description:
The minister detailed that the 2026-2030 Energy Roadmap translated this conviction into verifiable commitments.
"None of these announcements will produce a single metric ton of green hydrogen on its own, but together they determine whether that metric ton is produced here," she said.
“The most important aspect right now is that the factors hindering this industry's development have been evaluated extensively and consistently.
The current stage involves resolving these barriers to advance execution more dynamically,” says Vivianne Blanlot, president of Hyvolution Chile 2026.
One of the standout panels was "R&D+i on H2 and derivatives: advances in Chile and the world," moderated by Rowena Moreno, a member of Corfo's Green Hydrogen Committee.
text:
If the focus of Hyvolution Chile 2025 was laying the foundations for public policy, geopolitics, and attracting global investments, this year, the goal of Latin America's most important international green hydrogen and clean energy congress is moving to action, to project execution, financial viability, and the materialization of technologies on the ground.

Energy minister Ximena Rincón noted that while the country has unbeatable advantages for the sector, the challenge today is to turn tangible initiatives into reality with clear regulations, reasonable permit timelines, and a real impact on local employment and community wellbeing.

The minister detailed that the 2026-2030 Energy Roadmap translated this conviction into verifiable commitments. She highlighted the creation of an interministerial table for strategic energy investment to unblock timelines, the launch of a territorial logistics program for Magallanes, and the incorporation of the first hydrogen-powered bus assembled in Chile into the metropolitan transportation system by 2027.

"None of these announcements will produce a single metric ton of green hydrogen on its own, but together they determine whether that metric ton is produced here," she said.

“The most important aspect right now is that the factors hindering this industry's development have been evaluated extensively and consistently. The current stage involves resolving these barriers to advance execution more dynamically,” says Vivianne Blanlot, president of Hyvolution Chile 2026.

Meanwhile, Electricity and Fuels superintendent Marta Cabeza praised the role each actor is playing in the industry's takeoff. “Everyone involved, from civil society and the public sector to academia, contributes to developing this technology, which serves as a vital input for the country,” she said.

Matching supply with demand

In its fourth edition, Hyvolution Chile 2026 featured 15 main panels spread across the three days of the event, alongside keynotes, technical talks, sectoral agreement signings, and side events like the H2 Grand Prix, which involved students from technical and vocational institutions.

One of the standout panels was "R&D+i on H2 and derivatives: advances in Chile and the world," moderated by Rowena Moreno, a member of Corfo's Green Hydrogen Committee. Alongside experts and academic representatives, the panel included Leticia Frata, Sales Manager for Power Consulting at Hitachi Energy Brazil, the company's consulting unit that conducts feasibility studies and advises sector stakeholders on the electrical connection of their green hydrogen plants.

“Each project has specific characteristics and must therefore be structured from the prefeasibility stage, considering proper equipment sizing and grid integration studies,” says Moreno.

“Initiatives are being pushed forward quickly due to high expectations, but we have focused on having the product without ensuring we have the necessary input,” says Javier Quispe, director of the Department of Chemical Engineering at the Universidad Católica del Norte in Antofagasta. “Several projects have been developed, such as the Antofagasta locomotive, which requires hydrogen compressed at 350 bar, or vehicles requiring 700 bar, while current standard plant production exists at 30 bar.”

Leticia Frata says anticipating challenges related to power stability and quality is essential for selecting the most appropriate solutions, reducing risks, and supporting decisions that balance reliability, CAPEX, opex, and commercial viability. “In Brazil today, we have a project evaluating the origin of CO2, its quality, quantity, cost, and distance; evaluating all of this early on is crucial to guide investment decisions,” adding that this working experience can and likely will be replicated in the Chilean market.

Frata's statements align with the industry's transformation. This development is reflected in the international congress itself, which, starting in 2027, will be named Energyvolution, broadening its technological umbrella into a platform that more widely includes electrification, storage, new fuels, and renewable energies; aligned with Hitachi Energy's solutions for the energy transition, the executive said.

title: A 1,014-megawatt nuclear plant on the Finnish coast is pulling the casings and internals out ...
description:
“Tech company signs a deal with a nuclear plant” is basically its own genre now.
While a unit is down, crews are pulling the casings and the internals out of its low-pressure turbines.
This is the part I’d want explained if I were reading it cold, so here it is: a nuclear plant has two halves, and only one of them is nuclear.
All of it has to work for the 38 megawatts to show up.
The 38 megawatts are different.
text:
“Tech company signs a deal with a nuclear plant” is basically its own genre now. You’ve read a few of them, and they tend to land the same way: somebody needs electricity for AI, a reactor needs money, and everybody puts out a statement about the future of clean energy. Google signed another one in Finland on September 9, and I nearly scrolled straight past it.

Then I looked at what’s happening inside the plant this month, and that turned out to be the good part.

The plant is Loviisa, on the southeastern coast of Finland, about 62 miles from Helsinki. It’s been in its annual maintenance outage since August 2 and it won’t be fully back until October 18, which is a long one even by its own schedule. Fortum, the utility that owns it, takes the two units down one at a time so one of them keeps generating. While a unit is down, crews are pulling the casings and the internals out of its low-pressure turbines.

All eight of them are being replaced.

So what does eight new turbine casings buy you?

About 38 megawatts, and Fortum expects them to be live in 2028. The plant puts out 1,014 megawatts today from two reactors of 507 megawatts each, so the upgrade is worth roughly 3.7% more electricity.

The reactors get none of the credit. This is the part I’d want explained if I were reading it cold, so here it is: a nuclear plant has two halves, and only one of them is nuclear. The reactor boils water. The steam runs down into the turbine hall, spins a high-pressure turbine and then a set of low-pressure ones, and whatever energy the blades fail to catch on the way through ends up as warm seawater. Sharpen the blades and the tolerances, and you catch more of the same steam.

Fortum says the modernization is limited to the turbine island and has no impact on reactor operations or nuclear safety. The reactor keeps making the same heat it makes now. The plant just wastes less of it.

Over the current license period, that moves Fortum’s expected generation from 170 terawatt-hours to 177. The work is being delivered by Doosan Škoda Power, the Czech turbine builder that also supplied Loviisa’s high-pressure turbines in an earlier round of this, and it’s being fitted in stages during the 2026, 2027 and 2028 outages.

Adding capacity by machining better parts for a plant you already own is an unglamorous way to do it. It’s also, I’d guess, a fair bit cheaper per megawatt than anything anyone is building from scratch in Europe right now.

The rest of the turbine hall is coming apart too

The turbines are the headline job, but there are more than ten major projects packed into this outage, and around 1,000 contractor workers on site to get through them.

Valmet, a Finnish company, is replacing the turbine protection and control systems on both units along with the actuators that carry out their instructions. The generator auxiliary systems are being modernized at the same time, which gives the control room live monitoring it didn’t have before.

Then there are the pumps. Each unit has four main seawater pumps, so eight in total, and Andritz of Austria is replacing the lot. Those pumps push cold Baltic water through the condensers, where the steam that has already been through the turbines gets chilled back into water and sent around the loop again. Fortum says the existing pumps and motors are approaching the end of their technical life.

None of that adds a megawatt on its own. All of it has to work for the 38 megawatts to show up.

Why rip out parts that still run?

Fortum’s stated reason is partly age and partly supply. Some components are near the end of their technical life cycle, which makes spares harder to find. And the company says changes in the operating environment and geopolitical developments have increased uncertainty about support and spare parts from some of the original equipment suppliers.

Fortum doesn’t name a country in that sentence, and I don’t think it needs to. Loviisa’s two VVER-440 reactors, the turbines and the generators were bought from the Soviet Union. The safety systems, control systems and automation came from the West, and the steel containment and its ice condensers were built under Westinghouse licenses. It has been a hybrid machine since it was built, and the eastern half of the parts catalog got complicated.

The fuel went the same way. Fortum has been loading Westinghouse-made assemblies into unit 2 during recent outages and is doing it again in this one, and in April it joined three other European utilities in an agreement with France’s Framatome to develop a fully European fuel for VVER-type reactors.

Sasu Valkamo, who runs the Loviisa plant for Fortum, said the outage will “again ensure uninterrupted electricity production for the coming year.”

What the search company actually bought

Google’s agreement runs 22 years. It starts in 2028 with a smaller volume and scales to half of Loviisa’s capacity from 2030 through 2049, and it’s the company’s first nuclear power deal outside the United States. Alongside it, Google said it will put €13 billion, about $15 billion, into data centers and supporting infrastructure in Finland across 2027 and 2028, at Hamina, Muhos, Vaala and Kajaani. Loviisa sits about 34 miles from that Hamina campus.

What Fortum gets is predictable revenue, and it needs some. The program to keep the plant running to 2050 is costed at about €1 billion, roughly $1.15 billion, and around 80% of the projects in it, worth some €700 million, still have no investment decision behind them. Fortum’s own line is that without the lifetime extension work, Loviisa couldn’t run past 2030 at all.

The two reactors first pushed power into the Finnish grid in 1977 and 1980, and their original operating licenses ran out at the end of 2027 and 2030. The Finnish government relicensed both units to the end of 2050 in February 2023, which is why there’s anything here to extend in the first place.

So where does the extra 10 megawatts come from?

Fortum hasn’t said, and I can’t find a hardware answer anywhere in the announcement. The company states that the deal is expected to enable a new 10 megawatt increase on top of the 38 already under way, and leaves it there. My guess is that it lands wherever the remaining €700 million of undecided projects lands, but that’s a guess and you should treat it as one.

The 38 megawatts are different. That work is contracted, the first casings are being fitted right now, and it doesn’t depend on anyone’s AI forecast holding up.

Fortum says the outage ends on October 18, the turbine work carries on through the 2027 and 2028 outages, and the extra 38 megawatts should be on the grid in 2028. The license it’s all aimed at expires at the end of 2050.

What electricity costs in Louisiana

The EIA’s published residential average for Louisiana is 13.49 cents per kWh (June 2026), against a US average of 18.34. That puts Louisiana at 4th of 51 states and DC, cheapest first — the cheaper half of the country. For the Volkswagen ID.4 Pro, the median of the 15 EPA-rated cars here at 29.8 kWh per 100 miles measured at the wall, that is $4.02 per 100 miles, $45 a month at 1,125 miles and $543 a year.

Home charging stops beating petrol once electricity passes about 51 cents per kWh at $4.07 a gallon and 27 mpg. Louisiana is below that line by 37.09 cents, so the saving holds at the state-average rate before any overnight tariff is applied. The rate is an average across every household and every hour of the month; a time-of-use plan with an overnight window will beat it, a summer peak will not. Put your own tariff into the running-cost calculator for a figure that is yours rather than the state’s.

Every EPA-rated car, charged at home in Louisiana

Same rate, one row per car. The order never changes from state to state because efficiency belongs to the car; what Louisiana decides is how much the choice is worth. Here the gap between the most efficient car, the Hyundai Ioniq 6 Long Range RWD, and the least, the Rivian R1T Dual Motor, Large pack, is $26 a month.

These are the EPA combined figures from fueleconomy.gov, which are measured at the socket and so already include the energy lost in the charger and cable — a figure worked out from battery size and range instead would understate the bill by roughly a tenth. The four cars in the database without a US rating (the European-market Teslas, the BYD Seal and the VW ID.7) are on the national state-by-state page in kilometres.

Public fast charging does not follow the residential rate. At a typical network price of $0.48 per kWh the median car costs $14.30 per 100 miles — 3.6 times the cost of charging it at home in Louisiana, and still under the $15.07 the petrol car spends on the same 100 miles. Louisiana against its neighbours

How long the charge itself takes does not change with the state, only what it costs: the Ford Mustang Mach-E charging time, BMW i4 charging time and Porsche Taycan charging time are 32, 28 and 19 minutes from 10 to 80 per cent wherever you plug in, and each of those pages runs the same cost arithmetic as this one at the national average rate rather than Louisiana’s.

title: BRICS Summit foregrounds clean tech cooperation, value addition – says CSE
description:
As in previous declarations, the continued role of fossil fuels in energy systems reiterates BRICS’ position on prioritising energy security within the transition.
“Taken together, the bloc appears to be organising around competitiveness and forwarding a shared agenda in clean technology manufacturing for the Global South,” Dev adds.
Given that we are in mid-transition, BRICS countries have chosen to pursue the ambitious goal of shaping their green industrial futures and their position in global green value chains.
Who controls, produces and can access clean technologies and minerals needed for the transition will shape how quickly countries can switch from fossil-based to low-carbon infrastructure.
The New Delhi Declaration shows that the BRICS countries have their eye on this larger goal.”
text:
New Delhi Declaration shows that the BRICS countries have their eyes on the larger goal of prioritising energy security within the transition

New Delhi, September 13, 2026: The 18th BRICS Summit, underway in New Delhi, has issued a Declaration which covers a wide range of climate issues -- from clean technology to forests -- and reaffirms the group’s commitment to the multilateral regime: the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement. Commenting on the proceedings, Avantika Goswami, programme manager of the Climate Change and Green Economy unit at Centre for Science and Environment (CSE), says: “The BRICS nations comprise a diverse mix of developing and emerging countries with growing energy needs, industrialisation aspirations and multiple development challenges -- it is unlikely that we will hear a fossil fuel phase-out declaration any time soon.”

The Declaration calls for “just, orderly, equitable, and inclusive energy transitions” foregrounding diversified energy sources and resilient value chains. As in previous declarations, the continued role of fossil fuels in energy systems reiterates BRICS’ position on prioritising energy security within the transition.

Goswami adds: “However, BRICS’ rapidly growing adoption of clean technologies like solar energy and electric vehicles positions the bloc well to aim higher and aspire for a faster transition rather than lock in vast amounts of fossil fuel infrastructure. BRICS nations are already generating more than half of the world’s solar power. Doubling down on scaling up renewable energy and economy-wide decarbonisation is the need of the hour -- not only to cut emissions, but also to shield from volatility and supply disruptions like those precipitated by the Hormuz crisis.”

Hosted by the Government of India, the Summit has seen leaders from major emerging economies such as China, Iran, Indonesia, UAE and Ethiopia -- as well as Russia (which is a member of the grouping) – in attendance. It has been held at a crucial moment when the Global South leadership on climate ambition tailored to national circumstances, clean technology and innovation, and industrial strength is more evident than ever before.

The Summit Declaration addresses a number of barriers to scaling up climate action: high debt burdens, unequal governance of Bretton Woods Institutions, and climate funding gaps, especially for adaptation.

On trade, the bloc has reiterated its objection to climate-linked trade measures, expressing opposition to unilateral, punitive, discriminatory and protectionist measures, explicitly naming carbon border adjustment mechanisms.

“The opposition to unilateral climate-linked trade measures must be seen alongside the call for a broader and equitable cooperation between developing countries in global higher value manufacturing,” says Trishant Dev, deputy programme manager, Climate Change and Green Economy unit, CSE.

The Declaration adopts a Terms of Reference and Action Plan for the BRICS photovoltaic industry working group, opens a workstream on low-emission hydrogen, sets principles for smart grids and storage, and commits to global value chain action plans aimed at helping developing countries move up the value chain. The Declaration also talks about fair competition in renewable energy markets.

“Taken together, the bloc appears to be organising around competitiveness and forwarding a shared agenda in clean technology manufacturing for the Global South,” Dev adds.

The lack of lofty climate promises, therefore, does not necessarily signal a lack of ambition. Given that we are in mid-transition, BRICS countries have chosen to pursue the ambitious goal of shaping their green industrial futures and their position in global green value chains.

Goswami points out that “this, in some ways, could prove to be a more concrete commitment to decarbonisation than traditional emission-cutting goals. Who controls, produces and can access clean technologies and minerals needed for the transition will shape how quickly countries can switch from fossil-based to low-carbon infrastructure. The New Delhi Declaration shows that the BRICS countries have their eye on this larger goal.”

text:
WASHINGTON — In a defeat for the Trump administration, a federal court on Friday ruled that the Energy Department exceeded its authority when it forced a Michigan coal-fired power plant to stay open past its scheduled retirement date last year.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright had said the 64-year-old J.H. Campbell Generating Plant was needed to ensure reliable electricity in the region, and he used emergency powers to keep it operating. Environmental groups and three states — Michigan, Illinois and Minnesota — went to court to try to overturn orders keeping the plant online.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit sided with the states and the groups, saying there was no real emergency under the law.

The section of the Federal Power Act that allows emergency orders “is essentially a narrow, last-resort backstop,” Appeals Court Judge Cornelia Pillard wrote for a unanimous three-judge panel. Use of emergency authority “is triggered only when there is a need for immediate, essentially last-resort action and the circumstances require action by DOE in particular, as opposed to action by the state or states responsible for resource adequacy,” she added.

Reversing the Campbell plant’s “long and carefully planned retirement” is “disruptive,” Pillard wrote.

Trump administration order called ‘unlawful political stunt’ by critics

Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel said she was relieved the appeals court “threw out DOE’s order that had zero basis in reality.”

Nessel, a Democrat, said her office “has been fighting this unlawful political stunt at every turn, and this ruling proves what we have been saying all along: this administration does not get to invent fake emergencies to bypass the rule of law against the best interests of Michigan residents.”

The Michigan case is one of several legal disputes that have emerged across the country as the Trump administration uses emergency powers to force a half-dozen coal-fired plants to remain open.

Administration officials were undeterred by Friday’s court ruling and just hours later Wright announced another emergency order to keep online a coal plant in Centralia, Washington. That plant, operated by TransAlta, had been scheduled to shut down at the end of 2025.

The orders, which also apply to plants in Indiana, Colorado and Florida, are raising ratepayer bills and adding air and water pollution that could have been avoided, critics say. An oil and gas plant in Pennsylvania was also ordered to keep its turbines running as a hedge against electricity shortages in the mid-Atlantic grid.

President Donald Trump declared a national energy emergency in a January 2025 executive order, citing demand increases from artificial intelligence and data center growth.

Energy Department says coal-plant order saved lives during peak weather events

An Energy Department spokesperson said the emergency orders — including at Campbell — “prevented blackouts and likely saved hundreds of lives during peak capacity events this past year,” especially severe winter storms in late January and early February.

At the peak of the storms, coal generation in affected regions increased by 25% compared to the previous year, spokeswoman Emily Matthews said. The Campbell plant provided over 650 megawatts — enough power for hundreds of thousands of homes — every day from Jan. 21 to Feb. 1, she said.

The Energy Department “will continue to protect and defend energy security for all Americans,” she said.

Keeping the Michigan plant open beyond its May 2025 retirement has cost about $259 million so far, according to new financial filings. Those losses will likely be paid by families and businesses in the Midwest, opponents of the order say.

Consumers Energy, which operates the Campbell plant, said it was reviewing the court ruling. In the meantime, the utility will keep the plant operating under terms of a recent DOE order that extends its directive through mid-November, spokesman Brian Wheeler said in a statement.

Environmentalists say they’ll continue to fight the administration’s orders

Ted Kelly, U.S. clean energy director at the Environmental Defense Fund, said the court ruling rejected the Trump administration’s nationwide effort to force “unreliable, aging coal plants that are bleeding money and polluting communities to stay online.”

The Energy Department’s “unlawful actions attempted to make families and businesses in the Midwest wastefully pay hundreds of millions of dollars for a coal plant that should have been shut down over a year ago,” Kelly said Friday. The Campbell plant and other aging sites are “incredibly expensive, dangerous to our health and break down frequently,” he said.

Sanjay Narayan, a lawyer for the Sierra Club, called the ruling a victory for families across the Midwest who are “paying to keep this old, expensive and dirty power plant online.”

The Trump administration “has been pulling out all the stops to try to bolster dirty and expensive fossil fuels at public expense. This reckless agenda will not succeed,” Narayan said. “We will continue to fight back against the other illegal extensions across the country.”
