title: How To Know It's Time To Replace Your EV Battery - Yahoo Autos
description:
An electric vehicle battery doesn't have a universal age or mileage at which it suddenly needs replacing.
Gradual range loss doesn't automatically mean the battery is failing Some loss of usable battery capacity is expected over time.
This recent look at EV battery lifespan goes deeper into how modern packs are aging.
Tesla, for example, documents high-voltage battery alerts that can reduce maximum charge level and range when the car detects certain internal battery conditions.
If your EV otherwise works normally, gradual range loss alone is not a reason to replace the battery.
text:
An electric vehicle battery doesn't have a universal age or mileage at which it suddenly needs replacing. The high-voltage traction battery that powers the motors gradually loses some of its ability to store energy as it ages, which can reduce driving range without meaning the pack has failed.

Complete battery failure is also relatively uncommon in newer EVs. A Department of Energy analysis of about 15,000 plug-in vehicles found that 1.5 percent had batteries replaced because of failure, excluding recalls. Replacement rates were below 1 percent for every model year from 2016 through 2023.

The useful question, then, isn't whether your EV has lost any range. It is whether the changes you're seeing look like normal battery aging or a problem that needs professional diagnosis.

Read more: Are remote car starters still worth it in 2026?

Gradual range loss doesn't automatically mean the battery is failing

Some loss of usable battery capacity is expected over time. The Department of Energy estimates that today's EV batteries may last 12 to 15 years in moderate climates and eight to 12 years in extreme climates. Actual lifespan varies with battery chemistry, temperature, charging habits and how the vehicle is used.

A 2026 Geotab analysis covering more than 22,700 EVs across 21 models found average battery degradation of 2.3 percent per year, although individual vehicles can age faster or slower.

Battery state of health, often shortened to SOH, describes how much usable energy the pack can hold compared with when it was new. A lower state of health generally means less available range, but the number of miles displayed on your dashboard isn't a direct measurement of battery health.

Temperature, cabin heating and cooling, highway speeds, acceleration, hills and extra weight can all change how far an EV travels on a charge. Cold weather alone can produce a noticeable temporary drop. If your range suddenly looks worse, there are several ways to get more range out of your EV before assuming the battery itself is the problem.

What deserves more attention is a persistent decline under comparable conditions. If the same commute in similar weather repeatedly uses much more of the battery than it did before, degradation becomes a more plausible explanation. This recent look at EV battery lifespan goes deeper into how modern packs are aging.

Battery warnings and sudden changes are stronger signs of trouble

Gradual capacity loss is different from an abrupt change in how the car behaves. A sharp and unexplained drop in available range, a new limit on how much the battery will charge or reduced vehicle performance deserve more attention, particularly when it arrives alongside a battery or high-voltage-system warning.

The exact symptoms vary by vehicle. Tesla, for example, documents high-voltage battery alerts that can reduce maximum charge level and range when the car detects certain internal battery conditions. Its owner documentation tells drivers to schedule service if the relevant alert persists.

Other automakers use different warnings, so there's no universal dashboard symbol that means the battery needs replacing. What matters is that the car can detect internal battery faults that a driver can't diagnose from range alone.

Charging speed is similarly weak evidence on its own. Battery temperature, state of charge, charger power and the vehicle's charging curve can all slow a session, so a persistent slowdown matters more when it appears alongside a warning or another unexplained change.

Get the battery diagnosed before replacing the whole pack

If an EV is reporting a battery fault or has lost enough usable capacity to interfere with normal driving, the next step is a battery-health check. An EV-qualified service center can read diagnostic codes and battery data to determine whether the car has ordinary degradation, a repairable fault or a problem that calls for complete pack replacement.

Check the battery warranty before assuming the repair will be an out-of-pocket expense. Some EV manufacturers provide separate long-term coverage for the traction battery, although the mileage limits, duration and capacity guarantees vary by model.

If the entire pack needs replacing outside warranty, the cost can be substantial. Recurrent's survey puts many replacements at roughly $5,000 to $16,000, although pack size, vehicle design, labor and available replacement parts can push individual bills outside that range. A diagnosis may also uncover a smaller repair instead of a full-pack replacement.

Replacing an EV traction battery isn't a normal DIY project. The high-voltage pack requires specialized procedures, tools and protective equipment, so opening or removing it belongs with trained technicians.

If your EV otherwise works normally, gradual range loss alone is not a reason to replace the battery. A persistent warning, sudden unexplained change or range that no longer meets your needs is a reason to get the pack tested before deciding what comes next.

title: Explainer: How Laos' role as Southeast Asia's 'battery' is changing | News - Eco-Business
description:
In the long run, Cambodia aims to continue importing power from Laos at a stable level, according to its Power Development Plan of 2022.
But it hopes to eventually expand power sharing with Laos through one of the region’s most ambitious plans: a power grid connecting the member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean).
From Laos, energy largely created by hydropower is sent through Thailand, which acts as a “wheeler” country to send electricity through to Malaysia and subsequently Singapore.
The city-state began importing 100 MW from this system in 2022, making the LTMS-PIP’s first multilateral cross-border electricity trade through four Asean countries – all from Laos’ hydropower dams.
But Chinese involvement in Laos’ hydropower sector stretches back two decades.
text:
In the long run, Cambodia aims to continue importing power from Laos at a stable level, according to its Power Development Plan of 2022. This is expected to increase to around 3 GW by 2030 and remain the same until 2040.

But it hopes to eventually expand power sharing with Laos through one of the region’s most ambitious plans: a power grid connecting the member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean). The initiative, which has been in the works since 1997, is a plan to eventually share energy across all members of the bloc, in both mainland and maritime Southeast Asia.

In May 2026, the Asean Centre for Energy, Electricité du Cambodge and Electricité du Laos signed a joint study framework to advance cross-border connections, as part of a phased approach to advancing the Asean Power Grid. The framework involves collaboration on technical assessments, economic analysis and preliminary environmental assessments for future projects.

Laos and Cambodia took a major step towards regional grid interconnectivity in 2023 when they launched a high-capacity China-built 500-kilovolt transmission line linking a substation in Champasak province in south-western Laos to its border with Cambodia.

Malaysia and Singapore: End of the line?

Neither Malaysia nor Singapore share a border with Laos, so the Laos-Thailand-Malaysia-Singapore Power Integration Project (LTMS-PIP), launched in 2022, has been hailed as a broad advancement for the Asean Power Grid.

From Laos, energy largely created by hydropower is sent through Thailand, which acts as a “wheeler” country to send electricity through to Malaysia and subsequently Singapore. The city-state began importing 100 MW from this system in 2022, making the LTMS-PIP’s first multilateral cross-border electricity trade through four Asean countries – all from Laos’ hydropower dams.

The capacity of tradable electricity was increased to 200 MW in the project’s second phase, launched in January 2026. This phase introduced multidirectional electricity trading, with Singapore importing the additional 100 MW from Malaysia.

Imported hydropower from Laos is part of how Singapore seeks to achieve its climate goals, but experts have raised concerns about the environmental impacts of Lao and Mekong dams, noting that it is more than just counting carbon.

Nevertheless, Singapore’s energy needs are helping to drive the Asean Power Grid ever further as the Sarawak to Singapore undersea connection is expected to have some engineering design studies complete by end-2026. The hydropower produced for export will come from Malaysian Borneo, with the project estimated to transmit a proposed 1 GW of energy by around 2035.

China: The battery’s builder

In April, the China-Laos cross-border power transmission line began operations, opening China’s domestic electricity market to Laos’ renewable energy generators. But Chinese involvement in Laos’ hydropower sector stretches back two decades.

Today, many of Laos’ planned and completed Mekong mainstream hydropower dams have some involvement from Chinese companies, from ownership to loans and development at different levels. Major dam projects Pak Beng and Sanakham cost at least US$2 billion each to build and are majority-owned by Chinese companies, while others like Don Sahong and Pak Lay have Chinese infrastructure developers.

title: Federal Court Rules Trump Admin Can't Keep Aging Michigan Coal Plant Open | Truthout
authors: Zack Kligler, Kate Yoder, Derek Seidman, Nayanika Guha, Schuyler Mitchell, Kelly Hayes, Adam Mahoney, Shireen Akram-Boshar, Chris Walker, Amy Goodman
description:
The Department of Energy overstepped when it ordered an aging coal-fired power plant in Michigan to stay open past its planned retirement date last year, a federal court ruled on Friday.
This ruling represents one of the first successful legal challenges to how the administration has used its “energy emergency” powers.
“You can say there’s an ‘energy emergency’ as much as you want — even if you’re the president,” Kelly said.
Since it was forced to stay open, it has emitted 1,000 tons of nitrogen oxides, 2,000 tons of sulfur dioxide, and 140 tons of particulate matter as of the end of June.
Kelly hopes that the Trump administration voluntarily backs down, or if that doesn’t happen, that the court could force a shutdown.
text:
The Department of Energy overstepped when it ordered an aging coal-fired power plant in Michigan to stay open past its planned retirement date last year, a federal court ruled on Friday.

The J.H Campbell plant is one of seven fossil fuel plants around the country that the Trump administration has forced to stay in operation, despite the pollution they cause and the enormous costs of keeping them online. Just before it was about to close last May, Trump’s Energy Department invoked short-term emergency powers under the Federal Power Act to keep the 64-year-old plant running, arguing that the threat of outages, along with the need for more energy to power data centers, constituted an emergency. But the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit rejected that argument, with Appeals Court Judge Cornelia Pillard writing that the emergency statute “is essentially a narrow, last-resort backstop.”

When he declared a “national energy emergency” on his first day in office in 2025, President Donald Trump instructed federal agencies to use whatever emergency powers they had to increase energy production — specifically for fossil fuels. This ruling represents one of the first successful legal challenges to how the administration has used its “energy emergency” powers.

It doesn’t overturn the idea that there is an energy emergency, said Ted Kelly, director and lead counsel for U.S. Clean Energy at the Environmental Defense Fund, one group involved in the lawsuit. But it does limit its practical implications.

“You can say there’s an ‘energy emergency’ as much as you want — even if you’re the president,” Kelly said. “But what you can actually do depends on what the real facts on the ground are and what the law actually lets you do in different situations.”

Of all of the coal plants that the Trump administration has forced to stay open, the Michigan plant has emitted the most pollution, according to Kelly. Since it was forced to stay open, it has emitted 1,000 tons of nitrogen oxides, 2,000 tons of sulfur dioxide, and 140 tons of particulate matter as of the end of June. The Environmental Defense Fund estimates that mix of pollutants could contribute to about 100 new cases of asthma for the 3,000 people that live near the plant in West Olive, Michigan. Its continued operation since May last year has cost $259 million, which the utility, Consumers Energy Company, is seeking to recover from its customers in Michigan and 10 other states.

The court order doesn’t mean that the plant has to shut down immediately. Kelly hopes that the Trump administration voluntarily backs down, or if that doesn’t happen, that the court could force a shutdown. But the administration could challenge the ruling, delaying action by asking for a re-hearing or for a review by the Supreme Court, said Gavin McCabe, senior litigating counsel at the Natural Resources Defense Council, another environmental group involved in the lawsuit.

Either way, the D.C. Circuit Court’s ruling sets a precedent that there has to be a true emergency to keep these plants open. Several lawsuits against the other fossil fuel plants have been on hold as courts waited to see how the federal court ruled on the case, and the legal arguments there are pretty similar, Kelly said.

It’s hard to square the idea of an “energy emergency” with the Trump administration’s actions against renewable energy: By mid-August, the administration had committed about $4 billion in payouts to companies to stop offshore wind projects that could have, altogether, powered more than 15 million homes.

“Why would the administration be blocking sources of energy that are ready to come online in favor of keeping online something that has been set to be retired?” McCabe said. “I mean, there appears to be a pretext that the president wants to help coal industry supporters. And this is one of the ways to attempt to do that.”

text:
This Tier 2 disbursement under the Generation III+ SMR Pathway to Deployment Program is smaller than last year’s $800 million disbursement—which went to the Tennessee Valley Authority and Holtec to aid their deployment of, respectively, a GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy (GVH) BWRX-300 at Clinch River in Tennessee and two Holtec SMR-300s at the Palisades site in Michigan. The newly announced recipients come from different parts of the country and focus on key areas of SMR deployment, including equipment procurement.

The recipients: Two companies were chosen for site preparation and selection purposes:

A $17.3 million award to Constellation SMR Development LLC, to pursue a Nuclear Regulatory Commission early site permit (ESP) for a future SMR site in New York. (Recent actions in New York that could lead to new nuclear power plants include solicitations by the New York Power Authority for expressions of interest from potential host communities.)

A $27.9 million award to Nebraska Public Power District, to obtain an ESP from the NRC for a future SMR site in Nebraska. (Of note, NPPD hosted informational open houses across the state last year as it considered building a new nuclear power plant.)

The six other companies were selected for supply chain development endeavors:

A $21.4 million award to BWXT Nuclear Energy Inc., to acquire equipment for the final assembly of reactor pressure vessels and the manufacturing of large components for nuclear reactors at an existing facility in Mount Vernon, Ind. (Previously, BWXT Canada secured a contract to manufacture the reactor pressure vessel for the first of four planned BWRX-300 reactors at Ontario Power Generation’s Darlington site.)

A $547,900 award to Container Technologies Industries LLC, to expand nuclear quality assurance certifications at its Helenwood, Tenn., facility to produce steel for SMR deployments.

An $8.8 million award to Framatome U.S. Government Solutions LLC, to expand a Richland, Wash., fuel fabrication facility. Framatome wants to increase its number of ceramic pellet production lines; the expansion will add approximately 200 metric tons of uranium of annual capacity. (It is Framatome’s second major U.S. development in May, as the company announced the Richland facility had received NRC approval for a license amendment supporting fabrication of fuel with enrichment levels above 5 percent uranium-235, with manufacturing scheduled to begin in 2027.)

A $3 million award to Global Nuclear Fuel Americas (an affiliate of GVH), to establish a second production line for fuel rod fabrication for boiling water reactors, acquire capital equipment to automate the pellet inspection process, and implement automated pellet storage and handling capabilities at its Wilmington, N.C., facility.

A $2.9 million award to North American Forgemasters Company, to procure a new furnace for its New Castle, Pa., facility to domestically produce large-component forgings for Gen III+ SMRs.

A $12.3 million award to Scot Forge Company, to procure and install a large vertical turning lathe and gantry-style milling machine at its Spring Grove, Ill., facility to domestically produce and manufacture large components.

Plans span administrations: DOE Secretary Chris Wright said in Thursday’s announcement, “Advanced light water SMRs will give our nation the reliable, round-the-clock power we need to fuel the president’s manufacturing boom, support data centers and AI growth, and reinforce a stronger, more secure electric grid. These awards ensure we can deploy these reactors as soon as possible.”

The approximately $900 million in funding through the Generation III+ SMR Pathway to Deployment Program was originally offered in 2024 under the Biden administration, but the DOE modified the solicitation in 2025 to align with the energy policies and goals of the Trump administration.

Tier 2, or Fast Follower Deployment Support, was described in 2024 as providing approximately $100 million to address “key gaps that have hindered the domestic nuclear industry in areas such as design, licensing, supplier development, and site preparation.”

Another round of Tier 2 awards may be issued if additional funds become available, according to the DOE’s May 14 news release.

title: Texas business says record diesel prices are 'derailing' projects, and could raise food costs
description:
In Waco, businesses that transport essential materials and goods are facing new strain as diesel hits record levels.
National gasoline prices also stayed above $4.00, adding another layer of pressure on commuters already facing higher living costs.
Higher diesel costs can spread quickly through the economy because freight and delivery networks rely on the fuel.
Waco's diesel surge shows how swings in fossil fuel markets, power costs, and pollution pressures keep spilling into other parts of the economy.
For anyone watching record diesel squeeze Waco businesses, the impact of higher fuel prices also point to the bigger system driving costs, risks, and policy well beyond construction trucking.
text:
In Waco, businesses that transport essential materials and goods are facing new strain as diesel hits record levels.

The impact is likely to extend beyond trucking firms, since diesel underpins freight movement nationwide and can feed into grocery bills and other everyday expenses.

Here's what to know

KWTX reported that companies that depend on heavy-duty transportation are being squeezed as AAA's latest figures revealed diesel in Waco reached a record average of $5.59 per gallon, nearly 75% above the city's $3.21 average.

Across the U.S., diesel averaged $5.90 per gallon, up from $3.70 and above the June 2022 level of $5.82. The station reported that disruptions in Middle East energy flows and continuing conflicts affecting Russian refineries are still tightening global petroleum supplies.

Hunter Kosar, president and owner of Twisted Nail, a Waco- and Austin-based construction trucking company and aggregate supplier, explained the collateral damage.

"Looking back to the start of the year to today, I would say that our operation in general—every single project we've had—has been derailed," Kosar told KWTX. "Every single thing we projected in January is no longer the case today."

National gasoline prices also stayed above $4.00, adding another layer of pressure on commuters already facing higher living costs.

More background

Because Twisted Nail delivers materials such as limestone, road base, and recycled concrete to construction sites across the region, diesel affects nearly every part of its business, KWTX reported. When fuel prices jump, so does the cost of moving those materials, making it harder for contractors to keep projects on schedule and within budget.

"When fuel increases 70% in six months, obviously not only on our end, but the entire project... anything that burns diesel or fuel is impacted," Kosar noted to the station.

Higher diesel costs can spread quickly through the economy because freight and delivery networks rely on the fuel. The Independent Grocers Alliance says fuel can make up as much as 30% of total food costs.

Kosar suggested to KWTX that the impacts might be even more extensive for locals who don't use diesel. He pointed to ripple effects that ultimately don't even get off the ground because of changing economics.

"While we feel the hecticness—we feel the impact of it today—the end consumer is ultimately the person who is paying for it," he elaborated. "So all those projects we have planned, let's say a stadium, well that might not happen anymore."

Where can I learn more?

Waco's diesel surge shows how swings in fossil fuel markets, power costs, and pollution pressures keep spilling into other parts of the economy. A price jump at the pump can reach everything from investment decisions to household bills and the longer-term costs of relying on carbon-heavy fuels.

• New climate estimates suggest LNG can be worse than coal when its full toll on the environment is accounted for.

• In West Virginia, aging coal plants continue to impact consumers after 50 years in use.

• Communities near oil and gas sites still face premature deaths and asthma risks.

• In Colorado, regulators hit a critical milestone, forcing oil and gas firms to count methane.

For anyone watching record diesel squeeze Waco businesses, the impact of higher fuel prices also point to the bigger system driving costs, risks, and policy well beyond construction trucking. Seeing that bigger picture helps explain why fuel shocks can move so quickly into everyday budgets.

text:
source: Latitude Media

The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection has confirmed it issued no permits for any power generators at the DataOne Campus in Vineland, according to Latitude Media.

Investigative outlet Floodlight reported that 45 of the facility's 62 gas generators appeared to be operating anyway. The site, still under partial construction, is planned as New Jersey's largest AI data center.

No permit applications were under review at the time of the department's confirmation.

Bruce Buckheit, a former chief of air enforcement at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, told Floodlight the situation appears to break federal law. He said DataOne should halt the generators and face financial penalties for what he described as illegal emissions.

A $17 Billion Project With Microsoft Ties

DataOne Campus sits approximately 40 miles from Philadelphia and roughly a mile from two schools. Under a $17 billion agreement, Dutch AI infrastructure firm Nebius is set to use the facility to supply computing capacity for Microsoft. Construction began in 2025.

The scale of the project has drawn scrutiny well beyond the generator dispute. Since work began, the site has faced zoning disputes, separate allegations of unpermitted construction activity, and sustained noise complaints from neighboring residents.

Neighbors Report Constant Noise Disruption

Andrew Groetsch and his wife Stevi Groetsch live less than a mile from the facility. They told Floodlight the noise has disrupted sleep and daily life for their family. Andrew Groetsch said the sound is constant and never stops.

Their account illustrates the friction between large-scale data infrastructure development and the residential communities that border these sites in .

A National Pattern of Off-Grid Power

The Vineland situation reflects a broader trend documented by Floodlight, citing energy analytics firm Cleanview. Nearly 60 data centers across the country plan to build their own gas-fired power plants rather than connect to the electrical grid.

The push is driven by surging electricity demand tied to AI workloads, with developers unwilling to wait for grid connection timelines.

On-site generation allows faster buildout, but it also places those facilities outside the regulatory frameworks that govern grid-connected power sources, creating gaps in environmental oversight.

What Happens Next

Buckheit indicated to Floodlight that the likely regulatory response could be administrative enforcement action. Neither DataOne nor Nebius has been reported to have publicly responded to the specific generator allegations at the time of publication.

The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection's confirmation that no permits exist or are pending is a public-record finding. Federal air quality rules generally require permits before combustion equipment of this scale can operate. No application was filed.

That absence is notable in its own right.

Floodlight's investigation combined drone footage with records analysis to establish which generators appeared to be running. That reporting was subsequently covered by Latitude Media and aggregated widely, bringing the matter to broader public attention.

text:
General Motors is accelerating plans to develop next-generation battery cells in the U.S., aiming to slash dependence on Chinese materials for electric vehicles and energy storage systems, as reported by CNBC and TradersUnion on September 12, 2026.

Kurt Kelty, GM’s vice president of battery and sustainability, stated the company is building a domestic supply chain within two to three years to support market-ready technology.

"We're developing a supply chain such that, two years from now, three years from now, it will be domestic," said Kelty.

GM has partnered with Denver-based Peak Energy to produce sodium-ion battery cells, targeting commercial launch around 2029. The chemistry reduces reliance on Chinese-dominated materials like lithium, instead using abundant U.S. resources such as sodium from soda ash.

"It's going to take some time to build this industry up, but the potential for sodium-ion is just much greater than LFP," said Kelty.

The push follows criticism from the Trump administration over Ford’s ties to Chinese battery firm CATL. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy expressed concern over Ford’s licensing of CATL technology for LFP cells, despite Ford’s status as the top U.S. vehicle producer.

China currently controls 80% of global battery production, per the International Energy Agency, dominating cathode and anode material supply chains. GM’s existing LFP cells for energy storage are produced in the U.S. with LG Energy Solution, but other chemistries still use undisclosed Chinese-sourced materials.

"The better thing to do is try to leapfrog, come up with a different technology that's actually better that we can actually source here," said Kelty.

GM is investing $900 million in new battery lab facilities at its Detroit tech campus, including a 500,000-square-foot prototyping center set to open later this year. Sodium-ion cells, Kelty noted, could eliminate the need for active cooling in energy storage, reducing costs and complexity.

Battery expert Sam Abuelsamid of Telemetry said domesticating the supply chain will take years, even as China advances newer chemistries. "There's no reason why the LFP materials couldn't also be produced here," said Abuelsamid.

"It's going to take some time, but the sodium-ion would be even cheaper and easier to do."

text:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency granted 29 small refinery exemptions from 2025 Renewable Fuel Standard blending requirements and included a proposed plan to restore the lost renewable fuel volume in the near future.

Of the 34 pending exemption petitions, EPA granted full exemptions to 18 and partial, or 50%, exemptions to 11. It also denied three petitions and determined two petitions to be ineligible.

This represents a total of 1.76 billion exempted Renewable Identification Numbers, or renewable fuel blending credits.

EPA simultaneously announced a proposal to reallocate 100% of the newly exempted renewable fuel volume into the 2026 and 2027 renewable volume obligations before the end of October 2026. This will allow the market to appropriately account for the additional RINs.

In consultation with U.S. Department of Energy, EPA reviewed and considered information submitted by each petitioning small refinery. EPA then evaluated each SRE petition consistent with the Clean Air Act and case law.

In 2020, EPA established a methodology in regulation for predicting the expected volumes that would be exempted based on an average of the past three years.

Before that rule-making, SREs were not considered as part of the volumes — in other words, all SREs had the result of reducing volumes.

Following EPA’s methodology, the agency estimated that 990 million RINs would be exempted in 2025 in “Set 2” and put into the volumes.

However, due to more small refineries requesting exemptions and changes in financial circumstances, EPA is exempting more RINs than estimated in “Set 2.”

“Based on agency experiences, DOE is evaluating how it has historically utilized their 2011 disproportionate economic harm methodology and the information needed for future small refinery petitions to account for current market circumstances in this new phase of the RFS program. DOE will continue to seek public feedback from all impacted stakeholders on these analyses,” EPA noted in a release.

SRE Criteria

The Renewable Fuel Standard allows qualifying small refineries to seek an extension of the program’s original exemption when they can demonstrate disproportionate economic hardship.

An SRE allows certain small oil refineries to temporarily avoid part of all of the federal requirements to use renewable fuels, including ethanol and biodiesel.

“When exempted obligations are not reassigned to other refiners, the overall renewable fuel requirement effectively shrinks, reducing demand for RINs and weakening the incentive to blend renewable fuels,” Faith Parum, American Farm Bureau Federation economist, recently noted in Farm Bureau Intel.

“For farmers, un-reallocated exemptions mean weaker demand for agricultural products, particularly corn used for ethanol and soybean oil used for biomass-based diesel.”

name: EPA
title: EPA Pulls Scope 3 Emissions Guidance: What It Means for Automakers and Car Buyers
description:
Its Guidance section contains three items: Scope 1 and 2 inventory guidance, supply chain guidance, and management plan guidance.
EPA's surviving Scope 1 guidance still shows a diagram credited to the GHG Protocol's Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard.
Why Carmakers Should Care The final version of the Scope 3 guidance page, last updated in May 2022, walked companies through all 15 GHG Protocol categories.
The v1.3 dataset covers 1,016 commodities, uses 2022 emissions data priced in 2022 dollars, and was last updated in July 2024.
Fuel economy labels run through a separate regulatory process, and deleting a guidance page doesn't touch them.
text:
The Environmental Protection Agency has quietly edited Scope 3 emissions out of its corporate climate toolkit. There was no press release or Federal Register notice. The navigation simply changed. For anyone who follows the car business, that matters more than it sounds, because for an automaker, Scope 3 is where almost all of the carbon lives.

What's Gone and What's Left

Start with what EPA's own website shows today. The Center for Corporate Climate Leadership homepage, last updated September 8, lists "Scopes 1 and 2 Emissions Accounting" under Getting Started. Its Guidance section contains three items: Scope 1 and 2 inventory guidance, supply chain guidance, and management plan guidance. Scope 3 inventory guidance isn't listed anywhere on the page.

The section that used to hold it has been renamed too. The hub page is now titled "Scopes 1 and 2 Emissions Inventorying and Guidance," and its page metadata shows a last modification on December 4, 2025. EPA didn't hide Scope 3 in a subfolder. It rewrote the table of contents so Scope 3 no longer has a chapter.

Related Articles

The Chinese Car Ban Bill Also Outlaws Airbags Nobody Noticed

Volkswagen's Old Beetle Factory Is About to Build Iron Dome Parts. The Real Story Is Why It Had To.

There's an irony here. EPA's surviving Scope 1 guidance still shows a diagram credited to the GHG Protocol's Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard. The agency kept the picture of the value chain and removed the instructions for measuring it.

For a record of what used to be there, EPA keeps official web snapshots of its site taken every four years on January 19. The 2021 snapshot defines Scope 3 as emissions from assets a company doesn't own or control but influences through its value chain, and notes these emissions "often represent the majority of an organization's total GHG emissions."

Why Carmakers Should Care

The final version of the Scope 3 guidance page, last updated in May 2022, walked companies through all 15 GHG Protocol categories. It pointed them to EPA's spend-based supply chain factors for purchased goods. For Category 11, "use of sold products," it explained that no special factor was needed. Companies could apply EPA's existing combustion and electricity factors to the energy their products would use over their lifetimes.

Swap EPA's example product, electronics, for a pickup, and Category 11 becomes the lifetime fuel burned by every vehicle an automaker sold that year. A University of Michigan Center for Sustainable Systems project done with Ford found that value chain emissions account for more than 90 percent of an automaker's greenhouse gas inventory, with use of sold products the dominant source. That's why Ford's science-based target calls for cutting use-phase Scope 3 emissions 50 percent per vehicle by 2035 from a 2019 baseline. The factory smokestack is a rounding error next to the tailpipe.

The Tools Are Aging in Place

Some of the underlying tools still exist, but nobody seems to be maintaining them. The Emission Factors Hub still offers downloads, and its newest edition is dated January 2025. It was an annual update, and there's no 2026 edition listed. Oddly, the page still explains how to calculate a Scope 3 category using grid loss data, which suggests an editor missed a spot.

EPA's spend-based supply chain factors, the numbers companies use to turn purchasing dollars into estimated emissions, are still in the federal data catalog. The v1.3 dataset covers 1,016 commodities, uses 2022 emissions data priced in 2022 dollars, and was last updated in July 2024.

That 2022-dollar detail is worth understanding. Spend-based accounting multiplies what you paid by a kilograms-of-CO2e-per-dollar factor. If a tariff raises the price of an aluminum coil by 25 percent, a spend-based inventory reports 25 percent more emissions from that purchase, even though the smelter burned the same energy. Frozen factors plus volatile metal prices produce inventories that track the purchasing budget, not the carbon. The fix is primary data from suppliers, which takes years to build.

Part of a Broader Federal Retreat

The page edits line up with bigger moves.

On May 29, the SEC proposed rescinding its 2024 climate disclosure rules entirely, arguing they exceed the agency's statutory authority. That rule had already been stayed, and the Commission had voted in March 2025 to stop defending it in court.

EPA has also proposed ending reporting obligations for 46 source categories in its Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program, the facility-level database that underpins much of the country's Scope 1 data. In a separate final rule, it pushed the 2025 reporting deadline to October 30, 2026 while it considers the rest.

For car people, the biggest change came in February, when EPA finalized its rescission of the 2009 endangerment finding, the legal basis for regulating greenhouse gases from new vehicles.

There's history here, too. The 2021 snapshot shows EPA dropped out of the Climate Leadership Awards in 2018, canceling that year's awards and its conference sponsorship. And the January 2025 snapshot of EPA's homepage, taken the day before the inauguration, featured the 50th anniversary of the agency's Automotive Trends report, touting record gains in fuel economy and CO2 emissions. That homepage also listed Climate Change in the main navigation. The current menu doesn't.

California Didn't Get the Memo

A missing federal web page doesn't cancel anyone's legal obligations. California's SB 253 requires companies with more than $1 billion in revenue that do business in the state to disclose Scope 1 and 2 emissions starting in 2026 and Scope 3 starting in 2027, following the GHG Protocol. That describes every major automaker, most tier-one suppliers, and the big publicly traded dealer groups.

CARB's July workshop materials show where the state is heading. CARB has proposed moving the first Scope 1 and 2 deadline to November 10, 2026. For Scope 3 in 2027, staff want five categories to be mandatory: purchased goods and services, fuel and energy-related activities, waste, business travel, and employee commuting. Category 11, use of sold products, would be voluntary.

That leads to an odd result for the auto industry. Under California's proposal, an automaker's single largest emissions source, the vehicles it sells, would be optional to report. Its supply chain purchases would be mandatory. Category 1 covers steel, aluminum, glass, and battery cells, which is exactly where spend-based factors and tariff-driven price swings distort the numbers. CARB would also require companies to disclose what percentage of each category's emissions comes from primary supplier data, so leaning on stale federal averages will be visible to anyone reading the report. CARB even scheduled an August listening session specifically for manufacturers, including automotive.

Related Articles

Third Time's Not the Charm: Stellantis Just Re-Recalled 328,381 Jeep Grand Cherokees for the Same Spring That Keeps Falling Off

Tesla's Self-Steering Crash Save: The Rules Nobody Wrote Yet

The workshop deck includes one more notable line. CARB staff acknowledged uncertainty about how companies are preparing for mandatory reporting given the general rollback of federal support for climate initiatives. That's about as close as a regulator comes to saying Washington left the room.

What It Means Beyond the Boardroom

Nothing on your window sticker changes. Fuel economy labels run through a separate regulatory process, and deleting a guidance page doesn't touch them.

The effect shows up upstream. If you work for a parts supplier, expect more emissions questionnaires from your OEM customers, not fewer. With EPA no longer providing a common reference, each automaker will write its own supplier data requirements to satisfy California, European rules, and its own public targets. Suppliers that can document actual energy use per part will look better than those relying on dollar-based estimates, and that could eventually influence sourcing decisions.

For buyers, the market signal is subtler. With federal tailpipe greenhouse gas standards rescinded, one of the remaining pressures on powertrain mix comes from corporate emissions targets and state disclosure regimes. The pages EPA deleted were never binding law. They were free instructions for tallying the carbon in a value chain. Companies still have to do the math. Now they'll just be using someone else's instructions.

text:
“This bill coming to the House Floor proves that House Republicans are responding to the needs of the American people,” said Evans. “As the United States competes to win the global AI race and outcompete adversaries like Communist China, we must ensure that growth does not come at the expense of hardworking families.”

While the bill passed through committee unanimously, tech companies have raised concerns about provisions aimed at making them pay upfront for the energy infrastructure needed to serve their data centers. Environmental groups, meanwhile, think the bill does not go far enough.

They say the legislation would not force states to adopt the new reimbursement requirement. Instead, it would require states to consider the policy and decide whether to put it in place.

“The title of the Ratepayer Protection Act suggests it protects ratepayers from data center expansion; however, a more fitting title would be the Ratepayer Deception Act, since this legislation only speaks to a narrow category of utility costs. It leaves many costs from data centers unaddressed, including threats to water supplies, increased pollution, strain on local infrastructure, and land use,” Food & Water Watch wrote.

The House vote also comes as data centers have become an increasingly potent political issue ahead of November. The voter angst has complicated President Donald Trump’s effort to position the U.S. as the global leader in AI and data center development.

As opposition has grown, Trump has sent mixed signals about how Republican candidates should approach the issue.

‘If a Republican is against the data center, that’s OK with me,” said Trump, over the summer, offering room for Republicans to disagree with him as they have become an unpopular issue in many areas across the country.

Just weeks later, however, Trump suggested that communities that block the construction of data centers would end up “backwards and poor.”

The Trump administration has also sought to ease concerns about the effect of data centers on electricity bills by championing its Ratepayer Protection Pledge. So far, Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle, and xAI have already signed the pledge, committing to cover the power generation and infrastructure costs associated with their data centers rather than shifting them onto residential customers.

A White House official told the Washington Examiner that the bipartisan House measure set for consideration Tuesday builds on Trump’s efforts.

BRANDON GILL’S VIRAL RISE FUELS POTENTIAL BID FOR TOP HOUSE OVERSIGHT RULE

“American families should not see electricity bills rise to subsidize the infrastructure needs of data centers,” said the official. “The White House welcomes Congress to take steps to legislatively codify the President’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge to keep American families from footing the bill for big tech and data centers.”

Despite Tuesday’s vote, the bill faces an uphill path to President Trump’s desk this Congress. Similar legislation by Sen. John Husted (R-OH) has yet to advance in the Senate, which has just three weeks before recessing ahead of the November election.

text:
Between now and 2027, U.S. electricity generation is expected to surge to historic highs, according to the latest report from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).

The EIA highlighted that this year's projected 2.2% increase will result in a record energy output equivalent to an average continuous grid load of 498.63 GW (4,368 BkWh). An additional 1.7% growth is anticipated next year as capacity rises to meet expanding large-scale demand.

This demand, the EIA notes, is particularly strong in the West South Central region (along the Gulf of Mexico) amid an increase in manufacturing activity and AI data center development in the commercial and industrial sectors.

In August, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott issued a letter to the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) to pause new data center projects to conduct a thorough audit of power and water usage before interconnection onto the grid. But despite this pause, the West South Central region reportedly remains the largest regional contributor to electricity sales growth in the administration’s forecast.

Parallel to this grid expansion, the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and market researcher Wood Mackenzie (WoodMac) reported the U.S. solar power market added 11.4 GW of capacity in Q2 2026. It marks a 43% increase from the previous quarter, with enough generation capacity to supply power to 50 million homes.

“Solar and storage have grown to a scale most Americans have yet to fully realize and we simply can’t meet America’s growing energy needs without these technologies,” said SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty in a statement.

Together, SEIA and WoodMac noted that solar and storage accounted for 70% of all new capacity added to the grid in H1 2026, with the U.S. solar market expected to almost double over the next five years.

This growing momentum to add new renewable generation to the grid comes as global shifts accelerate in places like China. The country officially surpassed coal power for the first time, aligning with its broader goals to peak carbon emissions by 2030.

Wood Mac highlighted that the country's coal-fired power generation fell by nearly 2% in 2025, despite its rising energy demand. The U.S. aims to achieve its own renewable milestones in the race to modernize its aging grid infrastructure and meet soaring electrification needs in the years to come.

title: Pennsylvania and Texas warn AI developers: Build your own power, or stay off the grid
description:
Here's what to know Concern over the huge amount of electricity required by AI facilities is fueling state-level resistance, Grist reported.
Many proposed AI data centers are being paired with their own natural gas plants.
Texas and Pennsylvania are providing a preview of what a bring-your-own-infrastructure approach looks like as AI developers chase cheap land and quick approvals.
• In rural Texas, developers must bring their own power and water under Abbott's warning.
• Nationwide, AI facilities devour 6% of U.S. electricity, intensifying the power scramble.
text:
Pennsylvania and Texas are taking steps to ensure companies planning massive data centers should cover the power needs those projects create instead of pushing that demand onto everyday utility customers.

Here's what to know

Concern over the huge amount of electricity required by AI facilities is fueling state-level resistance, Grist reported. In response, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said he was imposing a moratorium on "any AI data center that does not bring, develop, and pay for their own power," and Texas Governor Greg Abbott has stopped additional data centers from connecting to the state grid.

The EPA issued a statement saying the Clean Air Act's Acid Rain Program does not apply to "islanded" power plants, or facilities built to serve a single site and not connected to the broader grid.

Many proposed AI data centers are being paired with their own natural gas plants. While this setup keeps new costs from being passed on to households and small businesses, it could also mean less transparency around air pollution and climate impacts.

Mindy Goldstein, who heads Emory Law School's environmental law program, said that removing Acid Rain Program coverage eliminates one permit requirement for some projects, even though other Clean Air Act rules can still apply, Grist reported.

More background

The AI boom is becoming as much an energy story as it is a tech story. Training and operating advanced AI systems can require enormous amounts of around-the-clock electricity, which is one reason utilities and developers are racing to add new power capacity.

AI could help optimize electric grids, improve wind and solar forecasting, and make buildings and factories more efficient. The technology also brings serious concerns, including massive utility use, higher energy costs for customers, security risks, misuse, and broader social disruption if its expansion outpaces safeguards.

OpenAI has announced plans tied to a 9.2-gigawatt natural gas plant in Ohio. Amazon is planning a 7.65-gigawatt gas plant in Texas, while Nexus has proposed a 6-gigawatt facility there. Smaller projects are also moving forward, including a 90-megawatt plant in Georgia for a Serverfarm data center.

David Spence, a University of Texas professor focused on energy law and politics, said, "For a long time, we just didn't have anybody building gas plants at all because wind and solar are cheaper. Then along came data centers with their incredibly large demands for power that has to be 24-7 and a lot of money to spend on these things," per Grist.

What's being done?

Much of the key decision-making is falling to state regulators. They will be responsible for permitting many of these projects, and Goldstein noted that EPA guidance is not the same as a binding rule. That means states can still choose to impose stricter requirements than the federal minimum.

According to Grist, the EPA said the guidance "expands opportunities for companies to develop and operate islanded power generation facilities for data centers. This will give developers greater flexibility in where and how quickly they can build new facilities while helping to protect the environment and reducing burdens on communities' electric grid." The agency has also proposed changes that would further streamline permitting for some "minor" pollution sources.

Still, some communities and watchdog groups are pushing back. In Georgia, state regulators issued violation notices to VoltaGrid and Serverfarm after construction reportedly began before permits were secured. A lawsuit by the NAACP alleges xAI built a 495-megawatt plant in Mississippi to power a Memphis data center without even applying for permits.

"This is a piecemeal approach to trying to clear the way for data center siting and for the siting of corresponding electric generating units," Goldstein said. "It seems like a continuous knockdown of dominoes to clear the way for these data centers, and they're leaving states and communities to hold it back."

Where can I learn more?

Texas and Pennsylvania are providing a preview of what a bring-your-own-infrastructure approach looks like as AI developers chase cheap land and quick approvals. Similar battles centered on gas plants, grid strain, and the huge amount of electricity these facilities use are emerging across the country.

• In rural Texas, developers must bring their own power and water under Abbott's warning.

• In Ohio, proposed data centers are pushing gas plants through before residents weigh in.

• Nationwide, AI facilities devour 6% of U.S. electricity, intensifying the power scramble.

These stories help explain why more state leaders want developers to shoulder the costs of their own expansion, showing how fast AI's power demands are changing utility policy, fueling local infrastructure fights, and prompting new fossil fuel build-outs.

And while there are ambulatory wheelchair users, the video’s framing that the Cybercab was designed for everyone suggests limited attention to universal design, given that some needs have been accommodated and others ignored. And while Cybercabs are now operational in several US cities and have been spotted further afield, NHTSA has already opened an audit into Cybercab, specifically how Tesla managed to self-certify a vehicle without any physical controls, which current Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards assume a vehicle has. Watch this space.

We’re off to Europe now, where Volkswagen is reporting that its dealer network has secured more than 30,000 confirmed orders for its brand-new Volkswagen ID. Polo. That’s great news for EVs, until you factor in the fact that Volkswagen isn’t producing a high volume of vehicles to quickly meet those orders, with wait times now predicted to be at least ten months, and deliveries haven’t even started yet. Off the back of that, you’d think Volkswagen would be accelerating its ID. Polo production plans, but last week its supervisory board approved its new Future Plan 2030. It calls on the entire Volkswagen Group to cut models, lay off as many as 50,000 additional staff between 2031 and 2034 on top of an already confirmed 50,000 people lay off, and then stop building EVs at four different plants in Germany. It’s not clear how this will impact future EV launches, but it doesn’t look good.

From bad Volkswagen Group news to good now, namely that Audi has officially unveiled its new A2 e-tron, the smallest Audi EV to date. Interestingly, it shares much of its underpinnings with the Volkswagen ID. Polo and, says Audi, is the most efficient car it’s ever made, with a stated energy consumption of 12.8 kilowatt-hours per 100 kilometers and a WLTP range of up to 646 kilometers. That’s about 4.8 miles per kilowatt-hour and 400 miles of range. The efficiency comes from the car’s notable Kammback and 0.24 coefficient of drag. It’ll be available with a choice of 52 kilowatt-hour or 61 kilowatt-hour LFP battery pack, with an 84 kilowatt-hour NMC pack for its higher performance models. Vehicle to load and vehicle to home is available as an option, and deliveries are expected to begin in December. It can be ordered now in launch markets from 38,200 euro.

We’re off to the US now, where Europe’s continued EV growth is matched by an equally rapid decrease in EV choices for the average car buyer. Late last week, Stellantis-owned Jeep and Ram both pushed back plans to bring range-extended models to market. With the Ram 1500 REV, a truck that’s been delayed multiple times, now due to launch in April next year, maybe, and the Jeep Grand Wagoneer EREV, now expected late 2027. Given how eager both brands have been to associate with the current administration, these delays are no surprise. But what is a surprise is news that Volvo has just confirmed it’s canceling the EX40 in the US, leaving just the EX60 as its only electric model until the promised EX50 launches late next year. And if that wasn’t enough, charging station manufacturer Wallbox is shutting down all US production four years after opening it. Now, the firm says it will make all products at its home facility in Barcelona, Spain, and maintains it won’t be pulling out of the US sales market. But the government may have other ideas. But that’s for later in the show.

Today’s show is pretty heavy and bad news, so let’s get to some good news now. EVs in Europe are, on average, a third cheaper to drive than gasoline vehicles. That’s the finding of the new EV Transition Check 2026 from the ICCT. Now in its second edition, it has been announced that the EV transition is saving EU owners around 4.5 billion euros a year in fossil fuel imports, and costs their owners about 33% less to drive than comparable ICE vehicles. That’s helped push battery electric cars to 22% of all new cars registered across the EU in the first half of this year. But it’s not just Europe. Despite the best efforts of the US administration to put people off EVs, a new report published this week by HERE and SBD Automotive shows more American citizens are showing interest too. The HERE-SBD EV Index 2026 found 31% of those questioned named better value for money as their single biggest reason to switch. Interestingly too, a third of all respondents said they’d consider buying a Chinese EV, which again, is coming back later in the show.

While the current US administration has been working hard to halt future solar and wind farm deployments, the industry has responded in the exact opposite way. And this week, as the SEIA and Wood Mackenzie detailed in their latest US Solar Market Insight report, Q2 2026 saw a 61% year-over-year increase in grid-scale solar and a 43% increase from Q1. It now says there’s enough grid-tied solar to power 50 million US homes, about one-third of all homes in the nation. What’s more, solar and battery storage made up 70% of all new US power capacity in the first half of this year. And despite claims to the contrary, a new Indiana study from Ball State University shows that new grid-scale solar and wind farm developments did little to impact real estate value. It examined home sales for the 20 years from 2004 to 2024 and said there’s no statistically significant negative effect on residential sales caused by utility-scale solar or large-scale wind farms. In fact, for homes within a half-mile of investor-owned utility solar farms, researchers found an increase in home value of up to 7.9%. The more you know.

Tesla may have launched its Cybercab last week, but despite some serious whataboutisms in the comments section, there’s increasing evidence suggesting Tesla’s full self-driving system and Autopilot is being abused by Tesla owners. This week, Illinois representative Raja Krishnamoorthi wrote to US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy demanding an answer to an increase in videos of Tesla drivers apparently asleep at the wheel of their vehicle, asking how it’s possible for owners to fall asleep when Tesla itself maintains its systems require active driver supervision and are not autonomous driving systems. He cited an NBC News investigation covering 43 different videos of apparently asleep Tesla drivers, 17 of which were from this year, and a message that appears in Tesla’s own vehicles prompting FSD use when drowsy. Neither Tesla nor the US DOT has officially responded to the letter, but it is worth calling out that Tesla just rolled out an OTA update with a safety feature that genuinely deserves praise. Its cars will now step in when you’re driving manually to avoid a collision, and intervenes if the system detects you aren’t paying attention, which, given everything I’ve just said, feels like it should have arrived sooner.

It’s no secret that the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, a massive US lobbying group representing automakers in the US, is no fan of EVs, and now it’s back on Capitol Hill campaigning to keep EV innovation out of the country. Just last week, John Bozzella, head of the group, pleaded with Congress to pass multiple proposed bills that would not only ban all Chinese vehicles from being sold in the US, but from entering and being driven in the US. And while you might think it’s just going to impact Chinese brands sold in Mexico and Canada, the bills he was calling for support on would also ban any automaker with partial Chinese ownership, potentially making all Mercedes-Benz and Volvo models illegal to drive and own. Given how feckless and disorganized Congress is right now, these bills are unlikely to pass, and in a stroke of sheer “bet you didn’t see that one coming,” Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin, one of the sponsors of some of the aforementioned bills, claimed on social media that President Trump was in talks with President Xi Jinping of China on a trade deal that would, surprise surprise, allow Chinese models to enter into the US. I severely doubt that claim, but hey, we are now living in the opposite universe.

Regulars to the channel will know I’m not afraid to call out automakers when they make bad choices, but I’m also more than happy to praise said automakers when they do things right, and Ford is a good example of this. I’m not a fan of Ford’s decision to cancel the F-150 Lightning in preference for a future range-extended Lightning model, and I’ve been more than happy with Ford’s plans for a smaller electric pickup as embodied by the Ford Fathom. And to ensure it’s competitive, Ford has been working on a domestic LFP battery facility using technology and expertise from the battery firm CATL. But this week, Sean Duffy, Secretary of Transportation, decided to pressure Ford on the partnership, calling it profoundly concerning and asking the automaker to cut all ties with CATL and Geely, who it’s recently signed a factory deal with in Spain. It’s worth noting here, as Ford itself did, that unlike some of its rivals who are importing Chinese-made batteries for their cars, Ford wants to build in the US for domestic production. The facility itself is not foreign-owned or operated, and instead, Ford is licensing tech and expertise — nothing more, nothing less. And if this sounds like an attempt to stop EVs… yeah, I agree.

And finally for this segment, we’re back to the root of everything seemingly happening to the EV industry in the US right now. President Trump. If posting AI-generated memes about Space Force, complete with a uniform based off the Starship Troopers send-up of Nazi uniforms didn’t get you, nor the map floating of a rename of New Mexico to New America, or the AI-generated map of the US swallowing all of North America, or indeed, the conceit that President Trump knows how to play ice hockey, there’s the threat he made last week that if the Federal Reserve doesn’t lower interest rates, he’ll halt all trade with countries the US runs a deficit with, i.e., countries that sell more stuff to the US than they buy. This week, his administration went further, arguing it can’t impose tariffs under emergency powers, but can ban imports outright. Why is this a big deal? Well, in addition to the expanded war on Canada, which is frankly getting very itchy — I even personally experienced it this week as a Canadian citizen when interacting with an immigration official — pretty much every nation that builds EVs for the US market runs a surplus with it, and most US-made EVs use components from said countries. Some analysts are saying the move could make the Great Depression look like an afternoon stroll, but I just want to remind US citizens that now is the time to make sure you’re registered to vote.

Our recall reminders are coming next, but first, a message from one of our most important channel sponsors, you. As one of the oldest and most independent YouTube channels in this space, we’ve spent over fifteen years distilling cleaner, greener, safer, smarter, and more equitable transportation and energy news into the information you need to make informed choices. We believe information should be free, and we don’t believe in handing over our opinions for money, whether that’s a company paying for them, or for readers paying to see or watch them. And since YouTube is getting worse, not better, in the way it treats creators, it’s no longer a viable revenue stream, it’s just a delivery medium. And that means we have to rely on you for our income. We have a tiny team of myself and two full-time staff, and while we are the leanest channel I know, even then, once we’ve paid the bills and everything else, there’s not a lot of money left. And while my wife’s salary used to cover our personal bills, her losing her job, thanks to a corporate reshuffle earlier this year, has put even more pressure on TE. We need to raise another two thousand dollars a month to be genuinely comfortable and cover TE and my own bills, or we won’t be able to continue in our current state. If you’re able, I would love you to consider supporting us from just one dollar fifty a month on Patreon or YouTube. And if just one percent of the people watching who don’t already support us gave that exact amount every month, we’d be in a far safer place. You can also send us Ko-fi, buy swag from our store, or just checks, or you can just engage with us and share our content. That also really helps. Right now, TE is the only thing keeping three people employed and four people housed, so if you can, we’d really appreciate your help. Thanks.

And now it’s time for our recall reminders. As usual, you’ll find links to all of the recalls in our show notes. Mitsubishi has included its Outlander PHEV in a wider recall campaign covering rear-view camera images failing to display properly when placed in reverse. Owners will be notified. Just nineteen Tesla Model Ys are being recalled to address a lateral link suspension separation that could shift the wheel alignment on affected vehicles, increasing the risk of a crash. The Chrysler Pacifica Plug-in Hybrid is among a number of Stellantis models being recalled for a fault in its stability control software. A recall software update is planned. And finally for the recalls, the Toyota C-HR is being recalled to address a fault that could cause vehicles to suddenly lose power while driving. A software fix is planned. And those were your recall reminders.

Now it’s time for our news shorts. As usual, you’ll find full links on our website at transportevolved.com.

Sany has expanded its electric truck lineup in Europe with plans to debut four new variants of existing models on the market. It will debut them all at IAA Transportation.

A team of engineers at Fraunhofer ISE have developed a new cell architecture for batteries that could increase cell energy density by 10 to 15 percent. It uses thicker electrodes.

Researchers at the German Federal Institute for Materials Research and Testing have discovered that the distribution of two different lithium isotopes in battery cells is directly linked to degradation. It could help advance cell state of health reports.

EV sales in the UK are on a roll, with August data showing a 29.8 percent market share among cars. However, the SMMT is now warning that that increase is still below the 33 percent target set by the UK government.

Dacia has begun production of its new Dacia Spring. Unlike its predecessor, the new model is made in Europe for the European market, helping it avoid tariffs on Chinese-made models.

Audi has made a decision to reorganize its Chinese partnerships. Its work with SAIC will focus on the new AUDI sub-brand, while FAW’s partnership will focus on Audi-branded vehicles.

Data from Canada shows that the EV import quota agreed on between China and Canada is mostly benefiting Tesla, which now imports its Chinese-made models to the nation.

Battery diagnostics company AVILOO has announced that it is extending its battery warranty product to 26 countries. The free coverage is linked to a qualifying flash battery test.

German company Vector has unveiled a new control board designed to fit in the handle of a CCS charging connector. It makes it possible for charging cables of up to 100 meters to be made.

BYD has commenced production at a new facility in Indonesia, where it will produce EVs for both the domestic and international markets. It’s located in West Java.

Witricity has opened up a new wireless charging laboratory in Florida. The new Stuart facility will focus on developing solutions for everything from passenger cars to autonomous vehicles and heavy-duty trucks.

The Future Is Neutral, a joint venture between Renault and Suez, is opening up offerings to the industry. It includes a refurbishment service for EV motors.

The Liverpool City Region in the UK has ordered a new fleet of low-emission buses, including 30 all-electric ones. The fleet will take ownership of its new buses next year.

Charging payment platform Paua and Zaptec have partnered on a way to work on a new EV charging ecosystem for fleet operators. It will cover employee, home and on-the-road charging.

New sales data from Russia shows that Russians are rapidly adopting electric and plug-in hybrid models as gas shortages bite as a consequence of its illegal war with Ukraine.

Swedish electric motorcycle firm RGNT has expanded its line-up with a new scrambler variant of its electric motorcycle. The RGNT Street Scrambler is now available to order in Europe.

Kia has officially launched three new GT variants of its existing EV models. The EV3, EV4 and EV5 GT models are now on sale across Europe, adding a sporty variant across the range.

Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles has confirmed that a longer-wheelbase ID. Buzz Cargo is on the way. It will share the same battery pack as the passenger-carrying long-wheelbase variant.

A new update to Transport & Environment’s ongoing analysis of plug-in hybrid emissions shows they’re not getting cleaner as PHEV drivers continue to not plug them in.

Polestar has confirmed that it’s planning on revealing a new concept car called the Formula 2030 concept car as part of a wider commercial strategy. It will preview both the next-generation Polestar 2 and Polestar 7.

Australia’s government is expanding EV infrastructure support for dealership and repair shops, offering them up to AU$3,000 per charging station installed and covering 80% of EV repair and maintenance equipment.

Volvo is moving forwards with its previously announced plans to become Lynk & Co’s official European distributor. Volvo dealerships will begin stocking the brand next year.

Mitsubishi has confirmed its Eclipse Cross EV in Europe will get a slightly larger 89 kWh NMC battery for the new model year, as well as a new, lower-capacity 67 kWh LFP variant.

Lucid has confirmed that it’s going to be working with Emil Frey to import its vehicles into France. The partnership will see Emil Frey provide sales and service.

Mercedes-Benz-backed solid-state battery firm ProLogium has confirmed it’s now making its Gen 3.5 lithium ceramic solid-state batteries at a new gigafactory facility in Taiwan.

Indian mobility company Ola has announced a new electric scooter model called the S1 Z, for Zyada, or Hindi for “more,” which features a new Indian-made LFP battery pack.

Bolloré has officially cancelled its Bluebus production. It never reached the scale it needed for profitability. A total of 700 buses were manufactured.

LG Energy Solution, working in collaboration with Seoul National University, has announced a breakthrough involving lithium manganese-rich batteries. LMR promises to lower production costs by replacing both cobalt and nickel in battery cells.

ZF has announced a new range of products in its ZF Aftermarket line, allowing for more after-sales repair of electrified drivetrains by trained independent garages.

Mercedes-Benz has announced an expansion to its VLE family, with the official launch of a VLE van with all-wheel drive. It’s also introducing more entry-level models as well.

VinBus, a Vingroup subsidiary specializing in public transit, has deployed 50 new electric school buses in Vietnam. It’s the latest in a line of public fleet switches to electric.

BYD UK has announced a new partnership with Vision to expand its after-sales repair network. 138 new approved repairers will join BYD’s official repair network.

Nissan has confirmed that its next electric car, the Pixo EV, will be revealed at the end of September. It’s based on the same platform as Renault’s Twingo EV.

Mercedes-Benz has handed over the first 27 of a total of more than 200 eActros 600 big rigs to Amazon. By the end of the year, 50 will be operating across Germany for the retailer.

UK firm Watt Electric Vehicle Company has confirmed that it will be designing two EVs in the UK for production at a new plant in Qatar. They will share the same aluminum skateboard chassis.

Google has announced a new partnership with Nevoya and the Center for Green Market Activation in Texas to deploy 25 new electric trucks in the Lone Star State.

Xiaomi has unveiled a new SkyNomad SUV family. A new range for Xiaomi, it will include four variants: the N70 Pro and Max, an N90 Max and Max Studio.

Rivian is pushing a new over-the-air update for all Rivian models called RivianOS 2. It brings R1 Gen 2 and R2 in line with one another, offering new graphics, new police and camera alerts and a new interface.

Supermarket chain Lidl has cut the price of charging if you’re a Lidl Plus app user. It’s part of an investment into EV charging in the UK and comes alongside a £10 million sterling expansion to its charging network.

And finally for the shorts, a production-spec Škoda Peaq has just travelled more than 580 miles on a single charge, setting a new record. But it did so by hypermiling on slower roads.

And those are your news shorts. There will be more next week.

Our final two stories are coming right up, but first a quick word from longtime channel sponsor, EnergySage. EnergySage is a great way to get trustworthy experts helping you, whether that’s for solar panels, getting a heat pump installed, or for those of you who rent, to join a community solar program. It was EnergySage who I used when we put solar panels on the roof of our house five years ago, and our panels are still churning out electrons every day. So it’s well worth it, as the cost of utility-provided power keeps going up. And while US federal incentives to solar aren’t around anymore, it’s worth using EnergySage’s network of local experts to help navigate the regional and state incentives that may exist in your area, as well as finding local financial institutions that have special deals for solar panel loans, allowing you to have a manageable monthly payment. And of course, if you choose to use an EnergySage provided installer for your project, we’ll also get a small referral fee, so you’ll be helping us out too.

And now it’s time for our final two stories. For a really long time now, Tesla fans have maintained that Tesla’s Optimus robot would revolutionize the world, with some even claiming that it would bring about the death of manual labor. To date, it hasn’t materialized the way it was promised, but it did spur rival XPeng into building its own humanoid, IRON. This week, XPeng commissioned a production line for it in China, though so far that means one robot walking off it, with mass production targeted for year’s end and sales in 2027. Fresh from a nine hundred million dollar raise valuing its robotics arm at six point three billion dollars, led by IDG Capital, with Tencent and Alibaba backing it, XPeng wants more than a thousand IRON units a month to be made, and a million built by 2030. I don’t know if it will get there, or even how I feel about it, and there’s certainly an uncanny valley vibe to IRON. I’m all for assistive technology, but the question we’ll need to ask is what is and isn’t okay in this new world, and more importantly, how we avoid the pitfalls science fiction keeps predicting.

And finally, for today’s show, it’s pretty standard wisdom that if you’re in the market for an EV, while leasing is a lot cheaper on a monthly basis than financing, if you have any wish to keep your car at lease end, it can prove extremely costly, so too can go over your mileage limit. As automakers in the US are moving away from EVs for… reasons I probably don’t need to explain, we’re seeing a weird phenomenon pop up. Dealerships and automakers encouraging customers to buy out their leases rather than hand their cars back. And for many, this is tempting but costly. Residual value payoffs are hardly pleasant, but this week, we learn that Audi is so eager for customers to buy out their leases and take over the associated risk of ownership that it is now offering up to US$10,000 in cash assistance for customers who buy out their lease. It avoids Audi being out of pocket for cars that are worth less than they once were, and it makes the maths a little more favorable. I’ve bought out leases before, but would you? I’m curious. Let me know in the comments below.

And on that note, we are done for today’s show, but first, a massive thank you to the Electric Vehicle Association for sponsoring us. The EVA has been around since 1967 and is firmly committed to a cleaner, greener future for everyone. Join the EVA today, become an EV educator, and find ways to accelerate your transition to electric. If you haven’t made the switch yet, head over to myeva.org for more info.

And thanks as well, go to EnergySage. Follow the link below to start planning your own energy-independent future today.

And of course, thank you. If you’re able, please consider supporting us using one of the methods I mentioned earlier in the show. Supporting us can also mean sharing our content, joining our Fluxr or Discord communities, promoting us on social media, or using our affiliate links, all of which are down below.

And if you are new to this channel, hi! Please give us a sub, either on YouTube or wherever you happen to see this.

Finally, you matter, you’re important, and we are all very glad that you are watching the show today.

For every week that goes by, things in the news cycle seemingly become more unbelievable, more suffocating, and for folks like us, more scary. I know that’s how it makes me feel, and I know it’s how it makes some of you feel too.

But I need you to know that as long as we keep showing up, change is possible. A better world is possible. A cleaner, greener, safer, smarter, and more equitable world must be one rooted in justice, fairness, and a shared goal, and that only happens when we all work together. And you being here today is that first step on a very important journey.

So until next time, be your authentic self, whoever you are, wherever you are, whoever you love. We’re all part of this amazing journey that we’re on together.

As always, keep evolving!
