text:
General Motors CEO Mary Barra has shed light on the company's long-term electric vehicle strategy, suggesting that EVs will eventually replace internal combustion-powered vehicles and hybrids.

The biggest hurdle to EV adoption remains charging infrastructure, which she believes is still inadequate in the U.S. By comparison, China and Europe have moved faster, partly because supportive regulatory policies have helped accelerate the development of charging infrastructure and the broader transition to EVs.

She also explained that a well-established charging infrastructure would give buyers greater confidence in switching to EVs, eventually helping drive higher sales. Speaking in an interview with Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell, Barra was asked about the pace of America's EV transition. She said:

"Every quarter, the number of chargers goes up, so I think over time we still believe EVs are the endgame- from just the styling, what it enables, you know, that instant torque and never having to go to the gas station. And so I think regulatory, though, when you look at Europe and China, that's really what's driven it along, with then, I'll say, other policies that enable the charging infrastructure to be robust."

Commenting on how rational customers are when making purchasing decisions, Barra suggested a robust charging infrastructure needs to be in place for buyers to feel confident about switching to EVs. She said:

"They're very rational, and most people don't have multiple vehicles. If there's two people in the family, they have two vehicles, but they both need them every day to get to work, to take care of their family. And so they're very rational about: is this going to meet my needs? Not just, you know, in a typical week, but when I want to go on vacation, or I've got to go drop a child off at college, or I've got to go visit my parents. They look at it holistically, and that's why charging infrastructure is so important for people to have confidence to switch to EVs.

"I think we'll get there. I think because of the policy in this country, it's going to take a little longer. And in the meantime, we have a great and very efficient internal combustion engine portfolio, and we have a very strong EV portfolio. And we'll have hybrids in the segments we think are important to give customers a full range, and they can pick what they want."

Barra was asked how she remains focused on GM's long-term goals amid a political landscape that can change every few years. In response, she revealed that President Donald Trump wants to give consumers the freedom to choose between different types of vehicles, including EVs, gas-powered cars, and hybrids. She said:

"Well, I don't think it's shifted our mission. Again, I think we still think EVs are the end game, and I think, you know, when I've had conversations with President Trump, he's talked about wanting to give customers choice, not wanting to force them into something. So we can definitely do that."

The GM boss added that her team has identified "no-risk" decisions it can make to prepare for potential shifts in the industry. She explained:

"We do constantly remind all administrations we're a capital-intensive, long-lead industry, and so people have to respect that. But what we've tried to do is, again, have a robust portfolio of both, but then also, you know, the minute we start to sense something might change, what are these no-risk decisions or these no-regret decisions we can make to say, okay, how can we prepare for this?

"We did that as we started to see the regulatory front changing. We also, as we started to see tariffs. What are no-regret moves, and then what are the shifts we need to make?"

text:
WASHINGTON—U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright today issued an emergency order to keep affordable, reliable, and secure coal generation in the State of Washington online to help address critical grid reliability issues facing the Northwestern region of the United States. The emergency order directs TransAlta Centralia Generation, LLC (TransAlta) to ensure that Unit 2 of the Centralia Generating Station in Centralia, Washington, a coal-fired power plant, remains available to operate. Centralia Unit 2 was scheduled to shut down at the end of 2025.

“America needs more reliable power, not less, and today’s order will help ensure reliable electricity generation remains available to help address periods of peak demand,” said Secretary Wright. “The Trump Administration remains committed to reversing the misguided energy subtraction policies it inherited from past leaders. Instead, we are advancing energy addition and expanding the American people’s access to affordable, reliable, and secure electricity. Similar actions preventing the premature shutdown of reliable power generation have prevented blackouts and likely saved lives."

Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, coal generating plants across the country are being saved from premature retirement. For example, in 2025, more than 17 gigawatts of coal-power electricity generation were saved from going offline.

The availability of Centralia to operate will continue to be an asset to maintain reliability in the Western Electricity Coordinating Council (WECC) Northwest region and is necessary to address elevated reliability risks in the WECC-Northwest region during extreme weather and reduce the risk of power outages that could threaten public health and safety.

As outlined in DOE’s Resource Adequacy Report, premature retirements of reliable generation resources increase the risk of power outages.

This order is in effect beginning on September 13, 2026, through December 11, 2026.

text:
A study published in May in the journal Nature Sustainability reports that the shoreline could eventually sit some 30 miles north of New Orleans. The finding does not come from a model. The authors dated a buried ridge north of the city and identified it as a shoreline from the last interglacial period, the last time global temperatures were about where they are now.

Three quarters of Louisiana’s remaining coastal wetlands are projected to be gone or going by around 2070. Two river diversion projects meant to rebuild that land broke ground and were canceled.

This week we ask what preparing actually looks like, and who gets to do it. Our guests describe a slow, generational shift inland rather than a sudden evacuation, and they push back on the idea that the people who stay are refusing to face facts. Insurance pricing, not scientific consensus, is how most people first learn what their home is worth in a warming Gulf. And in one researcher’s surveys, most residents who say they would relocate if flooding worsened also say they want to stay in the same parish.

name: North Carolina and Evs
title: VinFast fights NC effort to boot it from Chatham megasite, blames delay on 'the state's own failure'
authors: Will Doran and Jack Hagel, WRAL News, Will Doran, Jack Hagel, WRAL News
description:
State officials say they want to move on from the VinFast project to free up the land with the hopes of recruiting another company.
But VinFast, in its newly filed lawsuit response, says the state’s lawsuit is premature and that it’s still making good on its deal with economic developers.
It wants a judge to affirm that position, throw out the state’s lawsuit and award compensation for damages it says were caused by the state.
VinFast in March 2022 announced plans to invest more than $2 billion and create 7,500 jobs at the Chatham County site.
Therefore, it argues, the state’s lawsuit is premature.
text:
Electric-vehicle maker VinFast is fighting the North Carolina government’s efforts to claw back a Chatham County megasite, arguing in a new legal brief that the state’s actions are compounding delays on a multibillion-dollar factory while denying allegations that it violated its end of the bargain in one of the biggest economic development bets in state history.

Attorney General Jeff Jackson sued the Vietnamese automaker in May on behalf of the state Department of Commerce, alleging that the company missed a key contractual development deadline, triggering a buyback clause in the original sale agreement. State officials say they want to move on from the VinFast project to free up the land with the hopes of recruiting another company.

But VinFast, in its newly filed lawsuit response, says the state’s lawsuit is premature and that it’s still making good on its deal with economic developers. It wants a judge to affirm that position, throw out the state’s lawsuit and award compensation for damages it says were caused by the state. VinFast alleges that the state’s actions have hurt the company’s ability to obtain and maintain financing for the project, resulting in more delays and increased costs — barriers to meeting elements of its deal with the state.

“The state cannot rely on the absence of completed financing, additional construction spending, or related milestones to avoid its obligations … to the extent the state's own failure to cooperate prevented or materially hindered VinFast from satisfying those conditions,” the company wrote in its 80-page response, which was filed in state court this month.

A spokesperson for the state Department of Justice, which is suing on behalf of the North Carolina Department of Commerce, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment late Friday.

VinFast in March 2022 announced plans to invest more than $2 billion and create 7,500 jobs at the Chatham County site. At the time, it expected to begin construction that year and begin production by the middle of 2024.

VinFast’s plans were initially projected to grow the state’s economy by up to $71.59 billion over 32 years. The state agreed to a job-creation grant that would provide up to $316.1 million to the company in tax reimbursements over that span, provided it meets hiring and investment targets. So far, none of that proposed grant money has been paid out to the company.

Eight months after the announcement of VinFast’s plans, company executives agreed to the land-buyback deal. It gives the state the option to buy the property it originally sold to VinFast if the company failed to begin vertical construction by Jan. 1, 2024, or commence operations by July 1, 2026.

The state’s lawsuit, filed before the July deadline, focuses on vertical construction. The company and the state disagree over whether that has happened. The answer could factor into a judge’s decision over how to rule.

Vinfast says it completed the vertical construction obligation on time by pouring concrete into building footers — foundation work that’s typically measured in inches, not in stories — and that it has also built some retaining walls on site.

But the company is far from completing a project that would enable production at the site, which sits in a prime location: Off U.S. 1 in Moncure, just south of the Wake-Chatham county line. The state argues that vertical construction hasn’t begun. Separately, Chatham County officials voted in June to cancel their own incentives deal with the company, saying VinFast failed to meet project deadlines.

VinFast says it’s still trying to get up and running — and that other key deadlines tied to its deal with the state still haven’t passed. Therefore, it argues, the state’s lawsuit is premature.

The company has until Dec. 31, 2026 to create at least 1,750 jobs and make a “material investment” of at least $500 million in the site. VinFast says it has already invested about $229 million in the site, noting that meeting the investment target is feasible.

“The state's claim rests not on any positive, unequivocal statement by VinFast that it will not perform, but on [the state’s] own prediction that a delayed operational timeline will necessarily result in a future failure to meet the job-creation benchmark or an inability to meet the ‘material investment’ alternative,” the company said in its court filing.

Vinfast’s legal brief denies many other allegations lodged against it in relation to its efforts to get permits and otherwise clear bureaucratic hurdles necessary to build and start operating a factory. The company acknowledges that it doesn’t have plans to begin construction until 2028. But it says it still intends to build and that it has communicated that to the state.

“VinFast has never communicated to the state, in writing or otherwise, that it does

not intend to build a manufacturing facility on the site,” the company said in its brief. “In fact, VinFast has steadfastly communicated its position to the state that it wishes to perform under its obligations.”

The VinFast project was a key piece of former Gov. Roy Cooper’s economic development strategy. Cooper sought to recruit clean-tech companies that offered a dual benefit of helping the economy and the environment. Some projects, such as Toyota’s massive electric vehicle battery factory south of Greensboro, have been successful. Others have pulled out.

Softness in the EV market in the U.S. has complicated VinFast’s efforts. The company had warned investors of regulatory risks years ago, saying in a regulatory filing: “If current tax incentives are not available in the future, demand for EVs may stagnate or decline, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of operations, cash flows and prospects.”

The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, approved under Democratic President Joe Biden, offered buyers of EVs a $7,500 tax credit, provided a certain percentage of the vehicle was manufactured or assembled in the U.S. VinFast was hoping its North Carolina plant would have helped U.S. customers qualify for the credit. Republican President Donald Trump last year ended the $7,500 tax credit after vowing to do so in 2024. VinFast cited market factors as a reason to adjust its timeline in Chatham County.

“The decision is necessary given the well-publicized slowdown in the EV marketplace,” the company wrote in a 2024 letter to state economic development officials announcing its plans to delay construction until 2028 — a letter it quoted in the new court reply as well.

text:
By Nichola Groom

Sept 11 (Reuters) – A federal appeals court on Friday threw out an order from President Donald Trump’s administration that had forced a Michigan coal plant to remain open beyond its planned retirement.

The unanimous ruling by a three-judge panel of ​the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit found the Department ‌of Energy exceeded its authority under a rarely used emergency provision of federal law, according to court papers.

Michigan challenged the order after DOE instructed the 1960s-era J.H. Campbell plant in 2025 to remain online shortly before its planned closure.

The ruling is a setback for the administration’s efforts to preserve coal-fired generation at a time when ‌U.S. ​demand for electricity has soared due largely to the expansion ⁠of data centers. Coal-fired power is ⁠among the largest sources of carbon dioxide emissions that contribute to climate change.

“By forcing its continued operation, DOE tried a never-before-used tactic to illegally prop up the aging J.H. Campbell coal plant that nobody asked to keep, sticking ratepayers with a bill for a ​facility that should have been retired more than a year ago,” Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel said in a statement. “I am relieved that the Court saw through this facade and ⁠threw out DOE’s order that had zero basis in ⁠reality.”

Since 2025, the Trump administration has used emergency powers under the Federal ​Power Act to keep operating several aging power plants slated for retirement, including coal plants in Michigan, ​Indiana, Washington state and Colorado.

A DOE spokesperson did not comment on the ruling ‌but called the emergency orders essential to keeping the lights on during times of elevated demand.

“Rest assured, the Department of Energy will continue to protect and defend energy security for all Americans,” the agency said in an emailed statement.

The decision comes a month after DOE extended the emergency ⁠order to keep the aging J.H. Campbell Generating Plant open through November 14.

The Consumers Energy plant had been slated to close in 2025 because it was no longer economic. Its continued operation ⁠under the order cost the utility $295 ‌million from May 2025 through June 2026, according to the Michigan ⁠attorney general’s office.

Consumers Energy is reviewing the ruling, spokesperson Brian Wheeler ​said.

“While that ‌happens, we are continuing to comply with the current 90-day Department ​of Energy ⁠order that keeps the Campbell plant operating,” he said.

Environmental groups welcomed the ruling.

“The DOE needs to stay in its lane and use its emergency powers only in actual emergencies,” Michael Lenoff, an attorney with environmental group Earthjustice, said in a statement. “Preventing the market-driven retirements of coal plants to advance a coal-friendly agenda is not a proper use of emergency powers.”

(Reporting by Nichola Groom; Editing by Rod ​Nickel and David Gregorio)

Additional bills promote building electrification, mandate environmental review for polluting facilities, expand access to solar including plug-in solar, and increase oversight of utility spending to prevent companies from passing on unnecessary costs to customers. text:
Qcells opened its first Georgia plant in Dalton in 2019 when Trump’s first term tariffs on China raised a price on imports. Rollbacks in subsidies to solar construction in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act have raised questions about the future of solar expansion. But Republicans are being convinced by a different part of the pitch than clean energy: Qcells has brought nearly 2,000 factory jobs to Cartersville, where three quarters of the population voted for Trump.

This led Georgia State Republicans like Rep. Matthew Gambill to lobby for retention of federal consumer solar subsidies, and bonuses for American-manufactured solar panels. Tim Pawlenty, a former Republican Minnesota governor, now the president of the trade group Solar Energy Industries Association, has sharpened outreach to conservatives. His rationale is a potential $48 billion of announced investments and the 75,000 jobs that come with it.

It’s not all easy. Trump’s tariffs have put the squeeze on polysilicon supply: the key raw material for most solar panels. American manufacturers will need an expanded supply of domestic polysilicon, requiring billions of dollars in investment and plenty of time for manufacturing that is competitive with China. Qcells gets its polysilicon from Korea. But American manufacturers like REC Silicon have failed their quality control tests.

Companies investing now have benefited from expired subsidies and manufacturing subsidies still in force are set to end in 2033. Solar manufacturers must prepare for a world without tax credits or subsidies. Nearly three dozen House Republicans have voiced support for clean energy subsidies, Senate Republicans, however, voted against solar deployment incentives. But with subsidies ending, a stall in the rollout of factories could remove the incentives for Republican politicians to get on board with solar manufacturing.

Klimado – Navigating climate complexity just got easier. Klimado offers a user-friendly platform for tracking local and global environmental shifts, making it an essential tool for climate-aware individuals and organizations.

German environmental group sues over Russian involvement in nuclear plant

German environmental group BUND Niedersachsen has sued Lower Saxony over involvement of Rosatom, a Russian firm. The state has approved both Framatome, a French firm, and Rosatom, to produce nuclear fuel rods in Lingen.

BUND, working with anti-nuclear group .ausgestrahlt, allege errors in the procedure of granting the permit. They argue Rosatom could manipulate results given that they supply machines involved in quality control. They also contend the environmental screening relied on outdated documents, and that Rosatom’s involvement was not fully disclosed.

Framatome has described it as an interim step to allow customers to diversify, before they develop their own production technology. Lower Saxony’s environmental ministry granted approval, despite concerns. The environment minister Christian Meyer said he was ‘fundamentally opposed’ to working with Rosatom, but that he had no legal grounds to deny them administrative clearance. Berlin has said the decision was consistent with current EU laws, but that further EU sanctions would have to be implemented for the concerns to be addressed. The Lower Saxony environment ministry has agreed to assess the legal challenge raised by BUND.

No North Sea Oil decision before key by-election

Andy Burnham has postponed plans for the largest British gas reservoir ahead of key Holborn and St Pancras by-election. Zack Polanski, Green Party leader for the seat, previously occupied by Keir Starmer. Polanski has accused Labour of trying to keep the plans “under wraps”, in a by-election he claims will be influenced by climate concerns.

The election is set for the 8th of October, but the delay has the added bonus of bypassing the Labour Party conference set for the end of September. A Department of Energy Security and Net Zero spokesman defended the delay, stating that there was no agreed timing for a decision.

The project in the Jackdaw gas field is capable of boosting UK production of natural gas by around 6 percent. UK gas prices climbed to a four-year high on Thursday, as Jackdaw bosses warn of potential shortages this winter. Most of the work for the project has already been completed, and could be supplying gas “within weeks”, according to a spokesman for Adura, Equinor and Shell’s joint partnership.

Adura calls the project a “major opportunity,” noting it will contribute more than £28 billion to the economy and provide up to 3,500 jobs.

Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, warned delays could increase risks to offshore workers and push the project into deeper winter, and accused Burnham of “placing the interests of the Labour Party before the interests of Great Britain.” Zack Polanski has accused Labour of “dishonesty and betrayal.”

India proposes health labels on cheap packaged food

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSAI) floated on Thursday introducing red warning labels on food that exceeds limits on added sugar, salt or saturated fat. The All India Food Processors’ Association says 80% of packaged food in India could be flagged as high in fat, sugar or salt content. Countries such as Chile and Mexico have implemented similar policies.

Western packaged food has existed in India for about a century. Products such as Nestle’s condensed milk and Unilever’s “dalda”–a replacement for traditional, but expensive ghee–were introduced to the country around a century ago. A poor country, high quality ingredients are usually omitted from the Indian market. Nestle’s two-minute masala Maggie noodles launched in 1983. Now, around 6 billion meals eaten in India rely on the product. But in India, Maggi is made with palm oil, instead of sunflower oil as is used in Britain.

Lobbying of India’s government has been led by companies such as Coca-Cola and groups backing Nestle and PepsiCo who opposed warning labels. However, some businesses are also concerned that many traditional Indian products which could be subject to labelling are also high in sugar or fat.

Deputy Administrator Fotouhi began his visit with a tour of the Karns Meadow Stormwater Treatment Wetland in Jackson, Wyoming, alongside EPA Region 8 Administrator Cyrus Western, Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality (WDEQ) Water Quality Administrator Jennifer Zygmunt and local officials. The 40-acre wetland system was constructed with a combination of EPA and local funding to address longstanding water quality challenges in nearby Flat Creek. Today, the wetland captures and treats stormwater runoff from Jackson before it enters Flat Creek within the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. Post-implementation monitoring has demonstrated significant improvements in runoff quality, including an average 89% reduction in total settleable solids, a 95% reduction in nitrate, nitrite, and ammonia concentrations, and an 85% reduction in E. coli bacteria. The project demonstrates how targeted investments and innovative solutions can deliver measurable improvements in water quality.

The following day, Deputy Administrator Fotouhi delivered the keynote address at the Fall 2026 ECOS Meeting in Jackson, where he highlighted the Trump Administration’s environmental accomplishments during its first 18 months and EPA’s commitment to working with states to return ownership of environmental programs to state and local leaders. He was jregional administrators from all 10 EPA regions and numerous assistant administrators as they engaged with environmental regulators from all 50 states.

Deputy Administrator Fotouhi concluded his Wyoming visit with a tour of the Pinedale Anticline Natural Gas Field, one of the largest natural gas fields in the United States and a major contributor to Wyoming’s energy production for more than two decades. Supplying millions of homes with energy each day, the Pinedale Anticline is an important part of America’s domestic energy production and supports reliable, affordable power for American families. The field also demonstrates how technological innovation, combined with federal and state leadership and industry collaboration, can support environmental progress while strengthening domestic energy production. Deputy Administrator Fotouhi was joined on the tour by members of WDEQ, including Air Division Administrator Amber Potts.

text:
With help from Alex Nieves and Riley Ramirez

CARBON CLOCK: With the global climate math getting worse, California is increasingly trying to make carbon removal part of its climate strategy.

The United Nations released a new landmark report last week saying that global warming was going to blow past 1.5 degrees Celsius unless governments embraced technology to remove heat-trapping carbon dioxide from the atmosphere (see more from Corbin Hiar and Chelsea Harvey here).

But the technology remains expensive, and is controversial among environmental groups. It also hasn’t yet been proven to work at scale.

Vikrum Aiyer, head of global public policy at Heirloom Carbon, sees the U.N.’s warning as an opening for California, however. Heirloom, headquartered in the San Francisco Bay Area, develops technology to suck global warming-causing carbon dioxide directly out of the air. It has a plant near Tracy and is working on a major project in Louisiana.

Aiyer has been closely involved in California’s recent policy turn toward carbon removal, including the California Air Resources Board’s new incentives for carbon capture in its recent cap-and-invest overhaul. Now, the board is starting to write carbon storage permitting rules.

He talked to POLITICO about California’s role in the global development of ground-breaking carbon capture and storage technology, and what comes next.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Are California and the U.S. falling behind other governments in developing carbon capture policy and technology?

Brussels, the United Kingdom, Canada and Japan, they’re all leaning in, with very real, tangible forms of central industrial policy that help advance each of those countries’ case for energy security. And frankly, California started to get there, but we have more progress to make. We almost have it within our grasp.

What needs to happen in California now?

Right now we have a statutory mandate that says we need to hit a [net-zero] target by 2045. But in California, we are very clearly not on track to hit that target. So, what California represents is an opportunity to update the plan of action in a measurable way, and quite simply, our point of view is that we need to retool that climate architecture in order to actually meet our net zero mandates.

You can actually build and have California lead by making sure that you’re investing in community protections. I think that is the ultimate task in front of us. We have had these policy wins, but there have been real tensions. The onus is on us to show up in communities and demonstrate, hey, there can be community guardrails and there should be community guardrails on how you build these technologies, so there should not be a false choice between picking between the scale up of this tech and frontline communities.

Some buyers of carbon removal credits, like Microsoft, have slowed down. But then you have this big AI tech boom that will require more energy. What’s California’s role here?

I think that the AI boom makes the case for carbon removal stronger, not weaker. The buyers may be recalibrating how they think about purchases of removals, but the underlying challenge is actually getting bigger. They need extraordinary amounts of new power while still trying to meet climate commitments. That’s where California, in my mind, has an incredible opportunity. We invent much of the AI economy here. We should also be inventing the energy and carbon management infrastructure that allows it to grow responsibly.

The Trump administration has revoked a lot of funding for carbon capture and storage, but you’ve kept up negotiations on a grant for your Louisiana plant. What’s the status of those talks?

We continue to work in good faith with the Trump administration. After a long year-and-a-half review, the Department of Energy retained our project’s eligibility for up to $600 million. We actually credit that to a multifaceted coalition, workforce groups, community colleges, economic development advocates, congressional support for making the case to protect that funding. But to be straight with you, it isn’t fully closed out. We’re still updating the contract and the scope to make sure that it reflects DOE priorities while also kind of mapping to our core technologies.

Is it possible to appeal to both blue California and a red Trump administration?

I have to credit a remarkably agile and ambidextrous team that can use our left plane and right plane to talk to red states and blue states. Whether you’re Governor [Gavin] Newsom or Governor [Steve] Hilton or Governor [Xavier] Becerra, you get to create jobs and continue to move the ball on new climate technologies. Whereas, if you’re in Louisiana, and you’re in Texas, you really want to facilitate the exports of different forms of energy, and those energies currently, if they’re not low carbon intensity, will need to be adjusted for emissions mandates when they get exported into places like the European Union. Carbon management across all of these jurisdictions demonstrates real value, job creation, energy security, and the ability to continue to export.

What do you want out of the next governor, who will likely be Democrat Xavier Becerra, and how do you assess his interest in this technology?

I can’t speak on behalf of the Becerra team, but what I can tell you is that every time I hear the secretary and the attorney general campaign or stump, he is looking for win-wins, right? And I think that we are obsessed with California succeeding and leading the way. But Mr. Becerra offers a little bit of a tempering of expectations. Yes, we need to hit our climate ambitions, but no, we should not turn our backs on energy majors that are employers and communities. So, that might leave many scratching their heads. But I firmly do believe that our approach to carbon removal and California’s approach to carbon removal is exactly that win-win framework he’s looking for.

CALIFORNIA ON MY MIND: In a final legislative sprint before midterm campaigning, the House is turning its attention to California’s environmental regulations for ships.

The House plans to vote next week to axe two waivers that allow California to set strict emissions standards for ships and other harbor vessels, Amelia Davidson reports.

The two resolutions — H.J. Res. 210 and H.J. Res. 213 — were brought by California Republican Reps. Vince Fong and James Gallagher last month. They joined a widespread push by Republicans to roll back the EPA waivers that underpin California’s strict emissions standards.

Other resolutions introduced in both the House and Senate target California’s emissions standards for cars and off-road vehicles. Those are not currently slated for a House vote ahead of lawmakers’ planned seven-week departure beginning Sept. 17.

PUMP PAIN: It’s a bad day to own a truck that runs on diesel.

The average price for diesel nationwide reached $6 for the first time ever on Friday, according to AAA, as crude oil prices continue to skyrocket amid disruptions linked to the war with Iran. The price problem is even worse in California, where the average diesel price is now nearly $8.

A handful of gas stations around the state have raised their diesel prices to $9.99, fuel-tracking company GasBuddy says, the max price that can be advertised on digital displays.

Diesel prices have already exceeded $8 in Oakland and San Francisco, which have set records at $8.02 and $8.23, respectively, according to AAA.

Skyrocketing fuel prices have thwarted Republicans’ efforts to run on affordability issues as they attempt to hold Congress, and political strategists say it’s probably too late for the party to stem the fallout.

INTERNATIONAL CONNECTION: Climate change is increasing temperatures across the Tibetan Plateau. That’s led to record-breaking rainfall in California, according to a new UCLA study.

A team of atmospheric scientists found that unusually warm temperatures over the Tibetan Plateau — the world’s largest and highest plateau, located primarily in southwestern China — set up conditions that increase the likelihood of atmospheric rivers along the West Coast.

That’s a phenomenon the researchers observed while studying data from the winters of 2016-17 and 2022-23, which saw heavy precipitation in California despite these being La Niña years (a weather pattern typically associated with drier conditions).

Researchers say those higher temperatures aren’t driven by the ocean conditions that dictate La Niña and El Niño cycles, like the “super El Niño” scientists say we’re currently in. That means it’s not entirely clear what a hot winter in southwestern China would mean for California.

“While we wait to see how the current event unfolds, we must also closely monitor early winter surface temperatures on the Tibetan Plateau,” said UCLA Professor Yongkang Xue.

title: Opinion | Hampshire's Land: Zone for the Future, Not the Next Developer - Amherst Indy
description:
Hampshire College is closing, and now Amherst has a different problem: What happens to the land?
That is why the Hampshire campus zoning matters so much.
The July zoning-study information session made something very clear: Hampshire College owns the property and will ultimately decide what happens to it.
The town’s Master Plan lays out a long-term blueprint for land use, housing, economic development, natural resources, transportation, and municipal facilities.
Could UMass, Amherst College, and the remaining Five College institutions provide research partnerships?
text:
Hampshire College is closing, and now Amherst has a different problem: What happens to the land?

The easy answer is to say housing. Amherst needs housing. Amherst already has a stated goal of creating 200 affordable homes for households earning below 100% of area median income over the next five years. But if the answer to every Amherst land-use problem is simply to build more apartments, we should at least ask whether we are solving the problem or reproducing it on a different piece of land.

That is why the Hampshire campus zoning matters so much.

The town is now studying how the approximately 800-acre Hampshire campus could be used after the college closes. The July zoning-study information session made something very clear: Hampshire College owns the property and will ultimately decide what happens to it. But Amherst controls zoning. The town’s study is examining developable areas, water and sewer capacity, roads, housing-market demand, and economic-development opportunities before writing new zoning.

That means Amherst should not wait for a buyer to arrive with a proposal and then ask: “Can we make this work?”

The question should be reversed: What does Amherst need this land to do — and what zoning will make that possible?

Don’t Turn Hampshire into Another Student Housing Pipeline

Housing absolutely belongs in the conversation. But there is a huge difference between housing that Amherst needs and housing that happens to be financially profitable to build in Amherst. Amherst could add hundreds or thousands of units while doing very little to solve the town’s underlying problem.

The town has already been wrestling with the consequences of its college town housing economy. Downtown Amherst is being reshaped by large residential projects, while residents continue to argue about whether the community is losing too much of its year-round population. The Hampshire property gives Amherst an opportunity to be more specific.

If housing is permitted on the Hampshire campus, zoning should prioritize year-round housing, workforce housing, family housing, and genuinely affordable units, rather than simply maximizing the number of bedrooms that can be squeezed onto the property.

And the town should ask a brutally practical question before approving anything: What does this development contribute to Amherst after the ribbon-cutting?

More residents mean more demand for roads, emergency services, schools, utilities, and other municipal services. A development that produces housing but adds little recurring municipal revenue can still leave current taxpayers carrying much of the infrastructure burden.

The town’s Master Plan lays out a long-term blueprint for land use, housing, economic development, natural resources, transportation, and municipal facilities. That is exactly how Hampshire should be approached.

Then There Is the Farm

The other extreme would be to preserve the entire property as open space or agricultural land.

Amherst’s 2026 Open Space and Recreation Plan identifies the Hampshire campus as containing significant agricultural resources, including prime agricultural land. Agriculture could support farm businesses, food production, educational programs, agritourism, farmers’ markets, and outdoor recreation. It would also protect land that cannot simply be recreated once it has been paved over. But agriculture alone probably does not answer Amherst’s fiscal problem.

A farm can create jobs, generate economic activity and community value, and protect land. It does not necessarily produce the level of taxable commercial activity that a successful business district or innovation campus could.

So Amherst does not have to be all development or all preservation.

This Is Where Alex Kent’s Idea Gets Interesting

Alex Kent’s proposal to create an innovation incubator on the Hampshire campus deserves more attention than Amherst’s usual reaction: putting every new idea through the civic equivalent of a 12-step referral process.

His idea is essentially this: turn Hampshire into an economic engine rather than another residential development. And, importantly, the for-profit businesses it would house could potentially expand Amherst’s taxable commercial base.

A stronger economic base might be able to pay for the things residents already complain about: roads, public safety, Department of Public Works (DPW) facilities, schools, infrastructure, and housing.

The town’s current zoning study explicitly says it is examining opportunities for economic development alongside housing demand and infrastructure capacity.

So Alex’s proposal may be one of the ideas the zoning study should be considering.

There Are Real Precedents

The idea is not simply “build a tech incubator and hope.” Former institutional or industrial properties have been converted into economic-development districts that combine research, entrepreneurship, training, and commercial activity. Amherst should commission a serious feasibility study.

Could UMass, Amherst College, and the remaining Five College institutions provide research partnerships?

Could Massachusetts economic-development agencies help finance the infrastructure?

Could companies receive incentives tied to actual job creation, apprenticeships, and tax generation, rather than simply receiving another tax break?

Those are questions with measurable answers.

UMass Creates an Awkward Comparison

Amherst residents have watched the University of Massachusetts make substantial capital investments in athletics and recreation. The university built the $34.5 million Football Performance Center in 2014, and it has continued investing in McGuirk Alumni Stadium and other athletic facilities. UMass has also developed a much larger long-term capital plan that includes major athletics, recreation, academic, and infrastructure projects.

The point is that institutions invest in the economic and institutional assets they believe will generate value for their future.

Why couldn’t the Hampshire campus become an economic asset for the town?

If UMass can make a multimillion-dollar bet on a football program, Amherst should at least be willing to investigate whether a former college campus can become a multimillion-dollar bet on clean technology, agricultural innovation, advanced manufacturing, health research, and entrepreneurship.

That comparison of the two investments reveals that vision is not free, and neither is refusing to have one.

The Smartest Answer May Actually Be All Three

This is where I think Amherst should go. Not housing versus farms versus Alex Kent’s incubator. Rather, housing + agriculture + economic development.

Preserve the environmentally sensitive, agricultural, and forested portions of the property. Use the portions with appropriate infrastructure and development capacity for carefully planned housing — but make it housing Amherst actually needs, not simply another student apartment complex. Then create an economic-development district around research, technology, agriculture, clean energy, health care, and advanced manufacturing. Build paid apprenticeship and workforce-development programs into the zoning and development agreements.

And make one principle nonnegotiable: Development must produce public value. And that principle should be established before the land is sold.

text:
Gov. Whitmer joined the Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity’s Office of Future Mobility and Electrification (OFME) to announce $1.5 million in grant funding awarded through the Michigan Mobility Funding Platform to 10 mobility projects that will help companies bring new technologies to market, advance clean energy and transportation solutions and strengthen industries supporting Michigan jobs and economic growth.

The latest round of funding will help companies test and deploy technologies in real-world Michigan environments, reducing barriers to commercialization and creating new opportunities for businesses to develop, validate and scale their solutions in the state. Projects receiving funding span hydrogen production and fueling, electric vehicle charging, autonomous systems, accessible transportation, infrastructure inspection and other emerging mobility technologies.

“Michigan is the best place to invest in clean energy innovation,” said Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. “Today’s announcement reaffirms our commitment to supporting good-paying jobs, advancing clean energy solutions and helping Michigan businesses grow and compete on a global scale. This grant will help entrepreneurs create and test new mobility technology, making advancements in electric vehicles, accessible transportation options, infrastructure and more. Let’s keep working together to build the future right here in Michigan.”

Launched by OFME in partnership with the Michigan Economic Development Corporation (MEDC) and the Michigan Department of Transportation (MDOT), the Michigan Mobility Funding Platform focuses on catalyzing and scaling mobility solutions across air, land, space and water.

“Michigan continues to serve as the place where mobility innovation moves from concept to reality,” said OFME Chief Mobility Officer Justine Johnson. “Through the Michigan Mobility Funding Platform, we are helping innovators deploy, test and scale technologies while accelerating commercialization and supporting business growth. That gives companies more opportunities to validate new solutions and bring transformative technologies to market right here in Michigan, helping our state compete for the technologies, investment and jobs shaping the future of transportation.”

This latest round of funding supports projects through both Real-World Deployment Grants and Test Site Grants, helping companies validate technologies, accelerate commercialization and create stronger pathways from pilot to deployment. By connecting businesses with Michigan communities, infrastructure and testing facilities, the platform helps companies demonstrate solutions in real-world environments while bringing new investment and innovation into the state.

Real World Deployment Grant Recipients

Boston Dynamics — $150,000 [Detroit]

Boston Dynamics and Bedrock will deploy Spot robots to map and patrol challenging environments, develop reliable localization and inspection routines and define system requirements for enhanced mobility and anomaly response.

Detroit Hydrogen Exchange — $250,000 [Detroit]

This project will convert and deploy a hydrogen fuel cell Class 8 refuse truck under real municipal operating conditions in Detroit to validate performance readiness.

Neology — $250,000 [Detroit]

Neology will launch a mobility-grade hydrogen production and refueling site in Detroit to support real-world medium- and heavy-duty vehicle fueling.

Connected Traffic Intelligence – $150,000 [Oakland and Macomb counties]

Connected Traffic Intelligence will pilot their traffic signal optimization platform at intersections across Oakland and Macomb counties with the aim to reduce congestion, lower public infrastructure costs, and modernize transportation operations without requiring expensive roadside hardware investments.

Motmot – $75,000 [East Lansing, Meridian Township, Kalamazoo, Marshall]

Motmot will partner with municipal water infrastructure operators to conduct underground water infrastructure inspection pilots with their underwater robotics platform.

Test Site Grant Recipients

Cargility, Inc. — $75,000 [Detroit Smart Parking Lab]

Cargility is testing their portable, weight-bearing stabilization system aimed at enabling safer and more accessible entry and exit from passenger vehicles for people with mobility challenges.

Retrospect Autonomous Systems — $150,000 [American Center for Mobility]

Retrospect is testing real-time safety monitoring software for autonomous vehicle validation and fleet management.

Kodiak Technologies – $180,000 [Michigan Tech and American Center for Mobility]

Kodiak Technologies will pilot their plug-in hybrid diesel-electric heavy-duty snow blower aimed at supporting airport snow removal operations.

AmHyTech – $115,000 [Detroit Smart Parking Lab]

AmHyTech will deploy a modular ammonia-to-hydrogen refueling station to validate their hydrogen storage and generation solutions. This station will then be used to power a hydrogen bike or moped in a controlled test site environment.

OpenRoad Technologies – $135,000 [Kettering Mobility Research Center]

WASHINGTON (AP) — In a defeat for the Trump administration, a federal court on Friday ruled that the Energy Department exceeded its authority when it forced a Michigan coal-fired power plant to stay open past its scheduled retirement date last year.

READ MORE: As Trump throws lifeline to coal plants, critics warn of higher costs and health risks

Energy Secretary Chris Wright had said the 64-year-old J.H. Campbell Generating Plant was needed to ensure reliable electricity in the region, and he used emergency powers to keep it operating. Environmental groups and three states — Michigan, Illinois and Minnesota — went to court to try to overturn orders keeping the plant online.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit sided with the states and the groups, saying there was no real emergency under the law.

The section of the Federal Power Act that allows emergency orders "is essentially a narrow, last-resort backstop," Appeals Court Judge Cornelia Pillard wrote for a unanimous three-judge panel. Use of emergency authority "is triggered only when there is a need for immediate, essentially last-resort action and the circumstances require action by DOE in particular, as opposed to action by the state or states responsible for resource adequacy," she added.

Reversing the Campbell plant's "long and carefully planned retirement" is "disruptive," Pillard wrote.

Trump administration order called 'unlawful political stunt' by critics

Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel said she was relieved the appeals court "threw out DOE's order that had zero basis in reality."

Nessel, a Democrat, said her office "has been fighting this unlawful political stunt at every turn, and this ruling proves what we have been saying all along: this administration does not get to invent fake emergencies to bypass the rule of law against the best interests of Michigan residents."

The Michigan case is one of several legal disputes that have emerged across the country as the Trump administration uses emergency powers to force a half-dozen coal-fired plants to remain open.

The orders, which also apply to plants in Indiana, Colorado, Florida and Washington state, are raising ratepayer bills and adding air and water pollution that could have been avoided, critics say. An oil and gas plant in Pennsylvania was also ordered to keep its turbines running as a hedge against electricity shortages in the mid-Atlantic grid.

President Donald Trump declared a national energy emergency in a January 2025 executive order, citing demand increases from artificial intelligence and data center growth.

Energy Department says coal-plant order saved lives during peak weather events

An Energy Department spokesperson said the emergency orders — including at Campbell — "prevented blackouts and likely saved hundreds of lives during peak capacity events this past year," especially severe winter storms in late January and early February.

At the peak of the storms, coal generation in affected regions increased by 25% compared to the previous year, spokeswoman Emily Matthews said. The Campbell plant provided over 650 megawatts — enough power for hundreds of thousands of homes — every day from Jan. 21 to Feb. 1, she said.

The Energy Department "will continue to protect and defend energy security for all Americans," she said.

Keeping the Michigan plant open beyond its May 2025 retirement has cost about $259 million so far, according to new financial filings. Those losses will likely be paid by families and businesses in the Midwest, opponents of the order say.

Consumers Energy, which operates the Campbell plant, said it was reviewing the court ruling. In the meantime, the utility will keep the plant operating under terms of a recent DOE order that extends its directive through mid-November, spokesman Brian Wheeler said in a statement.

Environmentalists say they'll continue to fight the administration's orders

Ted Kelly, U.S. clean energy director at the Environmental Defense Fund, said the court ruling rejected the Trump administration's nationwide effort to force "unreliable, aging coal plants that are bleeding money and polluting communities to stay online."

The Energy Department's "unlawful actions attempted to make families and businesses in the Midwest wastefully pay hundreds of millions of dollars for a coal plant that should have been shut down over a year ago," Kelly said Friday. The Campbell plant and other aging sites are "incredibly expensive, dangerous to our health and break down frequently," he said.

Sanjay Narayan, a lawyer for the Sierra Club, called the ruling a victory for families across the Midwest who are "paying to keep this old, expensive and dirty power plant online."

The Trump administration "has been pulling out all the stops to try to bolster dirty and expensive fossil fuels at public expense. This reckless agenda will not succeed," Narayan said. "We will continue to fight back against the other illegal extensions across the country."

Associated Press writer Ed White in Detroit contributed to this story.

text:
In 2024, the Environmental Protection Agency administrator signed a regulation to sharply reduce toxic pollution from petrochemical plants.

Families in Louisiana's "Cancer Alley" say recent rollbacks of the rule under the second Trump administration are putting their health and future in danger.

Here's what to know

The concerns have to do with the Hazardous Organic National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants, often called the HON rule. It's a Biden-era regulation meant to curb toxic pollution from more than 200 petrochemical plants, many of them in Texas and Louisiana.

Just months into President Donald Trump's second term, the administration had granted temporary exemptions to dozens of these facilities. According to Yale Environment 360, the administration also plans to rewrite the rule.

In Louisiana's lower Mississippi River corridor, residents say the fight is personal.

Tish Taylor, who lives with her family in St. John the Baptist Parish, told Yale E360, "Everything that the Biden administration did to help protect us was pretty much just thrown in the garbage," and replaced by "a death sentence."

According to EPA estimates cited by the outlet, the rule would prevent about 6,200 tons of toxic air pollution each year, reduce ethylene oxide and chloroprene emissions by nearly 80%, and lower cancer risks linked to air toxins by 96% in affected communities.

St. John is one of the places where the situation is especially acute. The parish is part of the 85-mile stretch between New Orleans and Baton Rouge known as "Cancer Alley," where plants process about a quarter of the country's petrochemical products and where cancer rates are among the country's highest.

Across the region, Black residents make up a disproportionate share of the people facing the highest pollution burdens.

More background

The HON rule required petrochemical plants to improve pollution controls, monitor gases released at facility fencelines, and make repairs when dangerous chemical levels exceeded limits.

It also removed a major loophole that had let plants release extra pollution during startups and shutdowns, including before storms or during maintenance.

"We've fought for decades to close loopholes and get real checks on chemical leaks," Michele Roberts of the Environmental Justice Health Alliance said in a press release announcing a lawsuit over the exemptions in 2025. "These standards target the dangerous chemicals that create a huge cancer risk in communities like Mossville, Louisiana, and others throughout the country."

Tracey Woodruff, a Stanford University epidemiology and population health professor who previously worked on toxic assessments at the EPA, told Yale E360 about the chemicals covered by the rule, "We've known about their toxicity for decades."

What's being done?

Local and national advocacy groups are fighting back in court, suing the Trump administration over the exemptions and arguing they are based on false claims.

"The Trump administration is illegally offering chemical plants a free pass to pollute toxics," EDF attorney Rosalie Winn said in the 2025 release.

Annie Fox, an attorney at the Clean Air Council, told Yale E360, "These are supposed to be rare exceptions that are well-grounded in research and facts."

Where can I learn more?

Disputes over environmental regulations are unfolding in courtrooms and communities across the U.S. and around the world. These stories highlight some of the efforts to push back against industry power and seek stronger protections.

• In Louisiana, residents said permits for Formosa Plastics put polluters before people.

• In Georgia, families sued over catastrophic toxic chemical exposure near their homes.

• In New York, lawmakers urged a ban on biosolids as contamination fears grew.

These examples underscore how quickly environmental protections can unravel — and how much communities might rely on advocates and courts and more to step in.

title: When the sun sets on solar panel companies, can patent portfolios offer a new dawn?
description:
Traditionally, patent portfolios within the PV sector were accumulated primarily to protect technologies incorporated into products that companies intended to manufacture and sell.
However, as solar markets mature, the role of patent portfolios within the PV sector is increasingly expanding beyond product protection.
Portfolio value in a maturing solar market The increasing importance of patent licensing and portfolio transactions is not unique to the solar sector.
Following its withdrawal from solar manufacturing, LG reportedly transferred 352 US solar patents and more than 590 Korean solar patents to JinkoSolar, with industry reports suggesting that the wider transaction may have involved approximately 2000 solar patent assets globally.
The solar industry continues to evolve rapidly, and the role played by patent portfolios is likely to evolve alongside it.
text:
This growth has been supported by significant reductions in module costs and continued expansion of manufacturing capacity. Solar module prices reportedly fell by approximately 90% between 2015 – 2024, whilst 647 GW of new solar capacity was added globally in 2025 alone. As a result, photovoltaic (PV) technologies have evolved from an emerging renewable energy source into a major contributor to global electricity generation.

Patent ownership and transaction trends can often serve as a useful indicator for understanding how companies respond to changing market dynamics. Traditionally, patent portfolios within the PV sector were accumulated primarily to protect technologies incorporated into products that companies intended to manufacture and sell. Patent protection helped prevent competitors from copying commercially significant innovations and supported investment in bringing new photovoltaic products to market.

However, as solar markets mature, the role of patent portfolios within the PV sector is increasingly expanding beyond product protection. Patent portfolios are becoming tools not only for protecting what a company makes and sells, but also for generating value through licensing activities, portfolio sales, technology transfers, and other commercial arrangements. In this respect, patent portfolios can allow innovation to continue generating returns long after manufacturing activities have ceased or a company has exited a particular market. Whether a portfolio can continue to generate such returns will, however, often depend on how broadly and strategically the underlying intellectual property has been protected. Whilst patents directed narrowly to particular products may have limited residual value once those products leave the market, patents protecting broader technical concepts can remain valuable long after manufacturing has ceased.

Portfolio value in a maturing solar market

The increasing importance of patent licensing and portfolio transactions is not unique to the solar sector. The mobile phone industry provides a useful example. Former market leaders such as Nokia, Sony Ericsson, and LG invested heavily in technology development during periods of rapid growth. Whilst the handset market changed considerably over time, many of the patent portfolios generated during that period continued to retain substantial commercial significance through licensing and other monetisation activities long after the associated product lines had declined. Increasingly, similar dynamics can also be observed within the solar sector.

LG Electronics provides an example of how patent portfolios can continue creating value after a company has exited a market. In 2022, the company announced its withdrawal from solar manufacturing, citing increasing competition and continuing business challenges within the sector.

The decision was notable because LG had established a strong reputation for high-efficiency photovoltaic products and had invested heavily in advanced N-type cell architectures, a technology direction that has subsequently gained significant traction across the solar industry.

This example illustrates how those who pioneer new technologies do not always remain major market participants. As solar markets mature, factors such as manufacturing scale, supply chain efficiencies, and production costs have become increasingly important determinants of commercial success. Thus, companies with strong technological capabilities may conclude that resources can be deployed more effectively elsewhere whilst continuing to derive value from innovations developed within the sector.

This is where patent portfolios can become particularly important. Following its withdrawal from solar manufacturing, LG reportedly transferred 352 US solar patents and more than 590 Korean solar patents to JinkoSolar, with industry reports suggesting that the wider transaction may have involved approximately 2000 solar patent assets globally.

The transaction demonstrates that the end of a manufacturing operation does not necessarily mark the end of the commercial life of the underlying technology. Rather, patent portfolios may provide a mechanism through which value generated from earlier R&D investments can continue to be realised long after products have left the market.

The long commercial life of solar technologies

Recent high-profile disputes in Europe relating to TOPCon (Tunnel Oxide Pas-sivated Contact) solar cells provide a particularly interesting illustration of this principle.

TOPCon architectures utilise a thin tunnel oxide layer and passivated contacts to improve performance compared with earlier photovoltaic technologies and are expected to account for an increasingly large share of global solar manufacturing over the coming years.

Several important European patents relating to TOPCon technologies, including EP2787541 (Solar Cell) and EP4092759 (Solar Cell Panel), were originally filed by LG Electronics during its participation in the solar sector. Following LG's withdrawal from solar manufacturing, these patents were transferred through subsequent portfolio transactions, first to JinkoSolar and subsequently to JingAo Solar, and continue to form part of commercially significant patent portfolios within the solar sector.

Notably, these patents have continued to feature in high-profile disputes in Europe involving JingAo Solar and Astronergy, with parallel proceedings before both the European Patent Office (EPO) and the Unified Patent Court (UPC) examining aspects of the patents' validity and enforcement.

The continuing relevance of these patents shows that the commercial lifespan of a technology is not necessarily limited by the lifespan of the business that first developed it. Ownership may change, manufacturing strategies may change, and competitive landscapes may evolve, yet the underlying patents can continue influencing market behaviour and generating revenue for many years.

Strategic considerations for solar innovators

As solar markets continue to mature, several strategic considerations emerge for businesses developing the next generation of photovoltaic technologies. Firstly, businesses may wish to consider patent portfolios in the context of multiple potential commercial outcomes. Whilst protecting products remains an important objective, patent portfolios can also support licensing activities, collaborative development arrangements, acquisitions, divestments, and technology transfer opportunities. The relative importance of these outcomes will, of course, depend on the company's technology, market position, and broader commercial strategy.

Secondly, there may be advantages in focusing protection on technologies likely to remain commercially relevant as the industry evolves. Potential examples include advanced cell architectures, manufacturing processes, automation technologies, predictive maintenance systems, grid integration technologies, and future generations of tandem or perovskite-based devices, although, as with any technology forecast, the future direction of innovation remains difficult to predict.

Finally, as both the solar industry and other mature technology sectors witnessed, the commercial significance of innovation is not always reflected solely by market share or manufacturing output. In some instances, patent portfolios have continued to generate value long after the original business model, product line, or market position has changed.

The solar industry continues to evolve rapidly, and the role played by patent portfolios is likely to evolve alongside it. Whilst patents have traditionally been viewed principally as tools for protecting products and supporting commercialisation, recent developments suggest that they may also provide mechanisms for pre-serving and transferring value as markets mature. Although every business will face different commercial circumstances, patent portfolios can remain commercially relevant throughout a much larger portion of a technology's lifecycle than is sometimes assumed.

text:
By Abdul Ghani

The government is planning to introduce special electricity tariffs for new high-technology industries, including electric vehicles (EVs), batteries and data centres, under the proposed National Industrial Policy (NIP) 2026, according to the policy document available with Wealth Pakistan.

The proposed measure is part of the government’s broader strategy to improve the cost competitiveness of the industrial sector and attract investment into new and innovative industries.

According to the NIP, the government supports full implementation of the Energy Wheeling Policy and regular monitoring of its impact on export-oriented industries. The policy also proposes special tariffs for new high-technology greenfield sectors, with rates set just above marginal cost.

The proposed tariff framework specifically identifies electric vehicles, battery manufacturing and data centres among the sectors that could benefit from special power arrangements.

The move could help reduce one of the major structural challenges facing new industrial investment in Pakistan — high energy costs — while making emerging technology-intensive industries more competitive.

The NIP also proposes reduced tariffs for existing industrial units that consume incremental power beyond specified thresholds, potentially encouraging manufacturers to expand production and increase electricity consumption for productive activity.

Alongside tariff reforms, the policy calls for continued upgrading of transmission and distribution infrastructure, recognizing that reliable electricity supply is essential for industrial expansion and high-technology operations.

The proposal forms part of a wider supply-side reform programme under which the government intends to lower production costs, improve industrial infrastructure and encourage investment in sectors with high productivity and export potential.

The power-cost initiative comes within a broader 19-point industrial reform agenda designed to reposition Pakistan’s industrial sector as an engine of investment, productivity, employment and exports.

text:
The Albanese government has been accused of breaking a promise after it shelved a longstanding commitment to bring in packaging standards intended to force manufacturers and retailers to cut plastic waste.

The federal environment department told industry representatives via email last week that the promise would not be kept before the next election because the government did not want to “exacerbate cost of living pressures”.

The director of the Boomerang Alliance, Jeff Angel, warned “ongoing inaction and token measures won’t be tolerated”.

“The Albanese government’s failure to act on packaging reform as promised is a repudiation of the public’s support of recycling and concerns about the health and environmental impacts of plastic pollution,” he said.

“The scale and breadth of outrage across a broad set of stakeholders from green groups to industry to state governments is something I have not seen before.”

The packaging laws had been under development since a 2023 agreement between the federal and state governments that the then environment minister, Tanya Plibersek, described as “historic”. They would have required producers to cut waste and boost plastics recycling.

Clean Up Australia’s annual litter reports highlight the persistent problem of packaging in the environment, with packaging accounting for 59.5% of all litter reported.

A suite of potential rules would have set design standards for packaging, for example by prohibiting use of certain chemicals, restricting unnecessary or excessive layers of packaging, or limiting the amount of empty space permitted within packaging.

Other potential changes could have required producers to be responsible for the packaging across its full life cycle – from the design stage to how the packaging is used and then disposed of.

The government’s decision to shelve its plans were due to its concern that any costs arising from changes could be passed on to consumers when they bought products such as groceries.

The department email said the environment minister, Murray Watt, wanted to pursue reforms “in a way that balances environmental outcomes with the broader needs of the economy, with the government looking closely at its policies to ensure it does not exacerbate cost of living pressures”.

The email said “a new Commonwealth scheme for packaging will not be introduced in this term of government” and the government would instead work with the states and territories “on opportunities to improve Australia’s packaging regulations and policies in the nearer term”.

The plastics campaign manager at the Australian Marine Conservation Society, Cip Hamilton, said the decision was “deeply disappointing”.

“Recyclers want action, businesses want certainty, and environmental organisations want an end to plastic pollution,” she said.

“Almost everyone was at the table, and the government has walked away.”

Hamilton said the laws would have “put the cost and the responsibility back where they belong – on the businesses using the packaging, not the households stuck with it”.

“Plastic pollution is having very real consequences. Little penguins are choking, seabirds are starving, and corals are suffocating,” she said.

Australian Packaging Covenant Organisation chief executive, Chris Foley, said producers wanted certainty. He said a national packaging regime with clear rules would “unlock investment in recycling, and replace fragmented approaches with a more consistent system”.

The chief executive of the Australian Council of Recycling, Suzanne Toumbourou, said the sector was calling for a “nationally consistent scheme with real targets”.

“We are already seeing recycling facilities close, with others under growing pressure, and the investment that built them go to waste, because there is no policy certainty to keep them viable,” she said.

Watt said the government understood that waste and recycling firms faced a range of challenges.

“The Albanese government is working closely with industry, and state and territory governments to strengthen the systems that support recycling, and improve the circularity, of Australia’s packaging,” he said.

“We’re committed to delivering stronger environmental outcomes while keeping costs to consumers and wider industry in check.”

He said the government’s immediate focus was to work with the states and territories to “reduce waste by harmonising packaging and recycling policy in Australia”.

text:
The state's power grid managers plan to launch a survey of 461 data centers' water and energy usage next week as part of an audit ordered by Gov. Greg Abbott.

The governor's order has paused power grid connections for some large data centers until the audit is complete.

The Electric Reliability Council of Texas, or ERCOT, which manages the state's main power grid, said data centers will have until mid-October to complete the roughly 130-question survey. The survey includes questions about "financial assistance, power self-sufficiency, water and cooling, community impact, and ownership," according to ERCOT.

Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox.

The survey's participants include 247 large data centers, classified as projects that are requesting at least 75 megawatts of power from the Texas grid — enough to power 18,750 Texas homes during a hot summer day or cold winter night. It also includes 214 "medium" data centers, which are requesting between 25 and 75 megawatts of power from the grid.

Chad Seely, a senior vice president with ERCOT, said the agency will work with a consultant to present its findings to the governor, the Public Utility Commission of Texas and lawmakers.

"We’ll also be able to have essentially a report card where we think that there are deficiencies in responses and be able to make that public as well," he said during a presentation to the commission on Friday.

However, companies' individual responses will remain confidential and will not be released to the public.

ERCOT unveils “Batch Zero” estimates

ERCOT on Friday also gave preliminary estimates for how many projects will be included included in "Batch Zero," a group of data centers and other large energy consumers that the agency is evaluating so they can join the power grid.

The agency said 362 large energy consumers had been approved for inclusion in the Batch Zero study. Those projects represent requests for 191.8 gigawatts of power – roughly double the amount of energy used to power the entire state during record-breaking demand.

According to the agency, 373 projects were excluded from Batch Zero. The projects were requesting more than 300 gigawatts of electricity from the grid.

However, Seely cautioned that the number of projects included in Batch Zero is subject to change.

"We are going through dispute processes," he said. "These numbers will change."

Verification process

As part of the governor’s audit, ERCOT must verify that these Batch Zero projects are actually ready to be built — for example, by providing a lease or property deed and permits.

ERCOT was already planning to take that step as the agency simultaneously conducted an “interconnection study” to determine how much electricity each large data center project could actually receive. Now, it has to complete the verification process before beginning the interconnection study.

So far, the state's power grid managers have sent requests for information to 231 large energy consumers included in Batch Zero as part of the "verification" process. These data centers will have until Sept. 23 to respond to these questions, though they may request an extension.

ERCOT said it will create dashboards that track how many data centers have responded to its community impact survey and verification review. The agency will also release blank templates of the surveys on its website.

"We’ll be able to come back throughout the coming months and give you all kind of a real-time update on the progress of both these work streams and identify any issues," Seely told the commission Friday.

The state's power grid managers plan to present the final results of the audit in December.

text:
WASHINGTON — The Department of Energy exceeded its authority under the Federal Power Act when it ordered the continued operation of a coal-fired power plant in Michigan that had been scheduled for retirement, a federal appeals court ruled on Friday.

The decision challenges the legal basis for similar directives issued by the agency regarding fossil fuel-fired power plants in six states.

The U.S. Circuit Court of the District of Columbia found the Energy Department’s order extending the operations of the J.H. Campbell plant in Michigan was unlawful, stating that no emergency existed to justify the mandate.

The judges held that the directive was inconsistent with the text of the Federal Power Act, established regulatory precedents, and the division of authority between federal and state regulators.

The J.H. Campbell plant, in operation for over 60 years, was scheduled for retirement on May 31, 2025.

Following that date, Energy Secretary Chris Wright issued a 90-day emergency order, which was subsequently re-extended five times.

The facility has already operated for more than a year beyond its planned retirement date.

Financial documents filed by the plant’s owner, Consumers Energy, indicate that the continued operation of the facility has incurred $259 million in additional costs as of June 30, 2026.

The utility company has sought to recover these expenses from ratepayers in 11 states: Michigan, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Minnesota, Missouri, North Dakota, South Dakota, Wisconsin and Montana.

The legal challenge to the department’s order was brought by the states of Michigan, Minnesota, and Illinois, in conjunction with the Environmental Defense Fund and eight other public interest groups.

Ted Kelly, director and lead counsel for U.S. Clean Energy at the Environmental Defense Fund, said the court’s ruling was a rejection of the Trump administration’s nationwide push “forcing unreliable, aging coal plants that are bleeding money and polluting communities to stay online.”

“The Department of Energy’s unlawful actions attempted to make families and businesses in the Midwest wastefully pay hundreds of millions of dollars for a coal plant that should have been shut down over a year ago,” Kelly continued, adding. “That’s why these aging coal plants are scheduled to retire in the first place – they are incredibly expensive, dangerous to our health and break down frequently.”

The Department of Energy had maintained that the J.H. Campbell plant was essential for grid reliability.

However, grid operator data from June 2025, cited in the case, indicated that the Midwest grid possessed sufficient power capacity during a period in which the facility experienced partial failures.

The court emphasized that the emergency power granted to the department is intended for imminent situations that cannot be addressed by other regulators.
