Citing an “exceptionally difficult” year for Utah farmers due to drought, wildfire and animal disease, Utah Department of Agriculture and Food officials said they are taking an “unprecedented step” to give financial relief to producers with active department of agriculture loans.

“Utah’s farmers and ranchers have faced challenge after challenge this year, and we want them to know that we are in their corner,” UDAF Commissioner Kelly Pehrson said in a prepared statement in a news release issued Friday. “We know producers are hurting, and we want to help.”

Beginning Nov. 1, all existing UDAF loans will automatically be reduced to 0% interest for one year. Borrowers will also have the option to defer their loan payments for up to 12 months, the department said.

The 0% interest rate will run through Oct. 31, 2027. Borrowers don’t need to take any action to receive the temporary interest reduction, so long as they have an active UDAF loan during that time frame. On. Nov. 1, 2027, rates will revert back.

Cox issues emergency declaration over crops lost to unseasonal weather

Borrowers who need more relief may also apply to defer their payments, available in monthly, quarterly, semiannual and annual payment schedules, department officials said. Borrowers who have already made their 2026 payment may also choose to defer their 2027 payment instead.

Those who want to defer payments must fill out an online form by Oct. 31.

More information about how to apply is available on the UDAF’s loan website.

The new loan options will give farmers more flexibility as they recover from challenges posed by the 2026 production year, stricken by extreme drought, unprecedented water conditions, record-low snowpack, and historically high temperatures.

“UDAF’s job is to make agriculture work in Utah, and right now that means doing everything we reasonably can to give producers some breathing room and help keep their operations moving forward,” Pehrson said.

The department’s new loan options are temporary. They were approved unanimously by the Utah Conservation Commission last month, along with the Utah Agricultural Advisory Board on Sept. 9, according to state officials.

State agriculture officials noted in Friday’s release that Gov. Spencer Cox has “championed these unprecedented relief measures as a meaningful investment in the farmers and ranchers who feed Utah and sustain rural communities across the state.”

“By providing immediate financial relief during an exceptionally difficult year, state leaders are sending a clear message to Utah producers: we are committed to helping you weather today’s challenges and continue operating for years to come,” the department said.

State officials also pointed to the UDAF’s broader efforts to help farmers through this year’s challenges, including working to connect producers with disaster assistance, technical support, emergency loans and other tools meant to help keep their businesses viable

“Utah’s farmers and ranchers are being hit from every direction this year, and for some, the question is whether they can keep their operations going,” Sierra Nelson, executive director of the Utah Wool Growers Association and Agricultural Advisory Board member, said in a prepared statement.

Nelson applauded state agriculture officials and Cox for “recognizing the urgency of this moment and taking meaningful action.”

“This relief will provide a much-needed lifeline, but just as importantly, it sends a message to producers that they are not facing these challenges alone — that they have partners who understand what they’re going through and are willing to stand with them and advocate for them,” Nelson said.

title: Enabling Business Growth: The Environmental Advantage - LinkedIn
description:
Yesterday, we brought together leaders from across Scotland's business community to explore a shared ambition: how a thriving environment can help unlock sustainable economic growth.
Good regulation should protect people and the environment, but it should also support responsible investment, innovation and growth.
For us, it means being able to focus more effort where it has the greatest impact: tackling environmental harm, addressing non-compliance and supporting positive environmental outcomes.

text:
Yesterday, we brought together leaders from across Scotland's business community to explore a shared ambition: how a thriving environment can help unlock sustainable economic growth.

Hosted at Glasgow's Technology & Innovation Centre, the event welcomed representatives from sectors including energy, whisky, agriculture, construction and manufacturing, alongside trade bodies, partners and business organisations. It provided an opportunity to hear directly from SEPA's leadership team, connect with experts delivering change on the ground and take part in focused discussions on the environmental and economic opportunities ahead.

Scotland's environmental advantage

Opening the event, our Chair, Lisa Tennant , reflected on the unique strengths that position Scotland for success.

“Scotland has extraordinary strengths… We have abundant natural resources, world-leading expertise in many sectors, a strong culture of innovation and entrepreneurship, and an internationally recognised natural environment. Increasingly, these are not simply environmental assets. They are economic assets too.”

Acknowledging that businesses are navigating significant change, Lisa’s message was clear: regulation and environmental protection should help provide certainty during periods of transformation.

From the move to lower-carbon energy systems and climate-related risks to changing customer expectations, businesses are navigating a period of transition and need clarity, confidence and consistency. Good regulation should protect people and the environment, but it should also support responsible investment, innovation and growth.

Opportunities in a time of transition

As we mark our 30th anniversary, the event provided an opportunity to reflect on decades of progress achieved through partnership between industry, communities and environmental regulation. Building on that legacy, our Chief Executive, Nicole Paterson , reaffirmed the importance of the environment to our nation’s future.

Environmental protection and economic success are interconnected. Stewardship, leadership and working in partnership are critical for us to make decisions today that build resilience, create opportunities and protect Scotland's natural assets for future generations.

With the Scottish Government's ambition to establish a single overarching environmental body by 2029, the transformation we have started in line with public service reform becomes even more important. While the landscape may be evolving, we’ll maintain the vital services that businesses rely on every day. We’ll also continue to process applications, provide advice, undertake inspections, check compliance and support innovation.

You can read more about our approach to transformation supporting public service reform in our recent LinkedIn article by Angela Milloy, Chief Operating Officer, Finance & Commercial.

Reimagining regulation - focussing on outcomes

As keynote speaker, Ross Haggart, Chief Operating Officer, Regulation & Environment, outlined the regulatory transformation that’s underway to support businesses as they tackle complex environmental challenges and strive for growth.

"Too often, regulation is seen purely in terms of permits, inspections, compliance checks and enforcement. Those things remain important, but they're not the purpose of regulation. The purpose is the outcomes we achieve together: cleaner air and water, healthier communities, stronger economic performance, more resilient businesses and a thriving environment that supports long-term prosperity."

"Put simply, success isn't measured by how many applications we process. It's measured by the difference we make.

As businesses adapt to changing markets, climate risks, resource pressures and new expectations from customers and investors, regulation needs to evolve too. We won't solve today's environmental challenges simply by processing more paperwork, more quickly. We need to focus our efforts upstream, identifying risks earlier, supporting better decision-making and preventing harm before it happens.

The best environmental incident is the one that never happens and the best enforcement action is the one that never becomes necessary.

That's the thinking behind our Future of Regulation Programme and the introduction of the Integrated Authorisation Framework. By bringing Scotland's main environmental regulatory regimes into a single framework, we're making regulation simpler, more consistent and easier to navigate.

For businesses, that means greater certainty, more transparent processes, consistent timescales and digital services designed around user needs. It means spending less time navigating systems and more time focusing on investment, innovation and growth.

For us, it means being able to focus more effort where it has the greatest impact: tackling environmental harm, addressing non-compliance and supporting positive environmental outcomes.

Just as importantly, it helps create the level playing field that responsible businesses rightly expect. Businesses that invest in doing the right thing should never be disadvantaged by those who choose to ignore their environmental responsibilities. This is also about building a different kind of regulatory relationship. One that is increasingly based on trust, transparency and performance. A relationship where we work with businesses to understand challenges, support innovation and create the conditions for sustainable growth.

We want to spend less time processing paperwork and more time creating value. For businesses that consistently demonstrate high standards, that should mean a proportionate and constructive regulatory relationship. Where organisations are investing in improvement, environmental performance and responsible growth, we want to support those ambitions.

At the same time, we will continue to take robust action where businesses deliberately break the rules, damage the environment or undermine responsible competitors. Fairness matters. A modern economy depends upon it.

Good regulation should protect people and the environment. But it should also support investment, innovation and growth.

Done well, regulation creates confidence. It reduces uncertainty and rewards responsible behaviour, creating the conditions in which businesses can prosper. And by working together towards shared outcomes, we can help ensure Scotland remains both environmentally resilient and economically successful for generations to come.”

Read more about the conditions that make working in partnership successful, with a closer look at how we moved the focus upstream in the construction sector.

Continuing the conversation

Businesses weren’t just in the room. They were on stage with us to explore themes of climate change and economic growth, how our approach to engagement can impact outcomes and the importance of communities in deciding how we use our natural resources and grow operations.

Facilitated by Catherine Salmond, Editor, The Herald, our discussion panel featured insight and expertise from Ruth Piggin, Director of Industry Sustainability, Scotch Whisky Association, Junaid Ashraf, Co-founder, Scottish Asian Business Chamber and Paul Dale, Chief Regulator, SEPA.

With questions following from the audience, it really highlighted the shared ambition to create the conditions for a more resilient, competitive and sustainable Scotland.

Thank you to our speakers, panel members, delegates and colleagues that supported the event.

text:
The Trump administration is moving to accelerate oil and gas drilling across the Western Arctic with a new proposal that would slash environmental review and public input.

The proposal could bring industrial activity to wide areas of wilderness and subsistence hunting grounds for Alaska Natives before President Donald Trump leaves office.

The move is the latest in a sustained effort by the Trump administration to open access to the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska, 23 million acres of public lands on the state’s North Slope overseen by the federal Bureau of Land Management.

The proposed rule, published in the Federal Register this week, would require the BLM to issue a decision within 60 days of receiving an application for any “qualifying project.” Environmental groups said there were few if any restrictions on what types of oil and gas projects would qualify, other than lying within 25 miles of existing activity.

Under the proposal, the agency would no longer assess the environmental impacts of individual projects or allow public input. The rule, which was written in response to a request from the oil and gas industry, says it would allow “a gradual westward progression of development.”

Environmental groups say the proposal effectively requires BLM to issue rushed approvals.

“What this rule does is move forward with this industry-requested proposal that would essentially clear the way for Willow-sized massive oil and gas drilling projects,” said Ben Tettlebaum, acting senior legal director at The Wilderness Society, referring to a large Arctic oil project approved by the Biden administration in 2023. “If this rule is finalized there would be no more review, no more public engagement, for essentially any future drilling in the Western Arctic.”

The Trump administration has acted broadly to cut down public comment on oil and gas development. In this case, the BLM published only a portion of the environmental impact statement for the proposed rule and did not include the section that analyzes its environmental impacts.

“They’re not even telling the public what the impact of this regulation would be,” said Erik Grafe, managing attorney for the Alaska office at Earthjustice, an environmental law nonprofit.

A spokesperson for the Department of the Interior, which includes the BLM, said in an email that if the rule is finalized the bureau would assess each application and require environmental reviews if projects involve “new or different” impacts from what was considered for the rulemaking.

“The Department of the Interior has made major progress unlocking the energy potential of Alaska’s National Petroleum Reserve for the benefit of Alaskans and all Americans,” the spokesperson said. “As interest in the area continues to grow, the Department and the Bureau of Land Management are taking important steps to streamline permitting in the petroleum reserve. These efforts are about using decades of research, experience and analysis to create a more efficient, predictable, and effective process while upholding environmental standards.”

The Alaska reserve contains some of the largest intact wilderness areas in the country. It provides critical habitat for migratory birds, polar bears, wolves and many other species. It is also home to a caribou herd that is an important subsistence resource for Alaska Natives who live in the nearby community of Nuiqsut.

The Willow project sparked a national debate over drilling in the area and prompted fierce resistance from some residents and leaders of Nuiqsut. The drilling and related infrastructure will extend into high-density habitat for the caribou herd. As part of the Willow approval, the federal government set aside an area under a right-of-way agreement where Nuiqsut leaders could protect the habitat by prohibiting drilling.

But the Trump administration canceled that agreement, and in March it opened that area and others to leasing by oil companies, which secured 1.3 million acres of new access. Leaders in Nuiqsut have challenged the cancellation in court and secured a preliminary injunction that has prevented the BLM from issuing leases within the conservation area.

Other Alaska Native communities support more drilling in the reserve.

“Responsible onshore development is directly responsible for critical social services in the region including education, health resources, wildlife management, and water and sewage management,” said Nagruk Harcharek, president and chief executive of Voices of Arctic Iñupiat, in a statement. His group represents five of eight native communities in the North Slope borough. “We appreciate that our right to consultation has consistently been respected in this process, and look forward to continuing a productive relationship between the federal government and our local elected leaders.”

Other Iñupiat groups have joined with national environmental organizations to file lawsuits challenging the Trump administration’s efforts to expand access to drilling in the petroleum reserve. Those cases are pending.

The proposed rule comes after reporting by the news organization Public Domain that said the Interior Department is working on a separate proposal that would similarly strip environmental review from the approval of seismic testing and other oil exploration work.

The Interior Department confirmed that it is working “to speed up permitting for winter exploration, including seismic and exploratory drilling operations. That effort builds on what the BLM has learned from dozens of environmental reviews for winter exploration in the area: when conducted under established operating procedures and mitigation measures, those activities result in no significant impacts.”

Grafe, the Earthjustice attorney, said the proposed rule runs afoul of the requirement that the government provide maximum environmental protections in certain so-called special areas within the petroleum reserve.

“It seems very likely that if BLM tries to apply these regulations to a future project that that will be unlawful,” Grafe said.

The agency is accepting public comment through Nov. 9.

This story was updated Sept. 11, 2026, with a late comment from the U.S. Department of the Interior.

title: From Yeosu to Baku, Translating 2026 Climate Commitments Into Real-World Solutions
description:

It also covered the new Non-State Actor Zone for Climate Action (NAZCA) portal and a test project, the Net-Zero Recognition Framework, used to track climate promises made by cities and companies.
Knowledge holders and practitioners from Indigenous Peoples and local communities shared experiences and solutions developed through generations of environmental stewardship.
text:
Last April, governments, businesses, cities, Indigenous Peoples, local communities, international organizations and civil society gathered in Yeosu, Republic of Korea, for UN Climate Week 3 (CW3), to show how climate action has now entered the era of implementation.

These lessons are already feeding directly into UN Climate Week 4 (CW4), which started on 7 September and runs until 11 September 2026, in Baku, Azerbaijan. It is designed to close the climate loop of the year, consolidating the real-economy solutions showcased in Yeosu into a delivery-ready agenda before the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) opens in Antalya in Türkiye.

The central question in Yeosu was no longer what needs to be done. The world already knows that emissions must be reduced, resilience strengthened and vulnerable communities supported. Instead, the nearly 1,500 participants focused on a more practical challenge: how to turn climate plans into solutions that work in the real world, attract investment, deliver benefits for people and can be replicated at scale, becoming part of the real economy.

“To speed up and scale up, we must work together to turn commitments into more real-world implementation, delivering real benefits for people, communities and economies,” said Simon Stiell, UN Climate Change Executive Secretary in his opening remarks in Yeosu.

As part of the Paris Agreement, many countries have developed their climate strategies through their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and National Adaptation Plans (NAPs). However, transforming these commitments into concrete projects remains a challenge for some countries.

Several countries and institutions presented practical solutions to bridge this gap.

For example, representatives from Brazil showcased the Climate Investment Platform, a country-led mechanism that identifies priority projects and connects them with financing partners. By bringing together ministries, development banks, climate funds and private investors, the platform has already mobilised around $5 billion for 18 projects. The model offers a practical pathway for countries seeking to transform climate plans into investment pipelines.

Participants from Cambodia presented another innovative approach through the Climate Financing Facility, a blended finance mechanism anchored within a national public financial institution. Rather than creating parallel structures, the facility uses existing national institutions to channel finance towards priority climate investments while attracting private sector participation.

These examples demonstrate that climate implementation is increasingly about building the financial architecture that can support long-term transformation, but also that climate solutions are already underway and are already delivering results, such as in Nepal, where community forestry programmes have transformed forest management over the last three decades. More than 23,000 local forest user groups now manage over 2.4 million hectares of forest. The result has been increased forest cover, improved livelihoods, stronger biodiversity protection and greater climate resilience.

In coastal Bangladesh, climate-resilient water systems are helping communities adapt to rising climate risks. Combining rainwater harvesting, solar-powered infrastructure, water filtration systems and women-led governance mechanisms, the programme now benefits more than one million people. Importantly, it integrates adaptation, renewable energy and social inclusion into one coherent package.

Pakistan presented its National Biochar Accelerator Programme, which transforms agricultural waste into biochar (an organic charcoal product made out of biomass) while generating economic opportunities for rural communities. The initiative reduces emissions, improves soil health and creates new revenue streams, illustrating how climate action can also support economic development.

Clean Energy Requires More Than Technology

Renewable energy was a major theme throughout the week. However, discussions repeatedly highlighted that solar panels and wind turbines alone are not enough.

Participants emphasised the importance of enabling systems such as modern electricity grids, energy storage, supportive regulations, workforce development and affordable finance.

The International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) highlighted grid modernisation as one of the most urgent priorities for accelerating the energy transition. As renewable energy deployment accelerates, many countries are discovering that grid infrastructure is becoming the main bottleneck rather than generation technology itself.

The Global Offshore Wind Alliance presented practical approaches to helping emerging markets develop offshore wind industries through policy certainty, concessional finance and partnerships between governments, investors and industry.

The discussions made clear that successful energy transitions depend on integrated systems rather than isolated projects.

Innovation and Digital Tools Accelerating Climate Action

Among the key innovations that emerged during CW3 were participants exploring how artificial intelligence, digital platforms and advanced data systems are already supporting climate implementation. Examples included AI-assisted reforestation, climate risk modelling, satellite monitoring and digital decision-support tools.

Particular attention was given to ensuring that developing countries can benefit from these innovations. The Technology Mechanism Initiative on AI for Climate Action aims to support Least Developed Countries and Small Island Developing States through capacity building, knowledge sharing and locally adapted applications.

At the same time, participants stressed that technology must remain accessible, transparent and people-centered. Digital solutions can accelerate implementation, but only if countries and communities have the capacity to use them effectively.

That balance continued directly into CW4. This session focused on keeping climate information accurate despite the impact of AI, discussing how to safely scale the digital tools shown in Yeosu. It also covered the new Non-State Actor Zone for Climate Action (NAZCA) portal and a test project, the Net-Zero Recognition Framework, used to track climate promises made by cities and companies.

Climate Action Works Best When it is Locally Driven

Finally, across adaptation, loss and damage, food systems and social development, one lesson emerged repeatedly from that week in Yeosu, independently from the topic: solutions are most effective when they are grounded in local realities.

Knowledge holders and practitioners from Indigenous Peoples and local communities shared experiences and solutions developed through generations of environmental stewardship. Their contributions highlighted the importance of combining scientific knowledge with traditional and local knowledge systems.

Examples shared from Bhutan, small island states and mountain regions demonstrated how locally-led approaches can better capture the realities communities face and help design responses that reflect local priorities.

UN Climate Week 3 in Yeosu showed that this transformation is already underway, by presenting solutions that were not theoretical concepts, but operational models already delivering measurable impacts, designed to be shared, replicated and scaled.

Baku Picks Up Where Yeosu Left Off

CW3's themes carry straight into CW4's agenda. For example, Brazil and Cambodia's financing models fed into an implementation lab on climate finance for agriculture and food systems, as well as a COP31 Presidency session on access to finance. The energy-systems work from IRENA and the Global Offshore Wind Alliance continued in a lab on decarbonising construction and heavy industries.

The week ran from an opening ceremony on 9 September to a high-level dialogue on transparency, a “Final Mile” workshop to support parties finishing their Biennial Transparency reports, the 2026 Adaptation Forum and a Regional National Designated Entities Forum for Eastern Europe, to only mention a few – all building towards COP31 in Antalya and the second Global Stocktake (GST2).

text:
Old solar panels contain valuable silver, copper, silicon, aluminum, and glass. A new Texas solar recycling plant aims to recover nearly all of it without sending partially processed materials overseas.

We Recycle Solar (WRS) says it will open what it describes as the first US end-to-end critical-materials recovery plant dedicated to retired solar panels in Q3 2027.

The 10-acre facility outside Dallas will process one panel per minute and recover up to 96% of its materials, according to the Yuma, Arizona-based company. Those materials will then be cleaned and prepared for sale back into US supply chains.

That last part matters. Conventional solar recycling generally focuses on the aluminum frame and glass, which make up most of a panel’s weight but aren’t its most valuable parts. Recovering smaller amounts of silver, copper, and silicon in a usable form is more complicated and expensive.

Advertisement - scroll for more content

Solar panel recycling is already happening in the US, but it typically costs more than sending panels to a landfill. Improving the recovery of high-value materials could close that gap while reducing the need for newly mined materials.

WRS says its proprietary process will recover silver, copper, silicon, aluminum, and glass at commercial scale without requiring downstream smelting at an overseas facility. The resulting materials could be reused in solar equipment, electronics, the grid, and other US industries.

“Solar panels contain the exact critical materials the US supply chain desperately needs, but until now, no American company has been able to recover their full resources at such scale or efficiency,” said Adam Saghei, founder and CEO of We Recycle Solar. “Through our advanced process, we are achieving true, comprehensive material recovery entirely on US soil, and retaining these critical materials – and the value currently being lost to Asian processing – within our domestic supply chain.”

A lot more solar waste is coming

Most US solar panels are nowhere near retirement. The US Department of Energy says about 70% of the world’s solar projects have been installed since 2019, and panels now typically remain in service for 25 to 35 years.

But with hundreds of millions of panels already operating across the US, the volume reaching the end of its useful life will climb sharply over the next several decades. Weather damage, installation problems, and the early replacement of older panels with more efficient models will add to that stream.

WRS says it has already diverted more than 1 million panels from landfills through its existing decommissioning, recycling, resale, and remarketing operations.

The Dallas-area plant is intended to be the first in a larger network. WRS plans to invest around $100 million in four additional US facilities over the next four years, although it hasn’t yet disclosed their locations.

text:
ATLANTA — Communities across Georgia that were hit hard by Hurricane Helene will begin learning in November whether they will get a share of federal relief funding earmarked for water projects.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency awarded the state nearly $500 million to help improve water infrastructure after the hurricane. The bulk of the money, nearly $360 million, is for drinking water systems. The next largest portion, nearly $125 million, is for wastewater.

“As communities across Georgia continue to recover from the most destructive storm in state history, these funds will help accelerate that ongoing work,” Gov. Brian Kemp said in a statement.

The funding is from the federal 2025 American Relief Act. The Georgia Environmental Finance Authority is responsible for distributing the money.

Kemp’s office said the agency will present the first group of project awards to its board of directors in November, after calling for applications last fall.

The goal is to harden water systems against flood damage. Projects that are eligible for Helene Resilience Funding are supposed to either reduce the risk of flood damage or vulnerability to it or enhance resilience.

Examples of eligible projects include relocating or replacing equipment and facilities, decentralizing wastewater systems, installing backup power and planning.

text:
In its Short-Term Energy Outlook released on Sept. 9, the U.S. Energy Administration forecasts that the U.S. will use record amounts of electricity.

"We expect electricity sales in the United States to total 4,135 billion kilowatthours (BkWh) in 2026 and 4,211 BkWh in 2027, driven by data center development and increased manufacturing activity in the commercial and industrial sectors," EIA said. "Despite a pause in connecting new data center projects in Texas to the grid, the West South Central region accounts for the largest share of total electricity sales growth in our forecast."

"We forecast that commercial sector electricity sales will increase by 3.3% in 2026 and 2.7% in 2027, accounting for 63% and 56% of the increase in electricity sales in those years," it said.

EIA forecasts industrial sector electricity sales will rise 1.6% in 2026 and 2.6% in 2027, accounting for an additional 22% and 36% of increased electricity sales, respectively.

"Although Texas has paused the connection of new data centers to the grid to facilitate a regulatory audit of proposed data center projects, the West South Central region still accounts for the largest regional share of growth in total electricity sales, totaling nearly 20% of nationwide growth in 2026 and nearly 40% in 2027," it said.

With natural gas generation in the United States rising by 2% in 2026 and 1% in 2027, coal generation falls by 8% in 2026 and 6% in 2027.

As wind and utility-scale solar capacity continues to be added to the grid, we expect solar generation to grow by 21% in 2026 and by 18% in 2027, while wind generation grows 7% in 2026 and 5% in 2027.

We expect the PJM interconnection to account for nearly 45% of the growth in total U.S. generation in our forecast, with natural gas generation driving the increase in 2026 and natural gas, coal, and wind generation driving the increase in 2027," EIA said.

Meanwhile, the growth in solar generation is concentrated in the parts of the grid managed by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas and the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO).

text:
A Missouri-based company has confirmed it is considering building a data center near Coffey Road in Moss Bluff.

Representatives for Azimuth Renewables, headquartered in St. Louis, confirmed that the company is considering building a data center on 1,100 acres of land that it has an option to purchase.

Representatives said plans are still in the early stages and that nothing firm has been decided yet.

The news comes as Moss Bluff residents and local elected officials have launched a firm opposition to a proposed solar farm in the same area.

California-based Orion Renewable Energy Group intends to request a variance from the Calcasieu Parish Planning and Zoning Board to build its proposed 4,700-acre solar farm that would include up to 2.5 million solar panels.

The proposed site is currently zoned as Agricultural and would require the committee approve a variance to allow industrial development, which is exactly what Azimuth officials will have to do if they choose to move forward with a data center.

While there has been no proven connection between the solar farm and data center, Louisiana State Rep. Brett Geymann (R-Lake Charles) says the news of the considered data center has added fueled to the fight against the solar farm.

“It absolutely has elevated the opposition to (the solar farm), because that would almost certainly open a gateway for the data center, if it happens,” he said.

This week, State Rep. Dewith Carrier (R-Oakdale), Chuck Owen (R-Rosepine), and Sen. Jeremy Stine (R-Lake Charles) added their signatures to a letter to the planning and zoning board members imploring them to deny the rezoning variance request.

“This decision by the board will have consequences for decades and will set a precedent for future industrial variance applications — like a data center,” Geymann said. “Once you let one industrial development in the neighborhood, it will be hard to deny any others that come behind it.”

Sources tell the American Press Orion’s variance request could go before the planning and zoning panel as early as November.

name: Detroit and Evs
title: General Motors EV Transition Strategy and Timeline - Rare Earth Exchanges
description:
REEx Insight — Detroit Needs a War Chest The EV transition has an uncomfortable financial reality: car companies effectively have to finance two industrial systems at once.
A slower U.S. transition therefore has an overlooked benefit: time to build the war chest.
REEx's automotive-industry sources similarly indicate that the U.S. supply base is not ready for an overnight conversion.
The same problem extends upstream into NdPr → metals → alloys → NdFeB magnets → motors.
Globally, more than 100 countries recorded rising EV sales in 2025.
text:
Highlights

GM CEO Mary Barra reaffirms EVs as the long-term goal while acknowledging the U.S. transition will take decades

IEA projects EVs will reach nearly 28% of global new-car sales in 2026, even as U.S. adoption slows

Used EV wholesale values rose 11.4% year over year in May 2026, driven partly by elevated gasoline prices

A slower U.S. transition gives automakers time to build capital from ICE and hybrid profits, but China is not waiting

The NdPr-to-NdFeB magnet supply chain remains unready for rapid conversion, with qualification timelines spanning years

General Motors CEO Mary Barra (opens in a new tab) says EVs remain GM's long-term "end game," but America's transition will take decades. That slower clock may actually help U.S. automakers. They must continue investing in profitable gasoline-powered and hybrid vehicles while accumulating the capital and manufacturing capability required for EVs. Globally, however, electrification continues: the International Energy Agency (opens in a new tab) (IEA) expects EVs to approach 28% of worldwide new-car sales in 2026, even as U.S. adoption slows.

REEx Insight — Detroit Needs a War Chest

The EV transition has an uncomfortable financial reality: car companies effectively have to finance two industrial systems at once. GM cannot simply shut down profitable internal-combustion operations and redirect the money. It must maintain existing engines, transmissions, plants, and suppliers while simultaneously funding batteries, EV architectures, software, power electronics, motors, and new supply chains.

That takes enormous capital. A slower U.S. transition therefore has an overlooked benefit: time to build the war chest. Profits from ICE vehicles and hybrids can help finance the next generation of electric platforms while consumer demand, charging infrastructure, and domestic supply chains mature.

REEx's automotive-industry sources similarly indicate that the U.S. supply base is not ready for an overnight conversion. Qualification alone can take years. The same problem extends upstream into NdPr → metals → alloys → NdFeB magnets → motors.

But the breathing room carries a strategic risk. China is not waiting.

While Detroit manages two powertrain systems, Chinese manufacturers operate inside a far more mature EV ecosystem. Globally, more than 100 countries recorded rising EV sales in 2025. So delay has value only if America uses it to build.

Gas Prices Can Move the Clock

Consumer economics can accelerate that timetable unexpectedly. Cox Automotive reported used-EV wholesale values rising 11.4% year over year in May 2026, versus 3.3% for non-EVs, amid elevated gasoline prices. Higher gasoline—and for commercial fleets, diesel—prices can improve EV operating economics even when policy incentives weaken.

Contact: Gabrielle Levy, glevy@cacampaign.org

CAC’s Alt Applauds Appeals Court Decision Blocking Trump DOE’s Fake ‘Emergency’ Coal Order

WASHINGTON–Today, the DC Circuit Court of Appeals sided with the people of the state of Michigan in its challenge against the Trump administration’s order extending operations of the J.H. Campbell coal plant, which was slated to shut down last year. In the unanimous ruling, the court was "unpersuaded" by the Department of Energy’s "sweeping conception of its ’emergency’ authority" and acted "without regard to the multiple procedural and substantive constraints built into state reliability planning processes." CAC Director Marge Alt issued the following statement in response:

"The Trump administration manufactured an energy ’emergency’ to cater to their friends in the fossil fuel industry, overriding economic, environmental, and local concerns. Their decision was far from being in the best interests of the people of Michigan and the United States.

"The Campbell plant, and 6 others the DOE has forced to remain in operation, weren’t scheduled to shut down based on politics. They were slated to close because dirty, outdated fossil fuels can’t compete financially against other options, namely, clean sources such as wind and solar power, and because people have run out of patience putting up with the damage coal pollution does to the climate and public health.

text:
Maine Democratic lawmakers are pushing for more clean energy options as a solution to rising energy prices. Energy costs have increased 77% in the last five years in Maine. Solar and onshore wind, meanwhile, are about 40-50% cheaper than fossil fuel.

Speaker of the House Ryan Fecteau, Energy Committee Chair Melanie Sachs and committee member Rep. Kilton Webb took a "lower energy bills tour" through parts of the state on Thursday.

Speaking from Blue Ox Malthouse in Lisbon Falls, Fecteau said renewable energy and efficient appliances like heat pumps will be crucial as the colder weather arrives.

Sachs says a big part of pushing clean energy solutions forward in Maine is going to be helping small businesses secure the funding, through tools like Efficiency Maine's Green Bank.

"We need to put all of the tools in the toolbox that we have to move our energy independence and sustainability forward," she says.

The lawmakers say they are committed to continuing Maine's community solar program as part of an 'all of the above' approach to lowering energy costs.

text:
Charlotte’s faculty and staff can help promote a culture of sustainability on campus through the Sustainability Ambassadors program, a professional development initiative for employees administered through the Office of Sustainability.

The program gives participants an opportunity to learn about the University’s sustainability goals and practices, promote a culture of sustainability on campus and make a positive difference within their departments and beyond. It also supports the University’s strategic plan to “create a culture where all University employees and students embrace their roles for achieving sustainability goals.”

“When employees understand how their daily decisions connect to the University’s sustainability priorities, real change becomes possible,” said Jenny Washam, communications and employee engagement coordinator. “Ambassadors play a vital role in making sustainability visible, practical and achievable.”

Ambassadors often engage in hands-on projects that connect personal experience with campuswide sustainability efforts. One example is the Climate Change Quilt, a collaborative art project supported by a Charlotte Green Initiative Grant funded by SGA student fees. Through the project, the campus community is invited to create quilt squares that reflect their relationship to climate change.

For Christin Lampkowski, emerging technologies librarian, the project has become a powerful way to merge her sustainability values with her work supporting creative learning. Area 49’s Makerspace provides sewing machines, fabric scraps and other materials that make it an ideal location for quilt‑making sessions.

“The Sustainability Ambassador program helped me identify even more ways to bring sustainability into my professional life,” Lampkowski said. Area 49 has since added recycling stations and a Weird Recycling Bin for student projects, and she has incorporated sustainability themes into the classes and workshops she teaches.

Her ambassador experience also strengthened her collaboration with the Office of Sustainability. “Now when opportunities like the quilt project come up, they know they can reach out to me and Area 49,” she said.

Area 49 is also available to work with student organizations interested in scheduling a workshop for their members, as well as faculty who want to incorporate this project, creative reuse or quilting as a medium for message sharing into their courses. Email AtkinsArea49@charlotte.edu.

For Rachel Engstrom, costume lab supervisor and lecturer in the College of Arts + Architecture, the quilt project became a meaningful way to connect her professional skills with her passion for sustainability. She assisted with several quilt workshops, helping participants learn how to use the sewing machines and construct squares for the collaborative initiative.

“Environmental sustainability has always been part of my life and I strongly believe that we need to take care of the Earth,” she said. “The sustainability ambassadors program has allowed me to make professional connections with colleagues of a similar mindset and has also given me information and resources that I can share with my peers and colleagues.”

She encourages faculty and staff who are considering the program to take the leap. “I would encourage any colleague that is considering becoming a Sustainability Ambassador to do it sooner rather than later.”

text:
A gas export terminal on the Gulf Coast of Texas has routinely violated air pollution permits for years with little consequences from state regulators, according to a report released this week by Oilfield Witness, an environmental watchdog.

The Texas-based activist group cited thousands of pages of documents and a month of optical gas monitoring in its 27-page report on Freeport LNG, the nation’s third-largest exporter of liquified natural gas, where an explosion in 2022 caused an eight-month shutdown.

Oilfield Witness identified 532 unpermitted emission events reported by the company since 2019, along with more than 200 other permit deviations, but just seven penalty fines levied by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality.

“The findings in this report paint a stark picture of an out of control operator,” said the report. “This incompetence is enabled by regulators failing to act.”

The report tallied annual emissions more than 100 times greater than established limits. It also found that part of the $14 billion Freeport LNG complex reported emitting a staggering 1,500 pounds of the carcinogen benzene, known to cause leukemia, in 2024—five times more than its larger counterpart down the coast, Corpus Christi LNG.

A spokesperson for Freeport LNG, Heather Browne, said in a statement: “Freeport LNG’s unwavering commitment to safety, reliability and environmental stewardship and preservation are at the forefront of our operations. Our electric-drive LNG facility reduces plant emissions by over 90% relative to a typical LNG liquefaction facility, and our facility’s carbon footprint is the lowest of any LNG liquefaction facility in the world.”

Freeport LNG is currently expanding with a fourth liquefaction unit in development.

Earlier in September, Japan’s state-owned lender announced an investigation into its $2.6 billion financing for the project following complaints from community leaders and environmental groups, Global Trade Review magazine reported on Wednesday.

“Japanese financial institutions and companies are deeply involved in the Freeport LNG project,” said Ayumi Fukakusa, executive director of climate, energy, and development at Friends of the Earth Japan, in a press release Thursday. “They should re-examine the environmental and social risks.”

Fifty miles south of Houston, Freeport LNG is one of several gas liquefaction and export terminals that have cropped up along the coast of Texas and Louisiana in recent years. Through energy-intensive processes, the enormous installations super-cool methane gas into liquid at -260 degrees Fahrenheit, then load it onto tanker ships for consumption overseas.

“Texas remains the nation’s leading producer of natural gas and our state’s LNG export capacity plays a vital strategic role in strengthening America’s energy security,” Ed Longanecker, president of the Texas Independent Producers and Royalty Owners Association, said in a May newsletter.

A 2023 investigation by Inside Climate News showed how Freeport LNG, a project of New York billionaire Michael Smith, used a series of permit amendments to avoid a stricter review by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, known as the TCEQ. The facility was ultimately authorized to release almost 900 tons of regulated pollutants per year.

Chronic Emission Violations

Actual emissions from the facility appear much higher than the permitted limits, according to Oilfield Witness. For example, one flare at the complex was authorized to release 3.3 tons of carbon monoxide per year but reported emissions of 381 tons in the year after July 2019.

Another part of the Freeport LNG complex burnt off waste gas at more than six times its permitted rate for the most recent yearlong reporting period.

“Oilfield Witness makes a strong case that the facility has trouble following the law,” said Luke Metzger, director of Environment Texas. “With such a tepid response to their violations from TCEQ, it’s not hard to see why.”

According to Oilfield Witness, TCEQ has issued 76 violation notices to Freeport LNG since it opened in 2019, leading to seven fines totaling $610,000—about 2 percent of the facility’s estimated 2025 revenue.

Bobby Janecka, a former TCEQ commissioner, said the agency is doing the best it can with limited resources. It oversees thousands of industrial facilities across the state and lacks capacity to monitor them all. So the regulator depends on companies’ own emission reporting. Levying punitive fines on companies might only encourage them not to report violations, Janecka said.

“As much as this state relies on self-reporting and data collection from the industry itself, it’s imperative that TCEQ keeps in mind that long-term relationship,” he said.

Fines also make the agency vulnerable to long and expensive legal challenges from the companies, he said. Even when the TCEQ doesn’t impose fines, it puts companies through processes meant to correct the problems that led to unpermitted emissions.

“The agency is always quick to focus on achieving compliance even if it means doing so in lieu of a penalty,” said Janecka, who spent 12 years at the TCEQ.

At Freeport LNG, all of the largest emission events in the last two years resulted from units tripping, according to TCEQ data compiled by Texas-based oil and gas watchdog group Future Heist.

In the largest, on Nov. 1, 2024, three units at Freeport LNG “tripped due to an incoming power feed interruption. The trips resulted in unavoidable venting,” according to company reports. Gas was burned off for 62 hours at one part of the complex and for 55 hours at another.

On May 7, 2025, the same three units again “tripped due to an incoming power feed interruption,” leading the company to burn off gas for 19 hours.

On July 9, 2026, the facility “tripped due to a mechanical issue,” according to company reports, leading it to burn off gas for 14 hours. One week later the facility “tripped due to an incoming power feed interruption” and burnt off gas for 17 hours.

“Freeport frequently claims to have resolved deviations by adjusting operating parameters, only to report the same problem the following year,” said the Oilfield Witness report. “Each time, regulators accept the same parameter adjustments that failed to thoroughly resolve the problem previously.”

text:
“Suniva will continue to produce PERC cells,” Card told PV Tech this week, when asked about the cell technology that the new facility will use. “What this announcement validates is that PERC remains a workhorse product, particularly in the US market.”

PERC has been a key component of the company’s return to cell manufacturing, which began with the relaunch of its manufacturing facility in Georgia in 2024. Card told PV Tech Premium last week that this period was a “highly dynamic regulatory environment for the use of the TOPCon,” which improved the business case for other types of cell technology.

“PERC was tried and true,” he continued, pointing to the plethora of legal disputes that have embroiled the world’s leading TOPCon manufacturers in recent months. “It was a much more clean path, without the potential threat of legal or regulatory hurdles that you might have to overcome.

“What we did not want to do was build a facility and then immediately get enjoined by someone saying ‘you have a patent violation here, you have a patent violation there.’”

‘You can simply create more physical units of solar cells on PERC’

Last week, Card said that there were “three pillars” behind the company’s decision to use PERC, of which one was the legal landscape in the US. The second pertains to technology, as Card argued that “TOPCon is a much more volatile substance to build than PERC,” which again improves the business case for the latter technology.

The third, and perhaps most significant, pillar is the economic reality of producing PERC cells versus other cells, and the state of the current US supply chain, which incentivises production at scale, rather that production of the most efficient technologies.

“The reality is that, assuming PERC looks good and TOPCon looks good, TOPCon has multiple additional manufacturing steps that PERC does not have,” explained Card. “It physically takes several hours to make a single TOPCon cell than a single PERC cell. When you extrapolate those extra hours into volume over a year, or over three years, it becomes really meaningful, the number of physical cells you can create on one platform than another.

“You can simply create more physical units of solar cells on PERC than you can on TOPCon.”

This difference in scale is all the more significant in the US where, as Card put it, there is a “radically inverted and wide pyramid” of production capacity for various parts of the US solar supply chain; put simply, there is much more module deployment and module manufacturing capacity in operation in the US than there is cell manufacturing, so the most effective cell manufacturing process would be one that can produce the largest number of cells to address this imbalance.

Figures from PV Tech Research reflect this misalignment between cell and module manufacturing capacity, as the US currently has 77.3GW of module manufacturing capacity in operation, compared to just 26.5GW of cells; market analysts from the company published a series of guest blogs on PV Tech last week about exactly this disparity in US manufacturing capacity across the supply chain.

“There had been such a headstart in deployment and module manufacturing, and a lack in cell manufacturing, [and] what I think we correctly ascertained out of that was that the challenge in the US, in the intermediate term—meaning one to five or six years—was not power per unit, but it was sheer number of units,” explained Card.

During our conversation last week, Card said that if his company had 5GW of cell manufacturing capacity “I’d be sold out”; perhaps not unrelatedly, this week’s announcement of the financing for the South Carolina facility came with the news that Suniva has secured offtake agreements for the “majority” of the output of the new 4.5GW facility.

US policy drives manufacturing investment

The US policy landscape has been a crucial factor in recent changes in the US solar sector. The Biden-era Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) drove an 800% increase in US solar manufacturing capacity and even the more recent One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) “didn’t kill the 45X advanced manufacturing credit,” as Crux’s Hasan Nazar told PV Tech Premium last month.

While Card is less optimistic about the impacts of the policy landscape on deployment, he agrees that opportunities remain for manufacturers in the current environment.

“We needed a policy framework that supported growing US manufacturing. There is much with OBBBA that supports US manufacturing growth in solar,” he said. “You’ve seen a great uptick in announcements of factories since OBBBA—I’m not going to get into a debate if it’s good overall for solar deployment, everyone has views on what that is—but I can tell you that it is good, and Section 232 is good, for US manufacturing growth.”

Card added that policy has become a major talking point, and a driver of decisions, for companies that are looking to invest in US manufacturing at present.

“I heard over the summer at PV ModuleTech that there were a lot of end-use buyers saying their focus had shifted from a technology evaluation to a regulatory evaluation, and that has become the driver: am I qualified to participate in this market?” he said.

“It doesn’t matter what your product does—good, bad or otherwise—if you’re not qualified to participate in the market.”

Card claims US polysilicon production is ‘robust’

The disparity between module and polysilicon production in the US is even greater than the disparity between module and cell production, and is perhaps the greatest challenge to be overcome if the US is to build a robust domestic supply chain. Figures from PV Tech Research show that there is just 15.5GW of PV-allocated polysilicon production in the US, and just 5GW of US domestic wafer manufacturing capacity.

Suniva has already signed a deal with domestic polysilicon provider Corning to source its polysilicon and wafers from domestic producers, and while Card did not comment on the source of polysilicon for the company’s South Carolina facility, he said this week that Corning “continues to be a valued supply chain partner of Suniva’s”.

Indeed, when asked about the US polysilicon landscape more broadly, Card was bullish on the potential for domestic production.

“It’s robust on poly,” he said. “Certainly when you look at the US poly players, there’s more than enough polysilicon created in the US to support the US industry; there’s actually relatively synchronised capacity between polysilicon and deployment. The problem is that converting that polysilicon into wafers, and those wafers into cells and those cells getting deployed into modules.

“The reality is we don’t have the capacity to make wafers, we have very little capacity to make cells and there has to be more if you’re going to have a self-sustaining domestic supply chain.”

Perhaps the strongest evidence of the influence of policy can be seen in Suniva’s own history. The company was founded in 2007 and quickly expanded to cell and module manufacturing, but an influx of Chinese products into the US market in the 2010s proved stiff competition for domestic manufacturers; Card told PV Tech Premium that during this period, between 30 and 35 cell and module manufactures in the US went out of business.

Suniva, too, filed for bankruptcy in 2017, and it was only after significant policy shifts—such as the setting of tariffs on Chinese goods from 2018 following a Section 201 complaint from Suniva, and the passage of the IRA—that created the economic conditions for Suniva to return to manufacturing in 2024.

Policy challenges in the global supply chain

However, the policy situation is not perfect; Card himself admitted that there could “absolutely” be improvements made to the policy landscape in general, and Section 232 in particular.

Even the US’ policy history has rarely been to the benefit of all companies in the sector. In 2018, when Suniva launched the Section 201 petition, a number of US solar companies and influential trade body the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) objected to the petition, claiming that the tariffs would lead to Chinese manufacturers passing on costs to their US buyers, which would ultimately impede deployment.

While Card was optimistic that the current policy landscape would continue to support manufacturers, he said that, as the US has spent decades ‘offshoring’ its manufacturing capacity across a number of industries, bringing that capacity back to US soil, or even just to allied nations, would take time. For Card, onshoring will be an “evolution,” not a “revolution”.

“You can’t blame this on blue administrations or red administrations, but we’ve spent, as a country, 40 years offshoring our manufacturing,” he explained. “It was not an offshoring revolution, it was an offshoring evolution. So it’s reasonable to expect that, directionally, onshoring can’t be a revolution either; it’s an evolution.”

However, he still says that “we should do it.” Card points to initiatives such as ‘friend-shoring’, a process described by Nazar as the sourcing of materials and components from allied countries as a way to reduce reliance on Chinese goods without needing to rapidly build a robust manufacturing sector in the US, which would be particularly difficult to achieve for the upstream components, such as polysilicon and wafers.

“I don’t think that anyone is arguing for a truly exclusionary protectionist environment,” said Card. “They’re arguing for the US to have the ability to take care of its own energy needs. Some percentage of that is going to be home-grown, but it will always work on the global stage and we will work with friends.”

Again, Suniva’s past, which has ranged from bankruptcy to industry leading cell production, is perhaps instructive in this regard.

“When Suniva rebuilt it’s factory, we had to do it through friendshoring because, as a country, we spent so many years offshoring things that there was no industry in the US,” explained Card. “We were heavily reliant on European equipment in our first factory. It’s a perfect example.”

text:
McNeilus Truck and Manufacturing Inc. says Ace Recycling & Disposal, a West Valley City, Utah-based waste and recycling services provider, has added its first McNeilus Volterra ZSL electric side loader collection vehicle to its fleet.

Minnesota-based McNeilus says Ace serves more than 1 million people each week in Utah and Wyoming, adding the waste and recycling firm purchased the battery-electric vehicle from Siddons-Martin Environmental Group, which is based in Houston and has numerous locations.

“The vehicle marks an important step in Ace Recycling & Disposal’s commitment to sustainability, operational efficiency and providing drivers with advanced technology designed to promote safety and comfort,” McNeilus says.

The deployment of the vehicle also comes as fleet operators are confronting some of the highest diesel fuel and gasoline prices in American history.

McNeilus refers to the Volterra ZSL as North America’s most advanced fully integrated electric refuse and recycling collection vehicle (eRCV), saying it combines a purpose-built electric platform with advanced refuse collection technology to help customers reduce emissions while maintaining the performance required for demanding residential collection routes.

“Forward-thinking customers like Ace Recycling & Disposal are helping shape the future of refuse and recycling collection by investing in innovative technologies that support their operations today while preparing for tomorrow,” says Lee Dreas, president of McNeilus.

“The McNeilus Volterra ZSL was designed from the ground up to deliver an exceptional driver experience, dependable all-day performance and the sustainability benefits fleets are seeking,” Dreas says. “We’re proud to partner with Siddons-Martin Environmental Group to bring this vehicle to ACE.”

“We’re always looking for ways to operate more sustainably while improving efficiency across our fleet,” says Isaac Leituala, general manager of Ace Recycling & Disposal.

“After evaluating several electric refuse collection vehicles, we were impressed by the Volterra ZSL’s battery life and the overall driver experience,” Leituala continues. “Our drivers especially appreciated the 360-degree camera system, and we’re excited to continue to see the long-term operational and cost benefits as we integrate the truck into our fleet.”

McNeilus calls the Volterra ZSL purpose-built to meet the demands of residential refuse and recycling collection, saying it features an advanced electric drivetrain, smart battery management system and cooperative regenerative braking to enable all-day route performance on a single charge.

The truck provider says the model is certified as a zero-emission vehicle by the United States Environmental Protection Agency and the California Air Resources Board.

Regarding safety and operator comfort, McNeilus says Volterra features include nearly 38 percent more interior space compared with some other collection trucks; blind spot monitoring, 360-degree camera views and forward and rear collision notifications; a McNeilus Zero Radius vertical lift arm; and cloud-based telematics designed to optimize vehicle performance and maximize battery life.

title: Appeals Court Limits DOE Emergency Authority Tied to Power Plants
description:
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit on Sept. 11 vacated the Department of Energy's (DOE) order requiring Consumers Energy's J.H.
Campbell coal-fired power plant in Michigan to remain in operation beyond its planned retirement date.
The court concluded that DOE exceeded its authority under section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act, which grants the agency limited emergency powers to address immediate threats to electricity supply.
In a unanimous decision, the court rejected DOE's argument that its emergency authority could be used to preserve generation resources based on broader reliability concerns.
The panel emphasized that section 202(c) is intended to address actual emergencies involving imminent power shortages, not to allow DOE to override state and regional reliability planning processes or dictate preferred generation resources.
text:
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit on Sept. 11 vacated the Department of Energy's (DOE) order requiring Consumers Energy's J.H. Campbell coal-fired power plant in Michigan to remain in operation beyond its planned retirement date.

The court concluded that DOE exceeded its authority under section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act, which grants the agency limited emergency powers to address immediate threats to electricity supply.

In a unanimous decision, the court rejected DOE's argument that its emergency authority could be used to preserve generation resources based on broader reliability concerns.

The panel emphasized that section 202(c) is intended to address actual emergencies involving imminent power shortages, not to allow DOE to override state and regional reliability planning processes or dictate preferred generation resources.

The judges noted that Michigan regulators and the regional transmission organization had already determined that retiring the Campbell plant would not jeopardize grid reliability.

APPA said that the decision represents a significant limitation on DOE's ability to intervene in power plant retirement decisions and reinforces the primary role of states and regional grid operators in resource planning and reliability oversight. The court warned that accepting DOE's interpretation would effectively allow the federal government to compel operation of specific power plants without regard to the procedural and substantive safeguards built into state regulatory frameworks.

If the decision is upheld on appeal, it could shape the outcome of pending challenges to other FPA section 202(c) orders that require coal plants to continue operating.

title: Rhode Island Energy looks to Maine onshore wind farm to boost renewable electricity supply
description:

Rhode Island Energy announced Tuesday that it has tentatively agreed to buy 150 megawatts of wind-powered electricity from an onshore wind farm planned for northern Maine.
Onshore wind projects have not been spared from the Trump administration’s attacks on renewable energy projects.
“We are committed to helping advance a reliable, safe, affordable, and increasingly clean energy future for our customers, while supporting Rhode Island’s 2021 Act on Climate requirements,” Greg Cornett, Rhode Island Energy president, said in a statement.

text:
After a series of failed attempts to add more offshore wind power to Rhode Island’s energy portfolio, the state utility operator has turned landward.

Rhode Island Energy announced Tuesday that it has tentatively agreed to buy 150 megawatts of wind-powered electricity from an onshore wind farm planned for northern Maine. The conditional agreement with project developer Clearway Energy Group remains subject to pricing negotiations — a sticking point for past proposals on offshore wind projects — and also requires approval from the Rhode Island Public Utilities Commission.

Onshore wind projects have not been spared from the Trump administration’s attacks on renewable energy projects. Federal regulators paused permits on land wind and solar projects beginning in July 2025, setting off an escalating legal battle as project developers and Democratic attorneys general — including Rhode Island’s Peter Neronha — sought to overturn the federal freeze. A federal judge in Oregon ordered federal regulators to resume previews under a preliminary injunction issued on Aug. 6.

The 800-megawatt wind farm planned for Maine’s Aroostook County, near the Canadian border, was not listed as one of the 155 projects subject to the federal permit freeze. In August, Maine utility regulators authorized the onshore wind array, along with a high-voltage transmission line to connect the wind turbines to the regional electric grid. Both project developers were chosen from a competitive request for proposals that included input from Rhode Island, Connecticut, Massachusetts and Vermont.

Maine has tentatively agreed to buy 600 megawatts of capacity from the project, leaving the remaining 200 megawatts up for grabs. Rhode Island’s tentative power purchase agreement, if solidified, would generate enough electricity to power 73,000 homes while advancing the decarbonization mandates under the state’s 2021 Act on Climate law.

“We are committed to helping advance a reliable, safe, affordable, and increasingly clean energy future for our customers, while supporting Rhode Island’s 2021 Act on Climate requirements,” Greg Cornett, Rhode Island Energy president, said in a statement. “The proposed project offers the opportunity to secure a significant amount of renewable energy through a competitive regional procurement while supporting broader efforts to strengthen New England’s energy infrastructure and diversify the region’s energy supply.”

The project marks the largest onshore wind farm in New England, expected to create more than 2,500 construction jobs and $2.4 billion in economic output, according to Maine utility regulators. The benefits to Maine ratepayers — roughly $400 million including the transmission line — also offer stability to the regional electric grid that includes the rest of New England.

The timeline for Rhode Island Energy to finalize a contract agreement and submit the pricing proposal to the Rhode Island Public Utilities Commission was not immediately available.

text:
On September 4, 2026, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers issued a supplemental notice of proposed rulemaking (SNPRM) seeking additional public input on the definition of “waters of the United States” (“WOTUS”), and ultimately the scope of federal jurisdiction under the Clean Water Act (CWA).[1] The proposal builds on the agencies’ November 2025 rulemaking and the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Sackett v. EPA.[2] Most notably, the supplemental proposal would limit the WOTUS definition to perennial waters, under which tributaries would generally need to have standing or continuously flowing water every day of the year under ordinary conditions to qualify as “relatively permanent” waters. For wetlands, federal jurisdiction would generally require perennial surface water that is continuously connected to an otherwise jurisdictional water.

If adopted, the supplemental approach could significantly reduce the scope of federal CWA jurisdiction, particularly for intermittent streams and wetlands that currently qualify based on their adjacency to jurisdictional waters. The agencies anticipate that the greatest reductions could occur in arid regions and that the CWA Section 404 permitting program could see fewer permits and reduced mitigation requirements. At the national scale, the proposal may provide greater certainty for landowners, developers, and regulated entities, but it also could shift greater responsibility to states and Tribes, potentially resulting in greater variation among jurisdictions.

Specifically for Ohio, this could create some regulatory uncertainty. The definition, as proposed in the SNPRM, will likely result in more state regulation of direct impacts to wetlands, which would be covered by Ohio’s Isolated Wetland Permitting Program. However, any direct impact on intermittent streams might require additional state-level action. Intermittent streams would still be protected under state law, but there is no state-level permitting mechanism currently in place that could be used to authorize such impacts. Two options to address this are 1) Ohio could either implement a permitting program for intermittent stream impacts; or 2) redefine the definition of state waters to exclude intermittent streams, similar to what the state did after ephemeral streams were excluded from federal jurisdiction.

Comments are due on October 9, 2026, 30 days after the SNPRM was published in the Federal Register. The federal government received 220,000 comments to the November rulemaking, and one would expect that the federal government will receive a large number of comments to this SNPRM. Furthermore, it is almost assured that if the rule is enacted as proposed here, there would be legal challenges to the final rule.

text:
During the state visit of His Highness Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, President of the United Arab Emirates, to Germany, RWE and UAE partners signed two agreements: a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) regarding Offshore Wind between RWE and Abu Dhabi Future Energy Company PJSC – Masdar, and a Letter of Intent (LOI) between RWE and ADNOC regarding future LNG supplies.

The agreements reinforce the growing economic and energy relationship between Germany and the UAE and reflect the ongoing dialogue between RWE and UAE companies, as well as their shared interest in supporting the development of renewable energy opportunities and enhancing energy security in Germany and Europe.

Under the MoU, RWE and Masdar intend to consider joint participation in German offshore wind auctions in 2027. This agreement has an indicative investment value exceeding EUR 3 billion and builds on Masdar and RWE's long-standing partnership, reinforcing the UAE's role as a committed investor in Germany's energy sector and deepening bilateral cooperation in clean energy development.

Offshore wind is set to become one of the cornerstones of Germany’s energy system, combining large-scale renewable electricity generation with a high degree of reliability. With stronger and more consistent wind conditions at sea, offshore wind can make a significant contribution to a secure, climate-friendly and competitive power supply. Germany’s ambitious offshore expansion targets underline both the scale of the opportunity and the importance of strong partners.

The LOI between ADNOC and RWE Supply & Trading builds on ongoing discussions about long-term LNG supply opportunities established under the Strategic Collaboration Agreement signed in February this year. Both parties intend to agree on the terms of up to two LNG sale and purchase agreements, building upon key commercial terms covering deliveries to Germany and other European markets, as well as to Asian markets, supplied from ADNOC Gas’ and XRG’s growing LNG portfolio including Ruwais, Das, Rio Grande, Mozambique and Argentina, with supply commencing in the early 2030s.

His Excellency Dr Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber, UAE Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology, ADNOC MD & Group CEO, and Chairman of Masdar, said: “The UAE and Germany have built a strong partnership grounded in shared ambition, industrial cooperation and a commitment to energy security. The UAE’s intention to invest an additional €40 billion in Germany reflects the long-term confidence and ambition behind this partnership. Both offshore wind and LNG will play an important role in Germany’s future energy system, supporting industrial competitiveness and long-term economic growth. These agreements deepen our partnership with RWE and will help deliver the reliable energy infrastructure that will underpin Germany and Europe’s future prosperity.”

Dr Markus Krebber, CEO of RWE AG, said: “Offshore wind will play a central role in strengthening Europe’s energy security, accelerating decarbonisation and delivering reliable electricity at scale. Germany offers significant potential, and strong partnerships will be essential to turn that potential into future clean energy projects. We are therefore pleased to take another step with Masdar, a valued partner with whom we have built a successful, long-standing cooperation from London Array to Dogger Bank South. Together, we want to bring our complementary strengths and experience to the German market and support the country’s energy transformation with secure, sustainable and affordable power. We also welcome the Letter of Intent with ADNOC on potential future LNG supplies. It builds on the strategic collaboration we agreed in February and underlines our shared commitment to strengthening Germany’s and Europe’s security of supply while further diversifying RWE’s global LNG portfolio. We will now work together to further shape the potential commercial framework for long-term LNG deliveries to Germany, Europe and Asian markets.”

Mohamed Jameel Al Ramahi, CEO of Masdar, said: “Masdar has been investing in offshore wind for more than a decade, building deep experience across some of the sector’s most significant projects in the UK and Europe. From London Array to Baltic Eagle and Dogger Bank South, we have seen first-hand what can be achieved by combining long-term investment with strong partners and world-class technical expertise. Our partnership with RWE brings together complementary experience and a shared focus on disciplined execution, and we look forward to applying that expertise to new opportunities in Germany.”

RWE and Masdar jointly operate and develop offshore wind projects in the UK with a combined capacity of 3.6 gigawatts. Their long-standing partnership in offshore wind dates back to the London Array offshore wind farm, which has been operational since 2013 and has a capacity of more than 600 megawatts. In September 2022, the companies signed an MoU to explore collaboration on offshore wind projects in key global markets, which subsequently led to Masdar becoming RWE’s partner in the Dogger Bank South offshore wind projects. Dogger Bank South comprises the East and West projects, which together will have an overall capacity of 3 gigawatts, making it one of the UK’s largest offshore wind projects currently under development. Earlier this year, RWE and Masdar secured Contracts for Difference for the projects in the UK Government’s Allocation Round 7, marking an important milestone for their delivery.
